table.note: Clause references are to the editions named under Source. Jurisdictional requirements are set by the state or provincial authority and may adopt different editions; confirm the adopted edition before writing procedures.

facets.q: What changed in ASME B31.1-2022 for NDE personnel?
facets.a: Paragraph 136.3.2(a) replaced the previous, largely non-prescriptive programme with five defined qualification options: Level I, II or III under SNT-TC-1A; certification to ASME Section V Article 1 T-120(e) or (f); AWS QC1 inspector qualification; a programme based on SNT-TC-1A with employer-specified examinations; or an alternative approved by the B31.1 committee.

facets.q: Who may perform visual examination on power piping now?
facets.a: Under the earlier edition, visual examiners for boiler external piping needed only employer-designed written and performance examinations. B31.1-2022 requires SNT-TC-1A style qualification or AWS QC1 inspector status. Written practices that were never updated still authorise people the current edition does not.

facets.q: Which code governs NDE for a boiler repair rather than new construction?
facets.a: ASME Section I governs construction of the power boiler. Repairs and alterations to that boiler in service are governed by the National Board Inspection Code, and the NDE has to be performed under the R certificate holder's quality system. Two different systems own the same weld at different points in its life.

facets.q: Where do HRSG tube failures concentrate?
facets.a: Flow-accelerated corrosion leads, concentrated in low pressure economisers, preheaters and evaporator circuits including tubes, headers and risers. Thermal fatigue follows, concentrated at tube-to-header connections and dissimilar metal welds. Creep appears in high temperature sections. Scoping that ignores this ordering inspects the wrong circuits.

facets.q: Why do 18Mn-5Cr retaining rings need more than one inspection modality?
facets.a: 18Mn-5Cr is susceptible to stress corrosion cracking in the presence of moisture, with rapid initiation and growth once it starts. Cracking presents differently to ultrasonic and eddy current inspection depending on orientation and depth, so a single modality leaves credible crack populations undetected. 18Mn-18Cr replacements are resistant.

facets.q: What invalidates a traveller technician's certification mid-outage?
facets.a: Employer certification under SNT-TC-1A is deemed revoked when employment terminates, unless the individual holds third-party certification. A traveller arriving on a previous employer's card holds a document with no force under your written practice, and the badge issued against it fails the first records sample.

sections.heading: The outage window is the whole constraint
paragraphs: A utility outage is a fixed-duration event with a published return-to-service date, replacement power costs behind it, and a critical path that inspection sits directly on. Spring and autumn shoulder seasons carry most planned outages in the US because load is low and generation can be released. Everything about NDE scope, procedure approval, examiner qualification and records assembly has to be finished before the unit comes down, because the outage supplies no time to fix any of it.

That produces a specific failure signature. Procedures get approved in week one of the outage instead of six weeks before. Examiner qualification routes get checked when the jurisdictional inspector asks rather than at mobilisation. Findings arrive on day nineteen with no repair plan, no certificate holder engaged and no jurisdictional notification, so the repair extends the outage rather than fitting inside it. None of those are technical problems and all of them cost megawatt-hours.

The counter-discipline is a pre-outage records gate that mirrors the work scope: every procedure approved and issued at revision, every examiner matched to a named qualification route, every planned examination mapped to a permanent component identifier, and the repair pathway pre-agreed with the certificate holder and the jurisdiction for the findings most likely to arise. That package is assembled in the eight weeks before the unit comes down or it does not exist.

sections.heading: B31.1-2022 changed who may examine, and most written practices did not follow
paragraphs: The 2022 edition of ASME B31.1 rewrote NDE personnel qualification in paragraph 136.3.2(a), replacing a relatively non-prescriptive employer programme with five defined routes: Level I, II or III certification under SNT-TC-1A; certification to ASME Section V, Article 1, T-120(e) or (f); qualification as an AWS QC1 inspector; a programme based on SNT-TC-1A with employer-specified examinations; or an alternative programme approved by the B31.1 committee. Each is a real route with its own evidence trail.

The sharpest change hits visual examination. Under the 2020 edition, an organisation working boiler external piping could qualify visual examiners through instruction in the fundamentals, employer-judged on-the-job training, an annual visual acuity examination, and employer-designed written and performance examinations. The current edition pushes visual examiners toward SNT-TC-1A style qualification or AWS QC1 inspector status. Organisations that never revised their written practice are still certifying visual examiners under a route the code has moved past.

Fixing it is a written practice revision, not a retraining programme, for most organisations. The examiners often already meet a compliant route; what is missing is the document that says which route, applied to which people, approved by the Level III, and held on file as SNT-TC-1A requires. Getting that revision done before an outage costs a fraction of what it costs to discover the gap when a jurisdictional inspector samples the qualification records mid-outage.

sections.heading: Section I construction, NBIC repair: which quality system owns the record
paragraphs: A power boiler is built to ASME Section I under the manufacturer's quality system. Once it is in service, repair and alteration answer to the National Board Inspection Code, which is adopted into law across most US and Canadian jurisdictions and underpins the R certificate programme used by thousands of repair organisations. The weld does not change. The system that owns the record of examining it does.

That transition catches contractors who work both sides. NDE performed in support of a repair has to be controlled by the certificate holder's quality system, with procedures, personnel qualification and records that the certificate holder can produce during its own accreditation review. Subcontracting the phased array or the radiography does not move that responsibility, and a certificate holder who cannot show control over the subcontracted examination has a quality system finding independent of anything the examination found.

The jurisdictional inspector is the person the paperwork ultimately serves. He signs the National Board form on the strength of the examination records placed in front of him, and he decides what he needs to see. Contractors who present a complete, indexed NDE package structured around the repair rather than around their own report numbering get through that review quickly. Contractors who present a stack of individual reports get a long afternoon.

sections.heading: HRSG scoping starts from the mechanism, not last outage's list
paragraphs: Heat recovery steam generator tube failures are the leading source of unavailability in combined cycle plants, and the failure distribution is well characterised. Flow-accelerated corrosion leads, concentrating in low pressure economisers and preheaters and in low pressure evaporator circuits including tubes, headers and risers. Thermal fatigue follows, concentrating at tube-to-header connections and at dissimilar metal welds. Creep appears in high temperature sections operating outside the design envelope over long periods.

Cycling changes that distribution. Units built for baseload and now run as flexible plant see far more thermal transients than their design assumed, which drives creep-fatigue interaction at the same header and dissimilar-metal locations, particularly in circuits running above roughly 565 degrees C where T22 and T91 materials meet. A scope built from the previous outage's findings inspects where damage was already found. A scope built from mechanism plus operating history inspects where damage is being created now.

Turning that into an auditable plan means writing the reasoning down: which circuits are FAC-susceptible on chemistry and geometry, which header connections have accumulated the transient count that drives thermal fatigue, which sections have logged the temperature excursions that drive creep, and which technique addresses each. That document is what justifies scope to the asset owner when the outage budget is challenged, and it is what makes the next campaign comparable to this one.

sections.heading: Dissimilar metal welds and the demonstration record
paragraphs: Dissimilar metal welds are the hardest routine examination in a boiler or HRSG and the easiest to record badly. The joint pairs materials with different acoustic properties and different grain structures, the fusion line scatters and refracts sound, and a procedure that performs well on plain carbon steel can return clean results on a joint that is cracking. The technique has to be demonstrated on the material pair it will be applied to.

ASME Section V, Article 4 governs ultrasonic examination of welds, and the practical requirement that follows from it is a demonstration specimen representative of the actual joint: the same material pair, the same geometry and thickness range, and reflectors placed where the mechanism actually produces them, which for these joints is at or near the fusion line rather than mid-wall. A demonstration on a flat plate with side-drilled holes proves the instrument works, not that the technique detects the damage.

The record that matters at audit is short: the specimen description, the reflector positions, the technique parameters as run, the detection results, and the Level III approval tying the demonstration to the issued procedure. Contractors who hold that record can defend a clean result on a joint that later fails. Contractors who do not have a clean result and no way to show that the result meant anything.

sections.heading: Turbine and generator: what gets written down
paragraphs: Generator retaining rings sit under the highest stress in the rotor and carry a material history that determines the inspection. 18Mn-5Cr rings are susceptible to stress corrosion cracking in the presence of moisture, with rapid crack initiation and growth once conditions allow it, and that susceptibility drove a series of failures that changed industry practice. 18Mn-18Cr material replaced it and is resistant to the same mechanism. The inspection scope depends entirely on which one is fitted.

The technical consequence is that a single modality is not sufficient on susceptible material. Visual, penetrant, eddy current and ultrasonic each detect a different part of the credible crack population depending on orientation, depth and surface condition, and multimodal inspection is what industry practice on 18Mn-5Cr rings converged on. The record has to state the material, the modalities applied, the coverage achieved and what was excluded, because an incomplete coverage statement is what makes the next engineer repeat the whole job.

Rotor and blade root examinations follow the same records discipline. Positions must be located against a permanent datum on the machine rather than a temporary mark, results must be recorded so the next outage can compare the same indication rather than rediscovering it, and any indication carried forward must have an evaluation attached. Utilities that enforce this see indications tracked across a decade. Utilities that do not re-inspect from scratch every outage and learn nothing.

sections.heading: Badging travellers without importing a records defect
paragraphs: A large outage badges technicians from several employers on short notice, and each one arrives with a certification history the site did not create. SNT-TC-1A treats employer certification as revoked on termination of employment where the individual holds no third-party certification. A traveller presenting a card from a previous employer is presenting a document with no force under the certifying organisation's written practice, whatever the individual's actual competence.

Vision currency is the second traveller trap, and it is a calendar problem rather than a competence problem. An annual near-vision examination that expires in week three of a five-week outage means every examination that technician performs after the expiry date is challengeable. Checking vision dates against the outage end date rather than its start date takes minutes at mobilisation and removes an entire class of finding.

The third is qualification route. With five routes now available under B31.1, a badged examiner must be matched to one specific route with the evidence behind it, and crews assembled from three employers will present three different routes. The mobilisation record should list each name, the route claimed, the evidence sighted and the date checked. When the jurisdictional inspector samples the roster, that list is the answer, and producing it immediately ends the conversation.

sections.heading: Outage radiography and the night shift record
paragraphs: Radiography in a congested outage runs at night for access and exclusion reasons, which is exactly when records discipline degrades. 10 CFR 34.43 requires radiographers to be trained in specified topics, to complete a minimum period of on-the-job training, and to be verified as capable of working independently, with understanding demonstrated by written or oral examination. Those requirements do not soften at 02:00.

10 CFR 34.79 fixes the retention: training records kept three years after the record is made, certification documents and verification of certification status, copies of written tests, dates and names for oral and practical examinations, annual refresher safety training with topics and instructors, and semi-annual inspections of job performance for each radiographer and assistant. Utilities with a radiation safety officer audit that list directly, separately from the inspection group.

The defect that repeats is attribution. Exposures get logged under the name on the permit rather than the person who fired them, because the permit was raised on day shift and the work happened on night shift. That single habit invalidates the utilisation log, the survey record and the job performance inspections at once. Fixing it requires a shift handover that reassigns the permit, which is a procedure change rather than a technical one.

sections.heading: Outsourced Level III cover across an outage cycle
paragraphs: A retained Level III for a utility or an outage contractor works to the outage calendar rather than the accounting calendar. The heavy work sits in the eight weeks before the unit comes down: procedure authorship and approval at the adopted code editions, examiner qualification routes matched and documented under the revised written practice, demonstration specimens arranged for the difficult joints, and the records pack structure agreed with outage QA. Our outsourced Level III scope and retainer page describes how that engagement runs.

During the outage the role is availability and technical judgement: approving a technique change when access differs from the plan, evaluating an indication that outage QA cannot resolve, and standing behind the qualification records when the jurisdictional inspector samples them. After the outage it is the records close-out, so the package that supports the National Board forms and the next campaign's comparison is complete before the crew disperses.

Where the boundary sits matters as much here as in process plant work. Interval setting, run-or-repair decisions and fitness-for-service acceptance belong to the asset owner and the authorized inspector, and our page on what an outside Level III can and cannot do sets that out. Examination authorship and retention, which is the record most often requested years later, is covered on the exam oversight page. Nuclear Class 1, 2 and 3 work runs under a separate qualification and performance demonstration regime and is scoped separately.

faq.q: Can you write and approve our outage NDE procedures before the unit comes down?
faq.a: That is the intended sequence. Procedures written to the code edition your jurisdiction has adopted, demonstration specimens arranged for dissimilar metal and difficult-access joints, and examiner qualification routes documented under a revised written practice, all completed in the weeks before the outage rather than during it.

faq.q: Our R certificate holder subcontracts NDE. Whose quality system controls it?
faq.a: The certificate holder's. Subcontracting the examination does not move responsibility for controlling it, and a certificate holder who cannot demonstrate that control has a quality system finding regardless of the examination result. The subcontractor's procedures and personnel records have to be inside the certificate holder's system.

faq.q: We updated technician certificates but not the written practice. Is that enough for B31.1-2022?
faq.a: No. The written practice is the document that states which qualification route the organisation uses, applied to which personnel, approved by the Level III and held on file. Certificates issued under a route the practice does not describe fail the first records sample, even when the individuals are properly qualified.

faq.q: How do we justify HRSG inspection scope when the outage budget gets cut?
faq.a: With a written mechanism basis: which circuits are susceptible to flow-accelerated corrosion, which header connections and dissimilar metal welds have accumulated the transients that drive thermal fatigue, and which sections have logged the temperatures that drive creep. A scope tied to mechanisms survives budget review. A scope tied to last outage's list does not.

faq.q: Do you cover nuclear plant inspection?
faq.a: Nuclear Class 1, 2 and 3 work qualifies personnel and demonstrates ultrasonic procedures under a separate regime within the ASME code, with performance demonstration requirements that do not apply to conventional generation. Our utility work is scoped to fossil, combined cycle, HRSG, balance of plant and transmission-connected assets.

faq.q: Can one records pack serve both outage QA and the jurisdictional inspector?
faq.a: Yes, when it is indexed by component and repair rather than by report number. Outage QA reads it by scope area, the jurisdictional inspector reads it by the form he is signing, and both find what they need from the same index. A pile of individually numbered reports serves neither.

title: UT Level 1 Training: 40 Hours, 210-Hour Experience Path
description: UT Level I under SNT-TC-1A: 40 training hours, 210 hours of method experience, three exams, and annual vision checks. What the role may do and how to qualify.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing Level I Training Requirements
answer: UT Level I under SNT-TC-1A requires 40 hours of formal training and 210 hours of documented experience in ultrasonic testing, within roughly 400 total NDT hours. Your employer then certifies you through a general, specific, and practical exam plus an annual near-vision check. The hours are ASNT recommendations — your employer's written practice sets the binding numbers.
expansion: The 40/210 figures come from Table 6.3.1A of ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A, the document nearly every US industrial employer builds its written practice around. UT carries the heaviest recommended hour load of the common surface and volumetric methods — five times the classroom time of PT and more than three times MT — because pulse-echo ultrasonics demands working math: sound velocity, Snell's law refraction angles, and decibel drop calculations appear on the Level I exam. A UT Level I performs calibrations and records data under written instructions but does not interpret or evaluate results; that authority arrives at Level II. Candidates with two years of engineering or science study can qualify with reduced classroom hours under the same table. Full method-by-method hour comparisons are in our guide at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method, and the broader ultrasonic program is covered at /ultrasonic-testing-training.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2020), Table 6.3.1A — Recommended Initial Training and Experience Levels

facets.q: How long does it take to become UT Level I?
facets.a: Most candidates complete the 40-hour course in one intensive week, then accumulate the 210 supervised experience hours over roughly six to twelve weeks of full-time trainee work. From first class to certification, three to four months is typical for a full-time hire.

facets.q: Can I skip Level I and certify directly to UT Level II?
facets.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A allows direct Level II certification if you complete the sum of both levels' hours — 80 training hours and 840 UT experience hours — before the Level II exams. Many employers run new hires this way as documented trainees.

facets.q: Is online UT Level I training accepted?
facets.a: Online or hybrid delivery of the 40 classroom hours is widely accepted when the employer's Level III approves the course outline against the ASNT body of knowledge. The practical exam and supervised experience hours cannot be done remotely — hands-on instrument time is mandatory.

facets.q: Do I need a college degree for UT Level I?
facets.a: No. A high school diploma or equivalent satisfies SNT-TC-1A for the standard 40-hour path. Two years of university engineering or science study lets an employer reduce the training-hour recommendation, which mainly benefits career changers from technical fields.

facets.q: Is UT Level I certification portable between employers?
facets.a: No. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies you, so certification ends when employment ends. Your training certificates and experience logs transfer; a new employer re-examines and re-certifies you under its own written practice, usually quickly if your records are complete.

facets.q: What can a UT Level I not do?
facets.a: A Level I cannot interpret or evaluate indications, accept or reject parts, select techniques, or sign inspection reports. They perform calibrations and record readings strictly per written instructions under Level II or III oversight — the evaluation authority employers pay for starts at Level II.

sections.heading: The numbers US employers start from
paragraphs: Every US industrial UT program traces back to one table: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 40 hours of formal training and 210 hours of ultrasonic testing experience for Level I, inside a total of roughly 400 NDT hours. Those figures are recommendations, not regulations — SNT-TC-1A is explicitly a guideline, and each employer writes a 'written practice' that fixes the binding numbers for its own program. In practice, most employers adopt the table nearly verbatim because their customers' codes and auditors expect it. When a job posting says 'certified to SNT-TC-1A,' this 40/210 structure is what sits behind it.

sections.heading: What a UT Level I technician may do — and may not
paragraphs: A UT Level I performs specific calibrations, specific tests, and specific data recording, all according to written instructions and under the supervision of a Level II or Level III. In a working crew that means setting up the instrument to an approved calibration block, taking thickness readings or scanning per the technique sheet, and logging results. What a Level I may not do defines the role's ceiling: no interpreting indications, no evaluating against acceptance criteria, no accepting or rejecting material, and no signing reports. Employers structure Level I roles around high-volume, well-proceduralized work — corrosion thickness surveys are the classic example — where the evaluation decisions sit with a Level II reviewing the data.

sections.heading: Why UT training runs 40 hours when PT runs 4
paragraphs: Ultrasonics carries the heaviest Level I classroom load of the common methods because the physics does real work in the field. The 40 hours cover sound wave modes and velocities, acoustic impedance, Snell's law and refraction at interfaces, transducer construction and frequency selection, pulse-echo and through-transmission techniques, and instrument controls — gain, range, delay, reject. Calibration is a course within the course: IIW blocks, step wedges, and distance calibration consume significant bench time. Expect working math throughout — velocity-distance calculations, refracted angle problems, and decibel arithmetic all appear on Level I exams. Candidates who struggle with trigonometry should address it before the course, not during it. Compare hour loads across all methods at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

sections.heading: How the 210 experience hours actually accumulate
paragraphs: The 210 hours must be documented time performing ultrasonic work as a trainee — instrument setup, calibration, scanning, and data recording under supervision — not simply weeks on a payroll. Employers track it with signed experience logs that the certifying Level III reviews before scheduling exams. A full-time trainee doing daily UT work can log 210 hours in six to eight weeks; a technician splitting time across methods takes proportionally longer, which is why multi-method trainees often certify in staggered order. Keep your own copies of every log sheet. Under SNT-TC-1A your certification dies with your employment, but documented hours are yours forever and dramatically shorten re-certification with the next employer.

sections.heading: The three exams and who certifies you
paragraphs: Certification requires three examinations: a closed-book general exam on UT fundamentals, a specific exam on the employer's procedures and applicable codes, and a hands-on practical where you calibrate and test samples with known reflectors. SNT-TC-1A recommends a minimum composite grade of 80 percent. The employer's NDT Level III — in-house or a contracted outside agency — administers and grades the exams, and the employer issues the certification. This employer-based model is the crucial difference from central certification: ASNT's own exam-based credentials exist as a separate, fee-based route through asnt.org, but the overwhelming majority of US industrial UT Level I certifications are employer-issued under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis provides outsourced Level III examination services for companies without one on staff.

sections.heading: Vision requirements
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A calls for a near-vision acuity examination — Jaeger No. 2 or equivalent, read at not less than 12 inches with at least one eye, corrected or uncorrected — administered annually. A color-contrast differentiation exam is required at certification and repeated at intervals not exceeding five years. For UT the color requirement matters less than in PT or MT, but employers apply it uniformly because technicians typically cross-train into surface methods. Glasses and contacts are fully acceptable; document the correction. A failed vision exam suspends certification until corrected vision passes, so schedule the annual check before it lapses rather than after an auditor notices.

sections.heading: Where UT Level I gets hired in the US
paragraphs: The volume market for UT Level I labor is corrosion monitoring in oil and gas: thickness surveys on piping circuits, pressure vessels, and storage tanks feeding API 510, 570, and 653 inspection programs. Refineries and petrochemical plants along the Gulf Coast staff turnaround seasons with Level I techs taking thousands of thickness readings under Level II direction. Structural steel fabrication shops, shipyards, and power plants form the second tier. Employers in these industries ask for the same three things: SNT-TC-1A-compliant training certificates, documented experience hours, and a current vision exam — plus a TWIC card or site safety credentials for plant access. The role is deliberately procedural; it exists to feed data to Level II evaluators.

sections.heading: Pay at Level I — and why Level II is the real target
paragraphs: US Bureau of Labor Statistics data put the median for nondestructive testing specialists at $78,350 (May 2025), but that figure blends all levels and methods. Entry UT Level I positions sit well below it, while ZipRecruiter's NDT Level 2 data shows a $48,000–$90,000 range — the certification jump is the single largest pay lever in a UT career. Level I is best treated as a paid on-ramp: the 210 hours you log immediately count toward the 840 cumulative hours Level II requires. Full US, per-method, and per-industry bands are broken out in /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

sections.heading: Starting your UT Level I path with Atlantis
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT delivers 40-hour UT Level I courses aligned to the ASNT body of knowledge, with certificates and course outlines formatted for your employer's Level III review. For companies, our ASNT Level III consultants build written practices, administer qualification exams, and run the annual vision program — the full certification infrastructure without a staff Level III. Training is affordable, accessible, and fully customizable to your procedures and codes. See the complete ultrasonic curriculum at /ultrasonic-testing-training, the cross-method Level I picture at /ndt-level-1-training, and when you're ready, request a quote — we scope programs for individual candidates and full crews alike.

faq.q: Are the 40 training hours legally mandatory?
faq.a: No single US law mandates them. SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, and the employer's written practice is the binding document. But customer contracts, ASME and AWS code work, and audits effectively enforce the recommended hours, so almost all reputable employers require them.

faq.q: What score do I need to pass the UT Level I exams?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends a minimum composite grade of 80 percent across the general, specific, and practical exams. Many written practices additionally require no individual exam below 70 percent. Your employer's written practice states the exact passing rules that apply to you.

faq.q: How often is UT Level I recertification required?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends recertification at intervals not exceeding five years, by examination or by documented continuing satisfactory performance as the written practice allows. Interrupted service — leaving the method for roughly a year or more — typically triggers re-examination regardless of the interval.

faq.q: Can college coursework reduce the required training hours?
faq.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A's training table allows reduced UT classroom hours for candidates with two years of engineering or science study at a university or technical school. The employer's Level III decides whether to apply the reduction; experience hours are not reduced.

faq.q: Is thickness gauging a separate, shorter certification?
faq.a: Many employers issue a 'limited' Level I or Level II certification restricted to digital thickness gauging, with reduced training and experience hours defined in their written practice. It is faster to obtain but does not transfer to full pulse-echo flaw detection work.

title: UT Level 2 Training: Hours, Exams, and Evaluation Authority
description: UT Level II requirements: 80 cumulative training hours, 840 hours of experience, calibration and code evaluation authority, exam content, and current US pay data.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing Level II Training Requirements
answer: UT Level II under SNT-TC-1A requires 40 hours of training beyond Level I — 80 cumulative — and 630 additional hours of UT experience, 840 cumulative. Level II is where evaluation authority begins: setting up calibrations, interpreting indications against ASME, AWS, or API acceptance criteria, and signing inspection reports. Employers certify through general, specific, and practical exams at an 80 percent composite.
expansion: UT Level II is the highest-demand method-level combination in US industrial NDT because it is the minimum certification that can independently evaluate welds and sign reports — the deliverable clients actually pay for. The 40/630 increments come from SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A and stack on Level I's 40/210; candidates may also certify directly to Level II by completing the summed 80 training and 840 experience hours as a documented trainee. The Level II exam is a different animal from Level I: angle-beam weld inspection dominates, with trigonometry for skip distance and sound path, dB-drop sizing, and DAC or TCG construction all fair game — work through /blog/ut-level-2-practice-questions to gauge readiness. Method fundamentals live at /ultrasonic-testing-training, the cross-method Level II picture at /ndt-level-2-training, and hour comparisons at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2020), Table 6.3.1A — Recommended Initial Training and Experience Levels

facets.q: How long does it take to go from UT Level I to Level II?
facets.a: The 630 additional experience hours take roughly four to six months of full-time UT work, plus a 40-hour Level II course and exams. Most working Level I techs reach Level II inside a year; splitting time across methods stretches it.

facets.q: Does UT Level II include phased array or TOFD?
facets.a: No. Phased array (PAUT) and TOFD are separate techniques requiring their own training, experience, and examinations under most written practices — typically built on top of a conventional UT Level II. Employers advertise them as distinct certifications with distinct pay premiums.

facets.q: Can a UT Level II write inspection procedures?
facets.a: No. Procedure preparation and approval are Level III functions under SNT-TC-1A. A Level II works within approved procedures, selecting techniques and calibrations inside the limits the procedure allows, and may draft instructions for Level I use subject to Level III approval.

facets.q: Where can I practice for the UT Level II exam?
facets.a: Work through /blog/ut-level-2-practice-questions — it mirrors the general exam's weighting: wave physics, refracted-angle trigonometry, dB arithmetic, DAC construction, and code acceptance logic. Pair it with hands-on time on flawed weld samples before attempting the practical.

facets.q: Is UT Level II different for aerospace employers?
facets.a: Aerospace primes require NAS 410, which mandates the same 40+40 formal training structure for UT but roughly 1,200 experience hours for direct Level 2 — more than SNT-TC-1A's 840 — plus annual vision exams and stricter exam minimums. The classroom content overlaps heavily.

facets.q: What codes should a UT Level II know for US work?
facets.a: ASME Section V Article 4/5 with Section VIII or B31.3 acceptance criteria for pressure equipment, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and API 620/650/653 contexts for tanks. Job postings usually name the governing code — study the specific exam accordingly.

sections.heading: The requirement stack: 80 hours of training, 840 of experience
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A's table adds 40 formal training hours and 630 UT experience hours on top of Level I's 40 and 210 — 80 and 840 cumulative. There are two routes to the same certification. The ladder route certifies Level I first and upgrades later; the direct route takes a candidate straight to Level II exams once the summed hours are complete, working the entire time as a documented trainee. US service companies increasingly favor the direct route for promising hires because it produces a report-signing technician in nine to twelve months. Either way, every hour must appear in signed experience logs the certifying Level III can defend in an audit.

sections.heading: What Level II authority actually adds
paragraphs: The jump from Level I to Level II is not more of the same work — it is a different job. A Level II sets up and verifies calibrations rather than following them, selects transducer angles and frequencies within procedure limits, interprets screen signals as geometry or flaws, evaluates indications against code acceptance criteria, and signs the inspection report. That signature is the billable product of an NDT service company, which is why UT Level II is the highest-demand method-level combination in US industrial inspection. Level II also supervises: directing trainees and Level I technicians on data collection is an explicit SNT-TC-1A responsibility, and in practice the Level II runs the crew truck.

sections.heading: What the Level II exam actually tests
paragraphs: The Level II general exam shifts from fundamentals to application. Expect angle-beam weld inspection to dominate: calculating skip distance and sound path from refracted angle and thickness, locating a reflector from screen position, and sizing by dB-drop methods. DAC and TCG curve construction, transfer correction, and couplant and surface-condition effects all appear. The specific exam tests your employer's procedures and the governing code's acceptance tables. The practical puts flawed weld samples in front of you — detect, locate, size, evaluate, and document. Candidates fail the practical more often than the written exams, almost always on documentation gaps rather than detection. Calibrate your readiness against /blog/ut-level-2-practice-questions before scheduling anything.

sections.heading: The codes US employers test against
paragraphs: A UT Level II certification is only useful attached to code fluency, and US postings are explicit about which one. Pressure equipment work runs on ASME Section V Articles 4 and 5 with acceptance criteria from Section VIII or B31.3. Structural steel runs on AWS D1.1's UT provisions, with their distinctive attenuation-based rating system. Tank and piping integrity programs pull in API 650, 653, and 570 contexts. Pipeline girth welds reference API 1104. The specific exam exists precisely to verify this fluency, so a Level II changing industries should expect a new specific exam even with an unbroken certification history — and smart candidates ask which code governs before accepting an assignment.

sections.heading: Making the 630 experience hours count
paragraphs: Auditors and Level IIIs distinguish between 630 hours of thickness readings and 630 hours that include weld scanning, angle-beam setups, and assisted evaluations. SNT-TC-1A requires experience in activities appropriate to the level sought, so a trainee aiming at Level II should be rotated deliberately: calibration setups one month, angle-beam scanning under a Level II the next, then supervised evaluation practice. Techs stuck exclusively on corrosion surveys sometimes arrive at 840 logged hours and still fail the practical because they have never sized a real flaw. If that is your situation, ask for weld work rotations early — or use structured practical training to close the gap before exams.

sections.heading: Vision, recertification, and keeping the cert alive
paragraphs: Level II carries the same vision regime as Level I: annual near-vision at Jaeger No. 2 or equivalent from not less than 12 inches, with color-contrast differentiation checked at certification and at intervals not exceeding five years. Recertification comes due at a maximum five-year interval, by re-examination or documented continuing performance per the written practice. Interrupted service is the trap for working techs — leave UT work for an extended period and the written practice will typically demand re-examination. Because employer-based certification dies with employment, maintain personal copies of training certificates, experience logs, exam records, and vision results; a complete personal file turns a job change into days of re-certification instead of months.

sections.heading: What UT Level II pays in the US
paragraphs: PayScale reports certified UT Level II holders averaging roughly $70,000–$77,000 depending on employer, against a BLS median of $78,350 for all nondestructive testing specialists (May 2025). ZipRecruiter's NDT Level 2 band runs $48,000 at the 25th percentile to $90,000 for top earners, with turnaround and travel work at the high end thanks to per-diem and overtime stacking. Advanced technique endorsements move the number hardest: PAUT and TOFD-certified Level IIs command clear premiums in pipeline and pressure-vessel markets. Regional, industry, and global comparisons — including why US rates lead most markets — are maintained in /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

sections.heading: After Level II: the paths that branch from here
paragraphs: UT Level II is a platform, not a terminus. The technique path adds phased array and TOFD certifications — each with its own training and exam stack — and leads toward advanced weld-integrity work. The code path adds API 510, 570, or 653 inspector credentials, converting a technician into an inspection planner. The certification path accumulates the hours toward ASNT Level III, where you write procedures and run programs; UT experience counts directly toward Level III eligibility. Most Level IIs also cross-train a second method — MT or PT at modest additional hours — because multi-method techs win crew assignments. The full lateral picture across methods is at /ndt-level-2-training.

sections.heading: How Atlantis trains and certifies UT Level II
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT runs 40-hour UT Level II courses built around angle-beam weld evaluation, with practical time on flawed samples matched to ASME, AWS, and API acceptance criteria. For employers, our ASNT Level III consultants administer the full qualification cycle — written practice development, general/specific/practical examinations, and certification records that survive audits. Programs are affordable, accessible, and fully customizable to your procedures. Start from the method curriculum at /ultrasonic-testing-training, benchmark yourself with /blog/ut-level-2-practice-questions, and request a quote for individual seats or crew-scale programs — we scope both.

faq.q: Can I certify directly to UT Level II without ever holding Level I?
faq.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A explicitly allows direct Level II qualification when training and experience equal the sum of both levels — 80 hours of training and 840 hours of UT experience — completed as a documented trainee before examination. Many US service companies use this route.

faq.q: How much of the Level II exam is math?
faq.a: A substantial share. Refracted-angle trigonometry, skip distance and sound-path calculations, dB-drop sizing arithmetic, and DAC construction are core general-exam material. The math is applied and repetitive rather than advanced — candidates who drill it systematically rarely fail on it.

faq.q: Does UT Level II transfer if I change employers?
faq.a: The certification itself does not — it is employer-issued. Your documented training, experience hours, and exam history do transfer, and a new employer's Level III can typically re-examine and certify you within days if your personal records are complete.

faq.q: Is phased array Level II a replacement for conventional UT Level II?
faq.a: No — it is an addition. PAUT certification presumes conventional UT competence, and most written practices require conventional UT Level II first. Employers pay a premium for the stack, not for PAUT alone.

faq.q: What is the difference between SNT-TC-1A and ASNT central certification for Level II?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A certification is issued by your employer after employer-administered exams. ASNT's central programs examine and certify through ASNT directly, for published exam fees, and travel with you between employers. US industrial work overwhelmingly runs on the employer-based model; central certification is a portable supplement.

title: RT Level 1 Training: 40 Hours Plus the Radiation Safety Track
description: RT Level I needs 40 training hours and 210 experience hours under SNT-TC-1A — plus a separate radiation-safety qualification under 10 CFR Part 34 to work sources.
h1: Radiographic Testing Level I Training Requirements
answer: RT Level I requires 40 hours of formal training and 210 hours of radiographic experience under SNT-TC-1A, certified by your employer through written and practical exams. But method certification alone does not let you handle radiation sources: US industrial radiography also requires a separate radiation-safety qualification under 10 CFR Part 34, typically an IRRSP card plus licensee exams. You need both tracks.
expansion: Radiography is the only mainstream NDT method with two independent qualification tracks, and conflating them is the most common mistake entry candidates make. The SNT-TC-1A track — 40 training hours, 210 method hours, general/specific/practical exams — qualifies you in the testing method: exposure technique, film handling, image quality. The regulatory track under NRC 10 CFR Part 34 (mirrored by Agreement State rules) governs who may operate gamma and X-ray sources: certification through a recognized certifying entity such as ASNT's IRRSP program, licensee-administered radiation safety exams, mandated dosimetry, and the two-person rule at temporary job sites. A new RT Level I typically works as a radiographer's assistant under direct supervision while completing both tracks. Method fundamentals are covered at /radiographic-testing-training, the cross-method entry picture at /ndt-level-1-training, and hour comparisons at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020), Table 6.3.1A; US NRC 10 CFR Part 34 — Licenses for Industrial Radiography and Radiation Safety Requirements

facets.q: Does RT Level I certification let me operate a gamma camera?
facets.a: No. Method certification under SNT-TC-1A does not confer source-handling authority. Operating exposure devices requires the separate radiation-safety qualification under 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State equivalents — until then you assist under a qualified radiographer's direct supervision.

facets.q: What is an IRRSP card?
facets.a: The Industrial Radiography Radiation Safety Personnel credential, administered by ASNT as an NRC-recognized certifying entity. Passing its radiation-safety exam — gamma, X-ray, or both — satisfies the certifying-entity requirement of 10 CFR 34.43, alongside your licensee's own training and exams.

facets.q: How long does RT Level I take from a standing start?
facets.a: The 40-hour course takes a week; the 210 method hours take roughly two to three months of full-time work. The radiation-safety track runs in parallel — most new hires work as radiographer's assistants and complete both tracks inside four to six months.

facets.q: Can RT Level I read radiographs?
facets.a: No. A Level I exposes film and processes it per written instruction but has no interpretation authority. Film and digital image evaluation against code acceptance criteria is the defining Level II function — see /rt-level-2-training for that requirement stack.

facets.q: Is the radiation-safety training the same in every state?
facets.a: The framework is uniform — NRC rules or Agreement State programs that must be compatible with them — but licensing details, reciprocity filings, and card formats vary by state. Your employer's radiation safety officer manages state-specific requirements; your IRRSP exam is recognized nationally.

facets.q: What dose limits apply to industrial radiographers?
facets.a: The federal occupational limit is 5 rem (50 mSv) total effective dose equivalent per year under 10 CFR Part 20, with licensees required to keep exposures as low as reasonably achievable. Your three monitoring devices exist to prove compliance continuously.

sections.heading: Two tracks, both mandatory — the structure nobody explains first
paragraphs: US industrial radiography splits qualification into two independent tracks, and every entry-level plan should be built around that fact. The method track follows SNT-TC-1A: 40 hours of formal training, 210 hours of documented RT experience, and employer-administered exams covering radiographic technique. The regulatory track follows 10 CFR Part 34, the NRC's industrial radiography rule (mirrored in Agreement States): radiation-safety certification through a recognized certifying entity such as ASNT's IRRSP program, plus your employer-licensee's own written exam, practical exam, and documented on-the-job training. The method track makes you competent; the regulatory track makes you legal. Job-ready means both, and they can — and should — run in parallel.

sections.heading: The SNT-TC-1A numbers for RT Level I
paragraphs: Table 6.3.1A recommends 40 hours of formal training and 210 hours of method experience for RT Level I, inside roughly 400 total NDT hours — the same hour class as UT and ET, and for the same reason: radiography is technically dense. As with all SNT-TC-1A programs, your employer's written practice fixes the binding figures and its Level III administers general, specific, and practical exams at a recommended 80 percent composite. Candidates with two years of engineering or science study may qualify for reduced classroom hours. Direct-to-Level II certification is permitted by summing both levels' hours — 80 training, 840 experience — as documented at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

sections.heading: What a RT Level I may do on a crew
paragraphs: Within the method, a Level I performs specific setups, exposures, and film processing per written instruction under Level II or III supervision — no interpretation, no acceptance decisions, no report signing. Layer the radiation rules on top and the practical entry role becomes radiographer's assistant: working physically alongside a qualified radiographer, setting up shots, handling film, placing image quality indicators, and running darkroom or CR processing, while every source operation happens under direct personal supervision as 10 CFR Part 34 requires. Crews at temporary job sites must include at least two qualified individuals under 10 CFR 34.41, which is precisely why the assistant role exists as the industry's paid apprenticeship.

sections.heading: Inside the 40 hours: what RT training covers
paragraphs: The Level I curriculum divides into radiation physics and imaging technique. Physics covers X-ray and gamma production, isotope characteristics — Ir-192 and Se-75 dominate field work — the inverse square law, half-value layers, and attenuation. Technique covers exposure calculations, source-to-film distance and geometric unsharpness, film speed and screen selection, density fundamentals, and image quality indicators (penetrameters). Darkroom chemistry and film artifacts still get real hours because film remains standard in US pipeline and pressure-vessel work, with computed and digital radiography folded in as employers modernize. Expect exposure-calculation math throughout — inverse square and decay problems are Level I exam staples.

sections.heading: The radiation-safety track in detail
paragraphs: Under 10 CFR 34.43, before independently operating exposure devices a radiographer must be certified in radiation safety by a certifying entity — ASNT's IRRSP exam is the standard route, offered for gamma, X-ray, or combined — and must pass the licensee's own written and practical examinations, backed by documented hands-on training. Working radiographers carry three monitoring devices simultaneously per 10 CFR 34.47: a direct-reading pocket dosimeter, an alarming ratemeter, and a processed dosimeter (film badge, OSL, or TLD). Annual refresher training, internal audits, and the 5 rem/year occupational dose limit under Part 20 frame ongoing compliance. None of this appears in your SNT-TC-1A method exams — it is a parallel system with its own records.

sections.heading: Exams and vision requirements
paragraphs: The method track requires SNT-TC-1A's three exams — closed-book general on RT fundamentals, specific on employer procedures and code exposure requirements, and a practical demonstrating setup, exposure, and processing on real samples. The regulatory track adds the certifying-entity exam plus licensee exams focused entirely on safety: emergency procedures, survey techniques, posting and barricading. Vision follows the standard SNT-TC-1A regime — annual near-vision at Jaeger No. 2 or equivalent from not less than 12 inches, and color-contrast differentiation at certification and at intervals not exceeding five years. Good near vision matters operationally even at Level I: reading dosimeters, densitometers, and IQI placement is daily work.

sections.heading: Where RT Level I jobs are and what employers screen for
paragraphs: Pipeline construction is the volume employer — girth-weld radiography to API 1104 across every US pipeline spread — followed by pressure vessel and piping fabrication to ASME Section V, structural work, and castings. Postings for entry radiography roles read differently from other methods: employers screen for the radiation-safety track first, asking for an IRRSP card or eligibility, clean dosimetry history, driver's license for source-transport vehicles, and willingness to travel. Method certification progress matters second. Candidates who arrive with the 40-hour RT course and a scheduled IRRSP exam move to the front of the line, because the employer can put them to productive assistant work immediately.

sections.heading: Pay at RT Level I and the trajectory upward
paragraphs: Radiography assistants start modestly, but the trajectory is steep because the two-track barrier constrains supply: BLS puts the all-levels median for nondestructive testing specialists at $78,350 (May 2025), and pipeline radiographers with full qualifications routinely out-earn peers in other methods once per-diem and overtime stack on travel work. ZipRecruiter's NDT Level 2 band of $48,000–$90,000 brackets what the next certification step unlocks. The economics favor finishing both tracks quickly — every month as a half-qualified assistant is a month at the bottom of the scale. Full method and industry pay bands are maintained at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

For employers, our ASNT Level III consultants develop written practices that correctly separate the method and regulatory tracks, administer qualification exams, and structure assistant-to-radiographer progressions that survive both NDT audits and radiation-safety inspections. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable. faq.q: Do I need the IRRSP card before starting RT work?
faq.a: No — you can begin as a radiographer's assistant under direct supervision while preparing for it. You need certifying-entity certification plus licensee exams before operating exposure devices independently. Most employers sequence the IRRSP exam within your first months.

faq.q: Does the 40-hour RT course cover radiation safety?
faq.a: It covers radiation physics and safe practice as method knowledge, but it does not satisfy 10 CFR Part 34. The regulatory track — certifying-entity exam, licensee training and exams, dosimetry — is separate and additional. Budget time for both.

faq.q: Is RT Level I harder to obtain than UT or ET Level I?
faq.a: The SNT-TC-1A hours are identical — 40 training, 210 experience. Radiography is harder to enter overall because of the parallel regulatory track and licensing infrastructure, which is also why qualified radiographers are consistently scarce and well paid.

faq.q: What is the two-person rule?
faq.a: 10 CFR 34.41 requires at least two qualified individuals present during radiographic operations at temporary job sites — typically a certified radiographer plus a radiographer or qualified assistant. It shapes crew structure and guarantees the apprenticeship pathway.

faq.q: Can I count military or prior radiography experience toward the 210 hours?
faq.a: Yes, if documented. SNT-TC-1A lets the employer's Level III credit verifiable prior training and experience. Military NDT records, previous employer logs, and school certificates all count toward hours when the documentation is complete.

title: RT Level 2 Training: Film Interpretation Authority and Hours
description: RT Level II requirements: 80 cumulative training hours, 840 experience hours, film and digital interpretation authority, plus the separate radiation-safety track.
h1: Radiographic Testing Level II Training Requirements
answer: RT Level II requires 40 training hours beyond Level I — 80 cumulative — and 630 additional hours of RT experience, 840 cumulative, under SNT-TC-1A. Level II holds film interpretation authority: judging density, IQI sensitivity, and discontinuities against code acceptance criteria, and signing the report. Radiation-source operation still requires the separate 10 CFR Part 34 safety qualification — method certification never covers it.
expansion: Film interpretation authority is what the RT Level II certification exists to confer, and it is the scarcest skill in US radiography. The Level II reads each radiograph twice: first for image quality — density in the acceptable range, correct IQI and visible sensitivity, no masking artifacts — and only then for the weld, grading porosity, slag, incomplete penetration, and cracks against ASME Section V referencing codes or API 1104. The 40/630 hour increments stack on Level I's 40/210 per SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A, with direct Level II permitted at the summed 80/840. The radiation-safety track under 10 CFR Part 34 remains untouched by any of this: a Level II interpreting film in a viewing room needs no source authority, while one running field exposures needs full radiographer certification. Method fundamentals live at /radiographic-testing-training, the Level II landscape at /ndt-level-2-training, and hour tables at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020), Table 6.3.1A; US NRC 10 CFR Part 34; ASME Section V, Article 2 (referenced viewing and IQI practice)

facets.q: What does film interpretation authority actually mean?
facets.a: The Level II decides whether each radiograph is itself acceptable — density, IQI sensitivity, artifacts — and then whether the weld or casting it shows meets code. Both judgments carry the technician's signature and bind the inspection record.

facets.q: Does RT Level II qualify me to operate radiation sources?
facets.a: No. Source operation is governed entirely by 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules — certifying-entity certification such as IRRSP plus licensee exams. An RT Level II without that track can interpret film but cannot shoot it.

facets.q: Is there a film-interpretation-only certification?
facets.a: Yes. Many written practices define a limited Level II — often called RTFI or radiographic film interpreter — restricted to interpretation with reduced experience hours. It suits engineers and QC staff who review film but never perform exposures.

facets.q: How does digital radiography change Level II requirements?
facets.a: The hour structure is unchanged, but written practices add CR/DR-specific training covering detector characteristics, software measurement tools, and digital IQI practice. Employers migrating from film typically administer a supplemental specific exam rather than a full recertification.

facets.q: What codes govern RT Level II acceptance decisions in the US?
facets.a: ASME Section V Article 2 sets technique and image quality, with acceptance criteria from referencing codes like Section VIII or B31.3; API 1104 governs pipeline girth welds; AWS D1.1 covers structural steel. Your specific exam targets the code your employer works under.

facets.q: How long from RT Level I to Level II?
facets.a: The 630 additional experience hours represent roughly four to six months of full-time radiographic work, plus the 40-hour Level II course and exams. Pipeline crews working long turnaround seasons often bank the hours faster than the calendar suggests.

sections.heading: The requirement stack for RT Level II
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A adds 40 formal training hours and 630 RT experience hours to Level I's base — 80 and 840 cumulative — with direct-to-Level II certification available at the summed totals for documented trainees. The employer's Level III administers general, specific, and practical exams at a recommended 80 percent composite, and the written practice fixes the binding numbers. What makes RT Level II distinctive is where the practical weight falls: interpretation. A candidate can be a flawless field radiographer and still fail Level II exams on film reading, because the certification is fundamentally about judgment over images, not exposure mechanics. Hour comparisons across every method sit at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

sections.heading: Film interpretation: the authority Level II exists to confer
paragraphs: A Level II reads every radiograph twice. The first pass judges the image itself: is density within the viewing range — commonly around 1.8 to 4.0 under ASME Section V practice — is the correct IQI present with required sensitivity visible, is coverage complete, and are artifacts absent or identifiable as non-relevant? Only a technically acceptable radiograph earns the second pass: grading the weld or casting. Porosity, slag inclusions, incomplete fusion, incomplete penetration, undercut, and cracks each have code-specific acceptance limits, and distinguishing a crack from a scratch or processing artifact is exactly the skill the 630 experience hours exist to build. The Level II's signature on that judgment is the product the client buys.

sections.heading: What the Level II course and exams cover
paragraphs: The 40 Level II classroom hours shift from making images to judging them: densitometry and viewing conditions, IQI selection and placement logic, geometric unsharpness control, technique selection for varying thickness, and systematic discontinuity recognition across weld and casting radiographs. Exams follow the standard three-part structure. The general exam tests radiographic principles at depth — expect exposure technique, image quality variables, and discontinuity identification. The specific exam drills your employer's procedures and governing code tables. The practical is dominated by a film-reading exercise: a stack of radiographs to grade, with your dispositions scored against the Level III's master answers. Interpretation errors, not physics questions, are where candidates fail.

sections.heading: The radiation-safety distinction, restated for Level II
paragraphs: Nothing about advancing to Level II touches the regulatory track. Operating gamma or X-ray exposure devices in US industrial radiography requires radiation-safety certification through a recognized certifying entity — ASNT's IRRSP program is standard — plus licensee-administered exams, three-device dosimetry per 10 CFR 34.47, and the two-person rule at temporary sites per 10 CFR 34.41. A Level II who interprets film in an office needs none of it; a Level II running field exposures needs all of it, at any NDT level. Employers structure crews accordingly: field radiographers hold both tracks, while some interpretation specialists hold method certification alone. Confusing the tracks on a resume is an immediate credibility flag.

sections.heading: Film versus digital: where US practice actually is
paragraphs: Film remains the working medium across most US pipeline and much pressure-vessel radiography, so darkroom competence and densitometer fluency stay examinable skills. But computed radiography (CR) and direct digital arrays (DR) are displacing film steadily, led by shops chasing throughput and archiving advantages. For a Level II this means a widening skill set: digital detector characteristics, contrast-to-noise judgment, software measurement and annotation tools, and digital IQI practice under the same code logic. SNT-TC-1A's hour structure does not change, but written practices increasingly append CR/DR modules and supplemental specific exams. Candidates who can interpret confidently across both media are the most employable radiographers in the current US market.

sections.heading: Vision requirements — stricter stakes at Level II
paragraphs: The formal regime matches other methods: annual near-vision acuity at Jaeger No. 2 or equivalent from not less than 12 inches, color-contrast differentiation at certification and at intervals not exceeding five years. For an interpreting Level II, near vision is not a compliance checkbox but the working instrument — fine porosity and tight crack indications sit at the threshold of visual acuity under viewer illumination. Written practices for radiography frequently specify viewing-room conditions alongside personnel vision: calibrated high-luminance viewers, low ambient light, and dark adaptation time. A Level II whose vision exam lapses loses interpretation authority immediately, so the annual check belongs on a calendar, not a to-do list.

sections.heading: Demand and pay for RT Level II in the US
paragraphs: Interpretation authority is chronically scarce, and pay reflects it. PayScale reports certified RT Level II holders averaging roughly $65,000–$70,000, against the BLS all-levels median of $78,350 for NDT specialists (May 2025); ZipRecruiter's NDT Level 2 range of $48,000–$90,000 brackets the field, with pipeline radiographers at the top once per-diem and overtime stack. Employers hiring RT Level II ask for the complete package: SNT-TC-1A records, current vision exam, IRRSP card for field roles, code-specific film-reading experience, and a clean dosimetry history. Regional and industry breakdowns, including the pipeline premium, are maintained at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

sections.heading: Where RT Level II leads
paragraphs: Three paths branch from RT Level II. The technique path moves into CR/DR leadership and advanced applications as digital adoption spreads. The code path adds API 1104 fluency toward pipeline QC roles, or AWS CWI and API credentials that convert an interpreter into an inspection authority. The certification path banks the hours toward ASNT Level III in RT — the person who writes technique sheets, approves procedures, and administers the exams you just passed. Cross-training is the near-term multiplier: RT Level IIs who add UT read both volumetric methods and become the most flexible people on any integrity crew. The lateral view across methods is at /ndt-level-2-training.

paragraphs: Atlantis NDT's 40-hour RT Level II course is built around interpretation: graded film-reading libraries spanning weld and casting discontinuities, densitometry and IQI practice, and code acceptance drills against ASME Section V referencing codes and API 1104. For employers, our ASNT Level III consultants administer the full qualification cycle — written practices that correctly separate method and radiation-safety tracks, examinations with defensible film-reading masters, and audit-ready records. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable to your procedures and media mix, film or digital. Start at /radiographic-testing-training for the method program, then request a quote for individual certification or a full crew upgrade.

faq.q: Can I certify directly to RT Level II?
faq.a: Yes — SNT-TC-1A permits direct Level II at the summed hours: 80 training and 840 RT experience, completed as a documented trainee before examination. The film-reading practical is the gatekeeper; banked hours without supervised interpretation practice rarely survive it.

faq.q: What density range must a radiograph fall in?
faq.a: Under common ASME Section V practice, transmitted film density in the area of interest runs from about 1.8 (X-ray) or 2.0 (gamma) up to 4.0. Your governing code and procedure state the exact limits your Level II judgment must apply.

faq.q: Does RT Level II expire?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends recertification at intervals not exceeding five years, with re-examination typically required after interrupted service. The radiation-safety track renews separately — annual refresher training and periodic exams under the license — on its own clock.

faq.q: Is RT Level II certification portable between employers?
faq.a: The certification is employer-issued and ends with employment, but complete records — training certificates, experience logs, exam and vision history, dosimetry file — let a new employer's Level III re-examine and certify quickly. The IRRSP card, by contrast, is yours and travels.

faq.q: What is the hardest part of the RT Level II practical?
faq.a: Consistently, the film-reading exercise: distinguishing tight cracks from artifacts, grading rounded indications against the correct code table, and rejecting technically inadequate radiographs candidates are tempted to interpret anyway. Volume practice on graded film libraries is the only reliable preparation.

title: ET Level 1 Training: 40 Hours, SNT-TC-1A and NAS 410 Paths
description: ET Level I requires 40 training hours and 210 method hours under SNT-TC-1A — or 400 experience hours under NAS 410 for aerospace. Duties, exams, and vision rules.
h1: Eddy Current Testing Level I Training Requirements
answer: ET Level I requires 40 hours of formal training and 210 hours of eddy current experience under SNT-TC-1A, certified by your employer through general, specific, and practical exams. Aerospace work runs on NAS 410 instead, which keeps the 40 training hours but raises experience to 400 hours and mandates annual vision exams. Level I runs preset, calibrated scans — signal interpretation waits for Level II.
expansion: Eddy current is the one common method where the governing standard genuinely depends on industry, so an ET Level I plan starts with a destination question. General industry — tubing inspection, conductivity sorting, weld testing — runs on SNT-TC-1A's employer-based model: 40 training hours, 210 method hours from Table 6.3.1A, written practice, five-year recertification. Aerospace manufacturing and MRO run on NAS 410, a minimum standard rather than a recommended practice: the same 40 formal training hours for Level 1 but 400 experience hours, a mandated 40-question general exam, annual near-vision and color checks, and a Level 1-Limited category for single-task certification. Either way, Level I work is executing preset scans — lift-off compensated, reference-standard calibrated — with go/no-go thresholds, because impedance-plane interpretation is reserved for Level II. Method fundamentals are at /eddy-current-testing-training, entry-level context at /ndt-level-1-training, and hour tables at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020), Table 6.3.1A; AIA NAS 410 (minimum formal training and experience requirements)
