sections.heading: Three tracks, three kinds of credit for the same welding years
paragraphs: The decision is arithmetic before it is ambition. Count two numbers: documented welding-related years, and formal education. Five-plus years with a high school diploma makes you CWI-eligible today — the exam is the only barrier. One to four years points at the NDT track first, because employer-based Level I and II certification runs on training hours and logged OJT rather than a years-of-experience gate, and it pays inspection wages while your CWI eligibility clock keeps running in the background. Years spent fabricating pressure vessels, piping systems, or storage tanks additionally bank toward the API certificates — the long-game track with the largest equipment-specific paychecks.

The tracks also stack rather than compete. A CWI who adds MT and PT Level II becomes the shop's one-stop weld-quality resource; an NDT Level II with vessel fabrication history becomes an API 510 candidate the year the eligibility math closes. Sequencing them deliberately — rather than chasing whichever acronym a job posting mentioned — is what separates a two-year plan from a six-year wander.

sections.heading: The CWI track: your welding years are the eligibility
paragraphs: AWS built the CWI eligibility tables around welding-related work, so a welder's resume needs translation, not supplementation. The qualifying experience spans welding itself, supervision, quality control, and fabrication roles, on a sliding education scale: five years with a high school diploma or GED, four with a trade or vocational certificate, three with a qualifying associate degree, one with a qualifying bachelor's in engineering or a physical science. Welders short of the full requirement enter as CAWI — the associate credential on the same exam — and upgrade as years accrue.

The exam, not the eligibility, is where welders stumble: three parts in one sitting. Part A tests welding fundamentals in exam language rather than shop language; Part B is the hands-on practical, working replicas and measurement tools against a supplied specification book; Part C tests navigation of a code you select — D1.1 and API 1104 being the common picks. Pass rates differ sharply by part, and preparation should be weighted accordingly — the part-by-part failure pattern and how to study against it are broken down in the [CWI pass rate breakdown by Part A, B, and C](/blog/cwi-pass-rate-by-part-a-b-c-breakdown). A vision test and documented, verifiable experience complete the application.

sections.heading: The ASNT track: welding counts as advantage, not hours
paragraphs: Be precise about what transfers, because this is where career-changers get oversold. Under SNT-TC-1A's employer-based system, certification requires method-specific training hours and method-specific experience logged under qualified supervision — and ten years under the hood contributes zero of those hours. What welding experience does is compress everything around the hours: you already know how discontinuities form, where they live in a joint, and what a WPS controls, which is most of the interpretive judgment Level II exams actually test.

There is one conditional path to real credit: welders who performed documented visual inspection duties — examining their own or others' production welds against acceptance criteria, under a certified supervisor, with records — can have that time credited where the employer's written practice allows it. The operative words are documented and written practice: an employer's Level III decides what counts, and undocumented shop-floor checking counts nowhere. If you are still welding today, start creating that record now.

Method selection follows welding knowledge downhill: VT, MT, and PT are the natural first certifications because the discontinuities are the ones welders already recognize, and the training-hour requirements are the lightest. UT rewards welders who know joint geometry but demands real physics study; RT adds radiation safety qualification on top. A typical committed career-changer holds VT plus MT or PT Level II within their first year of NDT employment, with UT as the second-year target.

sections.heading: The API track: fabrication years on the eligibility table
paragraphs: API 510 (pressure vessels), 570 (process piping), and 653 (aboveground storage tanks) run on published eligibility tables that credit experience in the design, construction, fabrication, repair, or inspection of the covered equipment — which is exactly what a vessel, pipe, or tank welder has been accruing. The tables slide on education: more formal education, fewer required years; the no-degree rows demand the most. Every route also requires that a defined portion of the experience be supervising or performing inspection activities as the code describes, which is the piece pure fabrication history lacks — and the reason the API certificates work best as a second credential after NDT or CWI employment has put inspection duties on your record.

Equipment specificity is enforced, not implied: tank experience feeds 653, piping feeds 570, vessel experience feeds 510, and they do not substitute for one another. Each certificate has its own body-of-knowledge examination — a 170-question format — built on its code and the referenced standards. To be plain about scope: Atlantis does not sell API 510, 570, or 653 training; the eligibility structure is described here so you can sequence it into the plan, and API publishes the current tables and application requirements at api.org.

sections.heading: Document your welding years now — the future application depends on it
paragraphs: Every track above runs on verifiable experience, and verification decays: shops close, supervisors retire, and a 2019 job becomes unprovable by 2027. Build the file while the evidence is warm. For each employer: dates of employment, job title, the equipment and processes worked, and a duty description written in inspection-relevant language — joints welded to what codes, inspection or QC duties performed, WPS and PQR exposure. Get it signed by a supervisor or quality manager on company letterhead where possible.

Write duty descriptions the way an application reviewer reads them. "Welded and visually examined structural connections to AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria; maintained fit-up and interpass records" earns credit on three different applications. "Structural welder, six years" earns a request for more information. Add the corroborating layer — weld continuity logs, qualification test records, pay stubs establishing dates — and store it all somewhere that survives job changes. The single cheapest career move in this entire article is one afternoon spent getting letters signed before you need them.

sections.heading: The 2026 US market for welder-turned-inspectors
paragraphs: The demand side favors the switch. The US inspection workforce skews old — retirements across NDT and welding inspection are outpacing entries — while the work grows: refinery and petrochemical turnaround seasons, pipeline integrity programs, LNG and hydrogen buildout, fabrication reshoring, and the standing inspection load of aging pressure equipment. Third-party inspection firms and shop quality departments consistently prefer career-changers from the welding floor because the discontinuity recognition and code literacy arrive pre-installed; the credential is what they need added.

Practical hiring reality: shops and TPIs routinely hire welders as NDT trainees or QC assistants and sponsor the training, because growing an inspector from a welder is cheaper and more reliable than recruiting a finished one in a tight market. Turnaround contractors pay a premium for people who can hold both a torch card and a Level II — dual-capability heads reduce crew count. When you interview, lead with the documented welding record and the study plan; employers fund candidates who arrive with the file already built.

sections.heading: A realistic sequencing plan: months 0 through 24
paragraphs: Months 0–3: build the experience file — verification letters, duty descriptions, continuity records — and pick the entry track by the arithmetic: five-plus documented years means CWI preparation starts now; fewer means an NDT trainee or QC role is the move. Months 3–12: on the NDT route, complete VT and MT or PT training hours and log OJT toward Level II under the employer's written practice; on the CWI route, prepare for all three parts with study weighted toward the historically hardest, and sit the exam. Either route ends year one holding a paying inspection credential.

Months 12–24: stack the second credential. The new CWI adds MT/PT Level II to become the complete weld-quality package; the new Level II starts CWI preparation with the eligibility clock now well fed, or begins UT training for the deeper NDT ceiling. Vessel, piping, and tank welders map their fabrication years against the API tables and calendar the application for when the inspection-specific portion closes. For the ASNT side of that plan — Level I and II method training through Level III preparation — Atlantis delivers blended online theory with in-person practical arranged on-site at your employer or at an arranged venue, built around US codes and the exams you will actually sit. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable. Quote on request.

faq.q: Can I keep welding full-time while getting certified?
faq.a: Yes, and on two of the three tracks it is the optimal play: welding years keep feeding CWI and API eligibility while you study. The exception is the ASNT method-hours requirement — those accrue only in NDT assignments — which is why career-changers often move to a dual welder/QC role or an NDT trainee position partway through rather than at the start.

faq.q: Should I do CWI or NDT Level II first?
faq.a: Run the eligibility math. Five or more documented welding years with a high school diploma: CWI first — you are eligible now and the credential monetizes immediately. Fewer years: NDT first, because employer-based Level I/II has no years-of-experience gate for entry, pays inspection wages sooner, and the CWI clock keeps running underneath. The two stack; the order is just cash-flow optimization.

faq.q: If I fail one part of the CWI exam, do I retake everything?
faq.a: No — AWS scores Parts A, B, and C separately, and its retest rules let you re-sit the failed part within the allowed window rather than repeating the full exam. The part-by-part pass rates and the retake strategy are covered in the [CWI pass rate breakdown](/blog/cwi-pass-rate-by-part-a-b-c-breakdown).

faq.q: Does pipe welding experience help with API 1104 work as a CWI?
faq.a: Directly. Part C of the CWI exam is taken against a code you choose, and pipeline welders choosing API 1104 test on the document they have worked under for years. AWS also offers code endorsements, so a D1.1 CWI can add the API 1104 endorsement later — the standard setup for CWIs moving between structural and pipeline inspection markets.

faq.q: Will an employer pay for my training?
faq.a: Commonly, yes. Shops, third-party inspection firms, and turnaround contractors sponsor NDT training because growing inspectors internally beats recruiting them in a thin market — expect a service commitment in exchange. Arrive with your documented welding record and a specific training plan and you become the easy yes. Atlantis structures its ASNT-track training for exactly this employer-sponsored pattern, delivered on-site or blended. Quote on request.

faq.q: Is radiography a realistic first NDT method for a welder?
faq.a: Rarely first. RT adds radiation-safety qualification, badging, and regulatory oversight on top of method training, and most employers want a proven Level II in a surface method before investing in it. The standard welder's ladder is VT and MT/PT first, UT second, RT where the employer's work mix demands it.

title: NDT Software With QuickBooks Integration: What Actually Syncs
description: What syncs between NDT software and QuickBooks — invoices, customers, items, payments — what stays in the ERP, setup order, and causes of double-entry drift.
h1: QuickBooks Integration for NDT Inspection Software
answer: NDT software integrates with QuickBooks by syncing four objects: customers, service items, invoices, and payments. The ERP stays the operational system — jobs, technicians, reports — and pushes finished invoices to QuickBooks Online through Intuit's API. Payments recorded in QuickBooks flow back to close the job financially. Certifications, calibration records, and inspection reports never touch QuickBooks.
expansion: QuickBooks is where the small US inspection contractor's accountant, tax preparer, and banker already live, so the practical question is never whether to replace it — it is which system owns each record. The working rule: the NDT platform owns operations (jobs, technicians, equipment, reports, timesheets) and QuickBooks owns accounting (chart of accounts, tax, reconciliation, payroll). Integration means four objects cross the boundary. Customers and service items are matched or created once, then referenced by ID. Invoices are generated in the NDT platform — where the job data, per-diems, and mobilization charges live — and pushed to QuickBooks as drafts or posted invoices. Payments flow the other way, from QuickBooks back to the job record, so operations staff see paid status without opening the books. Everything outside those four objects stays put. Double-entry drift starts the day someone edits an invoice on the wrong side of that line.
source: Intuit QuickBooks Online API object model; Atlantis NDT Odoo ERP implementations for US inspection contractors

facets.q: Does NDT software integrate with QuickBooks Desktop or only QuickBooks Online?
facets.a: QuickBooks Online is the dependable path: Intuit's REST API exposes customers, items, invoices, and payments directly, and an Odoo-based NDT ERP connects to it over OAuth with no local agent. QuickBooks Desktop requires the Web Connector — a Windows-resident sync service that adds one more thing to break. A contractor still on Desktop gets a cleaner result by migrating to Online first, then connecting the ERP.

facets.q: Which system should create the invoice — the NDT platform or QuickBooks?
facets.a: The NDT platform, every time. The invoice is assembled from data QuickBooks never sees: report numbers, shift counts, per-diem days, mobilization charges, minimum call-outs. Building it in QuickBooks means retyping all of that, which is the double entry the integration exists to kill. QuickBooks receives the finished invoice, posts it to the right income accounts, and owns everything after — payment, deposit, reconciliation.

facets.q: What causes double-entry drift between an NDT ERP and QuickBooks?
facets.a: Drift has one root cause: the same object accepting edits in both systems. An invoice pushed to QuickBooks and then edited there no longer matches the job record; a customer created by name-matching instead of stored ID mapping spawns duplicates; a payment applied against a reused invoice number closes the wrong job. Lock each object to one owner, sync one direction, and drift stops.

facets.q: What is the correct setup order before the first invoice syncs?
facets.a: Four steps in strict order: clean the QuickBooks chart of accounts and confirm income accounts per service line; build the service-item list and map every ERP product to a QuickBooks item; deduplicate customers and store the QuickBooks ID on each ERP customer record; then pick a hard cutover date. Invoices before that date live only in QuickBooks; invoices after it originate only in the ERP.

facets.q: Should inspection reports or certificates be attached inside QuickBooks?
facets.a: No. QuickBooks has no revision control, no report numbering, and no link between an attachment and a technician's certification status, so a report PDF attached to an invoice becomes an orphaned copy the moment the report is revised. Keep reports, certs, and calibration records in the NDT platform and let the invoice reference report numbers as line-item text.

facets.q: Can an Odoo ERP for NDT replace QuickBooks instead of integrating with it?
facets.a: Odoo carries a full accounting module, so replacement is technically real — and the right call for a contractor whose bookkeeper works in-house. The integration exists for the more common case: an external CPA who works in QuickBooks and is not changing. Atlantis configures either mode; the deciding question is who closes your books, not what the software can do.

sections.heading: Why QuickBooks stays and the ERP adapts
paragraphs: In the United States, the small inspection contractor's accountant works in QuickBooks, files taxes from QuickBooks, and reconciles the bank feed in QuickBooks. Replacing it means retraining an outside CPA who bills by the hour and has no reason to learn an ERP's accounting module. So the sensible architecture for a five-to-fifty-technician NDT shop treats QuickBooks as fixed infrastructure. The operational software — jobs, technicians, equipment, reports — must integrate with it rather than compete with it, and the quality of that integration decides whether month-end close takes an hour or a weekend.

Most inspection software vendors treat the subject with one sentence — "integrates with QuickBooks" — on a features page. That sentence hides the four questions that matter: which objects sync, in which direction each flows, which system wins a conflict, and what happens to an invoice that gets edited after posting. Those answers are configuration decisions, and wrong ones surface as drift weeks later, when the books and the job list disagree by a few hundred dollars nobody can locate.

The division of labor that works: the NDT platform is the system of record for operations — job numbers, scopes, technician assignments, equipment usage, inspection reports, timesheets. QuickBooks is the system of record for accounting — chart of accounts, tax, deposits, payroll, reconciliation. Exactly four objects cross that boundary. This page walks through each one, the setup order that makes them behave, and the specific places drift creeps in when the boundary is drawn sloppily.

sections.heading: The four objects that sync, one at a time
paragraphs: Customers sync first because everything else hangs off them. The correct pattern is ID mapping: on first sync, each ERP customer is either matched to an existing QuickBooks customer and its QuickBooks ID stored on the ERP record, or created fresh with the new ID stored. From then on, every invoice references that ID, never the name string. Integrations that match by name create the classic QuickBooks disease — "Chevron", "Chevron Corp", and "Chevron Corporation" existing as three customers with three open balances.

Service items are the mapping layer between what you sell and where the revenue lands. Each ERP product — UT shift rate, MT technician day, per-diem, mobilization, report fee — maps to one QuickBooks item, and each QuickBooks item points at an income account. Get this right and the P&L reads revenue by service line with zero extra effort. Get it wrong and every invoice posts to a single "Services" account, which erases the answer to the one question worth asking: which methods make money.

Invoices flow one way: ERP to QuickBooks. The invoice is assembled in the NDT platform, where report numbers, shift counts, and job data live, approved by someone with billing authority, then pushed. It arrives in QuickBooks either as a posted invoice or — a defensible choice in the first months — as a draft the bookkeeper releases. The number sequence must have a single owner; two systems both assigning invoice numbers guarantees collisions with whatever the CPA created by hand.

Payments flow the opposite way: QuickBooks to ERP. Money is received, matched, and deposited in QuickBooks, where the bank feed lives. The integration reads payment events and marks the corresponding ERP invoices paid, so a project manager sees paid status on the job screen without asking the bookkeeper. The reverse event matters just as much — a voided or bounced payment must reopen the invoice in the ERP, or operations keeps treating a live receivable as closed.

sections.heading: What deliberately never syncs
paragraphs: Inspection reports, technician certifications, and equipment calibration records stay out of QuickBooks — not because syncing them is hard, but because they have no accounting meaning and QuickBooks gives them no revision control. A report PDF attached to a QuickBooks invoice becomes an orphaned copy the moment revision B is issued. The invoice line can and should carry report numbers as text — clients match invoices to deliverables that way — but the documents themselves live in the NDT platform, under its numbering and revision rules.

Timesheets and job costing deserve special caution. Labor cost belongs in job costing inside the ERP, and payroll belongs in QuickBooks or a payroll service — those are two different views of the same hours. Pushing raw timesheets into QuickBooks alongside payroll produces double-counted labor expense, one of the ugliest cleanup jobs in bookkeeping. Hours reach QuickBooks in exactly one form: as billable invoice lines after markup, never as cost entries duplicating what payroll already posted.

sections.heading: Setup order: the boring work that decides everything
paragraphs: Step one happens entirely inside QuickBooks: clean the chart of accounts and decide the income accounts — one per service line is the structure that makes the P&L useful for an NDT shop. Step two is the item map: list every distinct thing you invoice, create matching QuickBooks service items, and record the mapping. Contractors discover here that their invoicing has been improvised for years — the same mobilization charge entered five different ways. The integration forces the standardization that should have existed anyway.

Step three is customer deduplication, done before the first sync ever runs. Merge duplicates inside QuickBooks, then match ERP customers to the survivors and store the IDs. Skipping this step means the integration faithfully propagates the mess, and unwinding merged transactions later is worse than the original cleanup. Budget real hours for it: a ten-year-old QuickBooks file with hand-entered customers holds more duplicates than anyone expects, and every one left standing becomes a mis-posted invoice waiting to happen.

Step four is a hard cutover date. Invoices dated before it live only in QuickBooks; invoices after it originate only in the ERP. Resist backfilling history through the sync — pushing a year of old invoices into a file where they already exist creates duplicates by the hundreds, and duplicate revenue is the kind of error that surfaces at tax time. Historical reporting can read from QuickBooks directly; the integration's job starts at the cutover and runs forward.

sections.heading: Where double-entry drift comes from
paragraphs: Drift is the state where the ERP and QuickBooks disagree about a number and nobody knows which is right. Its root cause is singular: the same object accepting edits on both sides of the boundary. The bookkeeper "fixes" a pushed invoice in QuickBooks — adds a line, adjusts a rate — and the job record no longer matches the books. The fix is procedural, not technical: corrections happen in the system that owns the object, then re-sync. An invoice wrong in QuickBooks gets corrected in the ERP.

The second source is identity matching. Name-string matching spawns duplicate customers; reused invoice numbers apply payments to the wrong job; loosely matched items post revenue to wrong accounts. Every one of these disappears when the integration stores hard IDs — QuickBooks' own record identifiers — on the ERP side and matches on nothing else. Ask a vendor directly whether their sync matches on ID or on name; the answer sorts real integrations from checkbox ones in a single sentence.

The third source is arithmetic. Tax computed in two places with two rounding rules produces penny mismatches that block reconciliation and stack into real discrepancies across hundreds of invoices. The rule: QuickBooks computes tax, using its own jurisdiction tables, from taxable-status flags the ERP sends per line. Discounts and credit memos follow the same logic — issue them in the ERP, let QuickBooks post them, and the two systems stay in lockstep down to the cent.

sections.heading: NDT invoicing is why the ERP must build the invoice
paragraphs: An inspection invoice is not a product invoice. A single turnaround job bills straight-time and overtime shifts at different rates, per-diem days per technician, mobilization and demobilization, equipment charges for a PAUT rig, exposure counts on RT work, and minimum call-out charges when a two-hour job bills as four. All of that data originates in dispatch and timesheets — inside the NDT platform. Rebuilding it by hand in QuickBooks is where office evenings go to die, and every retyped line is a fresh drift opportunity.

Progress billing on long jobs follows the same principle. The billing schedule — a mobilization draw, progress draws against percent complete, retainage — lives on the ERP job. Each draw becomes an ordinary invoice pushed to QuickBooks, while the ERP tracks billed-to-date against contract value. What breaks is trying to run QuickBooks-side progress invoicing against a QuickBooks estimate, because the ERP cannot see the estimate and the two billed-to-date figures immediately diverge.

sections.heading: QuickBooks Online versus Desktop for inspection contractors
paragraphs: QuickBooks Online is the version built for integration: a REST API, OAuth authorization, event notifications for payments, and no software running on your machines. Every modern NDT platform that syncs at all syncs with Online. Intuit has also spent years steering Desktop customers toward Online — new US subscriptions for most Desktop editions stopped in 2024 — so the platform direction is settled, and new integration work targets the Online API.

Desktop integration still exists through the QuickBooks Web Connector — a Windows service polling on a schedule — or third-party bridges. It works, with more moving parts: a host machine that must stay on, a sync that runs on intervals rather than events, and file-locking quirks in multi-user mode. A contractor still on Desktop with an integration project ahead should sequence it deliberately: migrate to Online first, stabilize one full month of books, then connect the ERP.

sections.heading: How to test a vendor's QuickBooks claim before buying
paragraphs: In the demo, script four scenarios and watch them happen live. One: create a job, invoice it, push it, open it in QuickBooks. Two: edit that invoice inside QuickBooks and see what the ERP does — the honest answers are "flags a conflict" or "overwrites on next sync," and you need to know which one you are buying. Three: receive a payment in QuickBooks and watch the job close in the ERP. Four: void that payment and watch the job reopen. A vendor who cannot demo scenario four has a one-way sync wearing a two-way costume.

In writing, require the object list (customers, items, invoices, payments at minimum), the direction of each, ID-based matching, approval-gated invoice push, and payment-reversal handling. These belong in your requirements document verbatim — the full set is in the /erp/ndt-software-rfp-requirements-checklist. Contractors running API 510, 570, and 653 inspection programs alongside NDT services should also read /erp/api-inspection-contractor-management-software, because inspection-interval data adds its own integration questions on top of the accounting ones.

Atlantis configures its Odoo-based NDT ERP either way — synced to QuickBooks Online for shops whose CPA stays in QuickBooks, or running Odoo's own accounting for shops bringing the books in-house. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable. A working demonstration against a copy of your own QuickBooks file is the fastest way to judge any vendor's claim, ours included — a demo is available on request.

faq.q: Does the sync push invoices automatically or wait for approval?
faq.a: Approval-gated is the correct configuration. The ERP marks an invoice ready, a person with billing authority reviews it, and only then does it post to QuickBooks. Fully automatic push sounds efficient and produces posted invoices with wrong PO numbers that then need credit memos on both sides.

faq.q: What happens when a payment is voided or bounced in QuickBooks?
faq.a: The reversal syncs back on the next cycle: the ERP reopens the invoice and flags the job unpaid again, so operations sees the true receivable. Test this scenario in the demo — one-way payment sync that only handles the happy path is a common gap in inspection software.

faq.q: How is sales tax handled between the two systems?
faq.a: QuickBooks owns tax. The ERP sends taxable status and jurisdiction per line; QuickBooks computes the tax with its own rate tables so the filed return and the posted invoice always agree. Computing tax in the ERP and pushing a total invites penny-level mismatches that block reconciliation.

faq.q: Do progress invoices on long turnaround jobs sync correctly?
faq.a: Yes, when each progress invoice is its own document — a draw against the job, pushed like any other invoice, with billed-to-date tracked in the ERP. What fails is QuickBooks-side progress invoicing against a QuickBooks estimate, because the ERP has no visibility into that estimate. Keep the job's billing schedule in the ERP.

faq.q: How long does the QuickBooks connection take to set up?
faq.a: The OAuth connection itself is done in hours. The real timeline is the data work in front of it — cleaning the chart of accounts, mapping items, deduplicating customers — measured in days for a tidy file and weeks for one with years of freehand entry. The scoping questions are in /erp/ndt-software-rfp-requirements-checklist.

title: Calibration Tracking for NDT Equipment: Register to Recall
description: Calibration tracking software for NDT equipment — the register of instruments, probes, cables and blocks, due-date logic, out-of-cal quarantine, and audit answers.
h1: Calibration Due-Date Tracking for NDT Instruments, Probes, and Blocks
answer: NDT calibration tracking software holds a register of every item that touches a reading — flaw detectors, thickness gauges, probes, cables, and calibration blocks — with a due date, certificate, and status on each. When a due date passes, the item drops to out-of-cal, disappears from job assignment, and triggers a recall review of work performed since the last good calibration.
expansion: Search for calibration tracking and the results are calibration labs selling services, not software for the contractor who owns forty serialized assets and answers for every one of them at audit. An NDT calibration program is a register problem: the flaw detector has an accredited-lab certificate on a fixed cycle, the thickness gauge gets verified on a reference block every working day, the probe gets its exit point checked on an IIW block, the cable gets swap-tested when readings drift, and the calibration block itself needs periodic dimensional verification. Each class has its own clock, its own evidence, and its own consequence when the clock runs out. Software earns its place by doing three things a spreadsheet cannot: blocking an overdue item from job assignment, answering "which jobs did this serial number touch since its last good calibration," and producing the certificate in seconds when the auditor asks.
source: ISO/IEC 17025 laboratory accreditation framework; ASTM and ASME NDT method practices; Atlantis NDT Odoo EAM implementations

facets.q: What belongs in an NDT calibration register besides flaw detectors?
facets.a: Everything that influences a recorded reading: thickness gauges, probes and transducers, cables, calibration and reference blocks, MT yokes, UV-A lamps and light meters for fluorescent work, and survey meters on RT crews. Blocks are the item shops miss — an IIW block with a dinged radius quietly corrupts every angle-beam verification done on it, so blocks carry due dates for dimensional verification like any instrument.

facets.q: How should calibration due-date logic work — one fixed interval?
facets.a: Three clocks per item, not one. A certificate clock: fixed interval from the last accredited calibration, set by your written procedure. A verification clock: per-use or per-day functional checks — a thickness gauge proved on a reference block each working day. An event clock: a drop, a damaged connector, or suspect readings force status change immediately, regardless of the printed due date. Software that models only the first clock tracks paperwork, not fitness for use.

facets.q: What happens when an item goes out of calibration?
facets.a: Two actions, in order. Quarantine: the status flips, the item leaves the assignable pool, and dispatch cannot attach it to a job — with a physical tag matching the digital state. Then the recall review: pull every job that used that serial number since its last good calibration and have a Level III disposition whether the findings stand. The second action is the one auditors probe, and it is impossible without per-job equipment usage records.

facets.q: How should calibration certificates be stored for audit retrieval?
facets.a: One certificate record per calibration event, attached to the asset, carrying the lab name, certificate number, calibration date, due date, and as-found condition. The retrieval test that matters: given a job number from two years ago, produce the certificates for every instrument used on it, in minutes. Folder trees named by year fail that test; an asset register with per-job usage links passes it. A starting format is at /resources/calibration-certificate-template.

facets.q: Do probes and cables need accredited calibration certificates?
facets.a: No — they need documented verification, which is different. A transducer's exit point and beam angle are checked on an IIW block at the frequency your written procedure states, and the check is logged against the probe's serial number. Cables get continuity and swap-testing when signals misbehave, with replacements logged. The register still tracks both, because an auditor tracing a reading will ask which probe and which check, not just which instrument.

facets.q: What does ISO/IEC 17025 have to do with a contractor's equipment?
facets.a: Your clients expect the labs calibrating your instruments to hold ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation, with measurements traceable to NIST. Your own program then proves the chain: an accredited certificate on the instrument, documented verifications between calibrations, and control of nonconforming equipment. Client auditors borrow that framework even when auditing a contractor against ASNT-based programs, so a register organized around those three proofs answers audits from either direction.

sections.heading: The register is bigger than your instrument list
paragraphs: Ask a shop for its calibration list and you get flaw detectors and thickness gauges. Ask an auditor what they want to see and the list grows: every probe with its serial number, the cables in the kit, every IIW block, step wedge, and reference block, the MT yokes, the UV-A lamps and the light meter that proves them, and the survey meters the RT crew carries. The register's scope rule is simple to state: if the item can change a recorded reading or a probability of detection, it has an entry.

Blocks deserve the emphasis because they fail silently. A flaw detector out of calibration announces itself at the next linearity check; a calibration block with a worn notch or a dinged radius corrupts every verification performed on it while looking exactly like a block should. So blocks carry their own dimensional-verification due dates, their own certificates, and their own damage-inspection entries. The same logic covers reference blocks cut for specific procedures — sometimes the only physical standard a client's job ever sees.

Each register entry carries the same skeleton: unique asset ID and serial number, description and manufacturer, current status, the applicable check type, the interval, last-done and next-due dates, the certificate or verification evidence, and location or kit assignment. Location matters more than it looks — the audit question is never only "is it calibrated" but "which technician had it on which job," and a register that cannot say where an item was is only half a register.

sections.heading: Due-date logic: three clocks per asset
paragraphs: The first clock is the certificate cycle: a fixed interval from the last accredited calibration, with the interval set in your written procedure — a twelve-month cycle is the common baseline for flaw detectors and thickness gauges. The software's job is to hold whatever your procedure says and count down from the calibration date printed on the certificate, not from the date the unit came back in the door. That distinction quietly shortens the real interval by shipping time when it is gotten wrong.

The second clock runs faster: functional verifications between calibrations. A thickness gauge proved against a reference block each working day; an angle-beam setup verified on the IIW block at the start of the examination; sensitivity re-checked at the points the governing code section requires during the job. These checks are logged, not certificated — a dated entry against the asset's serial number with pass or fail and the technician's identity. Software that captures them from a phone in the field turns a compliance chore into a ten-second habit.

The third clock has no schedule at all. A dropped instrument, a crushed cable connector, a block that came back from a job with a gouge — any of these forces an immediate status change with the printed due date untouched and irrelevant. The register needs a one-tap way for a technician to flag an asset suspect from the field, because the alternative is the instrument riding along to the next job while the office waits for the annual date to catch the problem.

sections.heading: Out-of-cal: quarantine that blocks, not a color that warns
paragraphs: The difference between tracking and control is what happens the day after a due date passes. A spreadsheet turns a cell red; control means the asset's status flips to out-of-cal and the scheduling system refuses to assign it — the dispatcher building tomorrow's UT crew cannot attach that serial number to the job, the same way a certification gate refuses an expired technician. The digital state gets a physical twin: a quarantine tag on the unit and a quarantine shelf away from the ready kits.

Quarantine also covers the in-between states: sent-to-lab, awaiting certificate review, limited-use. The certificate-review state is worth modeling explicitly — a unit back from the lab is not automatically fit for use until someone reads the certificate's as-found data. As-found out-of-tolerance is exactly the trigger for the recall review of prior work, and a workflow that auto-restores status on the unit's physical return will skip the one reading of the certificate that matters most.

sections.heading: The recall review: reverse traceability
paragraphs: When a certificate comes back reading as-found out-of-tolerance, the question stops being about the instrument and starts being about the work: every reading that unit produced since its last good calibration is now suspect. Answering it requires reverse traceability — the register linked to job records, so one query returns every job, report number, and client that serial number touched inside the exposure window. Shops without per-job equipment logging reconstruct this from technicians' memories and truck sheets, in front of a deadline, with a client waiting.

The disposition itself belongs to a Level III: how far out of tolerance, in which direction, against what acceptance margins. A thickness gauge reading a few thousandths heavy is a different conversation from one reading heavy on a corrosion survey where readings sat at minimum wall. The software's role is the evidence package — affected jobs, the readings, the certificate — and the record that the review happened, was signed, and reached the client where notification was owed. That signed record is what closes the finding at the next audit.

sections.heading: Certificates: storage that survives an audit
paragraphs: A calibration certificate answers four questions: who calibrated the item, against what reference standards, what the as-found and as-left conditions were, and when it is due again. Storage that works means one record per calibration event, attached to the asset, with the certificate PDF plus its key fields — lab, certificate number, dates, as-found status — extracted into searchable data. The as-found field earns its keep: filed-and-forgotten out-of-tolerance certificates are how a shop learns about a recall obligation a year late, from an auditor.

The retrieval standard to design for: given a job number, produce the certificates for every asset used on that job, valid as of the job dates, in minutes. That query joins the asset register to per-job usage records, which is why folder trees named by year and instrument cannot answer it no matter how tidy they look. If you are formalizing what a certificate itself should contain, /resources/calibration-certificate-template breaks the required fields down line by line.

sections.heading: ISO/IEC 17025 and what clients actually expect
paragraphs: ISO/IEC 17025 accredits laboratories, not inspection contractors — but it shapes what your clients expect from your equipment program anyway. The working expectations: instruments calibrated by accredited labs, measurement traceability running back to NIST, documented control of equipment found nonconforming, and records that hold the whole chain together. Client auditors apply that frame to NDT contractors whether the formal audit basis is a quality manual, an ASNT-based program, or a corporate supplier standard.

The practical consequences: buy calibrations from accredited labs and keep the accreditation scope with the certificate, because an accredited lab calibrating outside its scope is a finding you inherit. Reference your own written procedure's actual requirements and the code sections your work is performed to, rather than dressing procedures up with clause citations nobody verified. A register organized around traceable certificates, logged verifications, and nonconformance control answers audits from any direction without pretending to an accreditation you do not hold.

sections.heading: The audit questions a client asks — and the report answering each
paragraphs: Audit questions about calibration follow a pattern, and each one maps to a report the software either produces in seconds or does not produce at all. Show me your equipment list with calibration status — the register, filtered live. How do you prevent use of overdue equipment — the quarantine gate, demonstrated on screen. Show me the certificate for this serial number — one click from the asset record. What equipment was used on this job — the per-job usage log.

The harder half: what happened the last time a unit came back out-of-tolerance — the recall review record, signed and dated. How do you verify between calibrations — the field verification log. Who decides your intervals — the written procedure, cited by the register's interval field. An answer that begins with someone opening a spreadsheet and scrolling is scored as a weakness even when the data eventually surfaces; the auditor is grading the system, not the search skills.

sections.heading: Why this is an ERP module, not another spreadsheet
paragraphs: Every capability above is a join between calibration data and something else: quarantine joins the register to scheduling, recall joins it to jobs, audit retrieval joins it to documents, field verification joins it to mobile data capture. Spreadsheets hold the register but cannot make the joins, which is why spreadsheet tracking works right up until the first out-of-tolerance certificate — and then fails all at once, in front of a client.

Atlantis builds this as the equipment module of its Odoo-based ERP for NDT companies — the register, three-clock due dates, quarantine gating on dispatch, per-job usage capture from the field app, and certificate storage with as-found flags — sharing data with the personnel-certification and job-costing modules beside it. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable. A demo against your own equipment list is available on request, and it is the fastest way to see the recall query run.

faq.q: Can calibration tracking work with equipment spread across trucks and site trailers?
faq.a: Yes — the register carries a location or kit assignment per asset, updated by check-out and check-in from the field app. That location trail is what makes the per-job usage log real: the recall query and the audit answer both depend on knowing which truck and which job held the serial number on a given date.

faq.q: What calibration intervals should we set for each asset class?
faq.a: Intervals come from your written procedure, the manufacturer's recommendation, and the codes your work runs under — the software enforces them, it does not choose them. Set the certificate interval per asset class, add per-use verifications where the governing code requires them, and shorten any interval whose as-found history shows drift. As-found data is the honest input for interval decisions.

faq.q: How does the software handle rental or client-supplied equipment?
faq.a: The same register, with an ownership flag. On receipt, the current certificate is verified and attached before the item becomes assignable; the return date acts as a hard due date. Rented flaw detectors used on your reports carry exactly the same traceability obligation as owned ones, so they cannot live outside the system.

faq.q: Does out-of-cal quarantine apply to calibration blocks too?
faq.a: Yes. A block that fails dimensional verification or takes visible damage quarantines exactly like an instrument, and triggers the same reverse-traceability question: which setups were verified on this block since its last good check. Blocks skip this treatment in most shops, which is why auditors have learned to ask about them specifically.

faq.q: What reports should the system produce for an ISO 9001 or client audit?
faq.a: Five: the live register with status per asset, a due-in-30/60/90 forecast, per-job equipment usage for any job number, out-of-tolerance history with signed dispositions, and certificate retrieval per asset. If a candidate system cannot produce all five without exporting to Excel first, the audit will still run on Excel — with the same old risks.

title: NDT Certification Tracking: The Tech-Method-Level Matrix
description: Tracking NDT technician certifications under SNT-TC-1A — the expiry matrix per method and level, annual vision tests, OJT hours, and the crew-assignment gate.
h1: Personnel Certification Tracking for NDT Technicians
answer: NDT certification tracking software maintains a matrix of every technician against every method and level — UT II, MT II, RT I — each cell carrying its own expiry date under the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice. Layered on top: annual near-vision exams, color-vision records, and OJT hour accumulation toward the next level. The assignment gate blocks scheduling any technician whose required credential lapses before the job ends.
expansion: Under SNT-TC-1A, certification belongs to the employer, not the technician — which means every US inspection company runs its own certification system and owns the paperwork burden that comes with it. One technician certified UT Level II, MT Level II, and PT Level II is three certification records, three expiry dates, one annual near-vision exam, a color-vision record, and a running OJT ledger toward RT. Multiply by twenty technicians and the matrix holds well over a hundred live dates, any one of which can invalidate a report if it lapses mid-job. Certification tracking software binds the matrix to the company's written practice, alerts ahead of every expiry, and — the part spreadsheets never do — gates crew assignment, refusing to schedule a technician onto work their current credentials do not cover through the job's end date. Cell by cell, that is the difference between an audit finding and a clean one.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended practice; ANSI/ASNT CP-189; Atlantis NDT outsourced ASNT Level III consulting practice

facets.q: What does the certification expiry matrix actually look like?
facets.a: Rows are technicians; columns are method-level pairs — UT II, MT II, PT II, RT I, VT II; each cell holds an expiry date and a status. A twenty-technician shop running five methods manages a hundred-cell matrix before counting vision exams, radiation-safety cards, and site badges. Software renders it as a heat map — green current, amber inside the warning window, red lapsed — so the renewal pipeline plans itself off one screen.

facets.q: How is SNT-TC-1A certification different from ISO 9712?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A is employer-based: your company certifies its own technicians under its own written practice, and the certification dies when the technician leaves. ISO 9712 is central certification — a body certifies the person, portably. US industry runs on the employer model, which is exactly why tracking software matters here: every US inspection company is its own certifying body, holding examination records, OJT ledgers, and expiry dates that no external registry maintains for it.

facets.q: How should annual vision examinations be tracked?
facets.a: As a separate credential per technician with its own expiry, because it lapses independently of every method certification and takes all of them down with it. SNT-TC-1A-based written practices call for near-vision acuity examination annually, with color and contrast differentiation testing at the interval the written practice sets. The tracker alerts ahead of the date, stores the examination record, and gates assignment the day it lapses — a lapsed eye exam grounds the technician, not one method.

facets.q: How does software accumulate OJT hours toward the next level?
facets.a: Hours flow from timesheets: each time entry tagged with a method becomes creditable experience against the trainee's running total, split by method, with the supervising Level II or III identified. The ledger shows hours-to-date against the requirement in the written practice, so the Level III sees exactly when a trainee becomes examinable. Hand-built OJT logs assembled at exam time are the alternative, and they are the records auditors challenge first.

facets.q: What is the crew-assignment gate?
facets.a: A scheduling rule that answers one question before a technician lands on a job: does this person hold every credential the job's methods require, valid through the job's end date, not just its start? The gate checks method certifications, vision status, radiation-safety credentials for RT, and site badges, and refuses the assignment on any miss. The end-date check is the part manual scheduling gets wrong — a certification expiring mid-turnaround fails silently until the client's auditor finds it.

facets.q: Why does the written practice drive the software configuration?
facets.a: Because under SNT-TC-1A the written practice is the law of your certification program — it fixes training hours, experience hours, examination composition, vision requirements, and recertification intervals for your company. The software must be configured from that document, not from a vendor's defaults: intervals, warning windows, OJT targets, and gate rules all trace to written-practice sections. Version-bind each certification to the practice edition it was issued under; when the practice is revised, the bindings show which certifications need review.

sections.heading: One technician is a stack of expiry dates
paragraphs: Start with one real technician: UT Level II, MT Level II, PT Level II, working toward RT. That is three method certifications, each with its own expiry under the written practice, an annual near-vision examination, a color-vision record, an OJT ledger accumulating radiography hours, plus a TWIC card and two client site orientations. Nine live credentials, six of which can ground him — and every US inspection company holds a stack like this for every technician on the payroll, because under SNT-TC-1A the company itself is the certifying body.

Scale that to a crew of twenty and the matrix crosses a hundred cells of method certifications alone before the vision exams and badges are counted. The failure mode is never ignorance — every Level III knows what the written practice requires. It is arithmetic at scale: some cell in the matrix is red today, and finding it requires checking all of them. That is a software problem, and the near-total absence of credible products addressing it is the gap this page maps.

Rendered properly, the matrix is one screen: technicians down the side, method-level pairs across the top, each cell colored by status with the expiry date visible — green current, amber inside the warning window sized to real renewal lead times, red lapsed. That single view answers the operational question (who can I send tomorrow) and the planning question (whose renewals cluster next quarter) at once, and it is the first screen a client auditor should be shown.

sections.heading: SNT-TC-1A: the employer is the certifying body
paragraphs: The US answer first: American industry certifies NDT personnel under the employer-based model of SNT-TC-1A, ASNT's recommended practice, or its mandatory-language sibling ANSI/ASNT CP-189 where contracts invoke it. The employer writes a written practice, trains and examines its own people, and issues certifications valid only inside that company. When a technician changes employers, the new company certifies them again under its own practice. Aerospace runs the parallel NAS 410 framework; the structure — employer responsibility, controlled document, per-method certification — is the same shape.

Contrast ISO 9712, the central-certification scheme common outside the United States: a certification body examines the person and the credential travels with them. Under that model, a registry tracks expiry for you. Under the US model, nobody outside your company tracks anything — the examination records, the OJT evidence, the vision results, and every expiry date exist only in your files. Employer certification is why certification tracking software is not an optional convenience for a US inspection contractor; it is the certifying body's own record system.

sections.heading: The written practice is the configuration file
paragraphs: Every number the software enforces comes out of one document. The written practice fixes, for your company: initial training hours per method and level, experience hours, examination structure and grading, vision-examination requirements and frequency, interruption-of-service rules, and recertification intervals — with three-year and five-year cycles both standard choices for Levels I and II. Configuring the tracker means transcribing those decisions faithfully: interval per method-level pair, warning windows sized to renewal lead times, OJT targets per method, and the gate rules that act on them.

Bind the versions. Certifications issued under revision C of the written practice should carry that fact on the record, because when revision D tightens an experience requirement, the audit question becomes which certifications were issued under which rules. A tracker that stores the practice edition on each certification record answers in one query. This is also where a Level III earns their retainer: Atlantis's outsourced Level III service maintains written practices and their software bindings for contractors who do not keep a Level III on staff.

sections.heading: Vision examinations: the annual date that grounds everyone
paragraphs: Near-vision acuity is examined annually under SNT-TC-1A-based written practices, and color and contrast differentiation at the interval the practice sets. The operational teeth: a lapsed vision exam does not suspend one method — it suspends the technician, because every method's certification presumes current vision. In the matrix it is a row-level credential, one date that turns every cell in the technician's row red at once, which is exactly why it deserves its own alert stream rather than a note in a personnel file.

Tracking it well means treating the exam as a first-class record: examination date, examiner, the test used, corrected or uncorrected, result, and next-due date. Batch the renewals — an annual company-wide vision day collapses twenty individual expiry dates into one scheduled event, with stragglers visible on the matrix afterward. Size the alert window to how the exams are actually delivered: thirty days is workable when a visit to the occupational clinic closes the gap the same week.

sections.heading: OJT hours: the ledger that starts before the certification exists
paragraphs: Experience accumulation is the untracked half of certification. A trainee's creditable hours accrue shift by shift, per method, under documented supervision, until the written practice's requirement is met and examination becomes possible. The clean implementation ties the ledger to timesheets: a time entry tagged UT on a job under a named Level II supervisor is one creditable increment, captured the day it happened. The alternative — reconstructing two years of hours from memory at exam time — produces exactly the OJT logs auditors challenge first.

The ledger should show, per trainee per method: hours to date, hours required, projected examination date at the current pace, and the supervision trail behind every entry. That projection is workforce planning — it tells the operations manager which month a fourth UT Level II appears and whether the RT pipeline is empty. The hour requirements themselves come from the written practice, built from SNT-TC-1A's recommended tables; /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method breaks those requirements down method by method.

sections.heading: The crew-assignment gate: can this tech legally do this job today?
paragraphs: The gate is one question asked automatically at scheduling time: can this technician legally perform this work, today and through the job's end date? Decomposed: does the job's method-level requirement match a current certification; is the vision examination current; for RT, are the radiation-safety credential and dosimetry in place; does the site require badges or orientations the technician holds. Any miss blocks the assignment with the reason displayed — not a warning to click through, a block, for the same reason out-of-cal instruments leave the assignable pool.

The end-date clause is the difference between a gate and a report. A four-week turnaround assigned to a technician whose UT II expires in week three passes every start-date check and fails on site — mid-job, when replacement means demobilizing one person and qualifying another. The gate evaluates expiry against the job's whole window and either blocks the assignment or drives the renewal to happen first. Every report signed by a technician whose certification had lapsed becomes a client-notification conversation; the gate exists so that conversation never starts.

sections.heading: Audit day: what the client's Level III pulls
paragraphs: Certification audits run on sampling: pick two technicians from last month's jobs, produce the files. A complete pull per technician: the current certifications with issue and expiry dates, the examination records behind each — general, specific, practical, with scores and the administering Level III — the vision-examination record, the OJT evidence supporting the level held, and the written-practice edition each certification was issued under. The software's test is producing that pack in minutes, assembled from records that already existed rather than gathered overnight before the audit.

The sharper questions target the seams. Show me anyone who performed work in the gap between expiry and renewal — a query joining certifications to job assignments, and the exact query a company without assignment-gating dreads. Show me the written practice in force in March of last year — version binding again. Auditors who find clean answers to the seam questions shorten the audit, because the sampling is a proxy for whether the system runs itself or runs on heroics.

sections.heading: The renewal pipeline: where tracking meets training
paragraphs: Tracking expiry dates without a renewal pipeline is just scheduled bad news. The working loop: the matrix's amber band feeds a renewals queue; the queue drives examination scheduling and refresher training; completions write back to the matrix. Recertification under the written practice — by examination or by the continuing-performance evidence the practice specifies per level — gets planned in the quarter before expiry and batched where renewals cluster, so the Level III administers one exam session instead of five.

Atlantis runs both sides of that loop: the certification-tracking module inside its Odoo-based NDT ERP, and the Level I, II, and III training programs that feed the renewals queue — see /corporate-ndt-training for the employer-side programs. The combination closes the loop the matrix exposes: the software finds the red cells coming, and the training calendar erases them before they arrive. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable, with a demo of the matrix built against your own roster available on request.

faq.q: Does the software handle CP-189 and NAS 410 programs as well as SNT-TC-1A?
faq.a: Yes — all three share the same structure: employer certification against a controlled document. What changes between them is the content of the requirements, not the shape of the tracking. The engine is identical; the configuration transcribes whichever document governs, and a shop serving both industrial and aerospace clients runs both rule sets side by side.

faq.q: What happens to certifications when a technician leaves or joins?
faq.a: Employer-based certifications terminate on departure — they do not travel. A new hire enters as a candidate: documented prior training and experience can credit toward hour requirements where your written practice allows it, but examination and certification happen under your practice before they work unsupervised. The software models this as an onboarding state with its own checklist, not as a transferred certification.

faq.q: Can it track site-specific credentials like TWIC cards and client orientations?
faq.a: Yes. Site credentials sit alongside method certifications as separate credential types with their own cycles — TWIC on its five-year federal cycle, client orientations on whatever the site dictates. The assignment gate checks them only when the job's site requires them, so a missing refinery orientation blocks that refinery's jobs without touching the technician's shop availability.

faq.q: How far ahead should expiry warnings fire?
faq.a: Size each window to its renewal lead time rather than setting one global number. A vision exam closes in a week, so thirty days is comfortable. A recertification examination needs the Level III scheduled and refresher training delivered, so ninety days is the working minimum. Radiation-safety renewals with external examinations deserve longer still. Per-credential windows are a configuration item, and the written practice's renewal provisions are the input.

faq.q: We track all this in Excel today — what breaks first?
faq.a: The join. Excel holds the dates but cannot see the job schedule, so the assignment gate does not exist — and the first failure is a technician on site with a credential the spreadsheet knew was lapsed. The second failure is OJT reconstruction at exam time. Both are joins between certification data and operations data, which is exactly what a spreadsheet cannot maintain and an ERP module exists to do.

title: NAS 410 vs SNT-TC-1A: 4x the Training Hours in Surface Methods
description: NAS 410 requires 16 penetrant training hours where SNT-TC-1A recommends 4. Side-by-side hours tables, exam-timing rules, and a contract-type decision matrix.
h1: NAS 410 or SNT-TC-1A: Which Standard Binds Your NDT Program?
answer: NAS 410 is a mandatory aerospace standard; SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice your written practice can tailor. The training gap sits in surface methods: penetrant Level 1 takes 16 formal hours under NAS 410 against 4 under SNT-TC-1A 2020 — 32 versus 12 cumulative to Level 2. UT, ET and RT match at 40 hours per level. Aerospace flow-downs bind NAS 410; ASME, API and AWS work follows SNT-TC-1A.
expansion: NAS 410, published by the Aerospace Industries Association and harmonized with EN 4179, sets mandatory minimums for NDT personnel on aerospace hardware; SNT-TC-1A is ASNT's recommended practice, and the employer's written practice gives it force. The measurable gap is formal training in surface methods: penetrant needs 16 hours at Level 1 under NAS 410 versus 4 under SNT-TC-1A 2020, and 32 versus 12 cumulative to Level 2; magnetic particle runs 32 versus 20. Ultrasonic, eddy current and single-format radiography match at 40 hours per level. NAS 410 also times examinations — the specific exam only after 75% of experience hours, the practical only after 100% — and requires structured, documented courses. Which document binds you is a contract question: aerospace prime flow-downs and Nadcap audits invoke NAS 410, while ASME, API and AWS fabrication work references SNT-TC-1A. Dual-market shops run to the stricter standard.
source: NAS 410 Revision 5 (Aerospace Industries Association, September 2020); ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020 edition), Table 6.3.1A
