facets.q: Which standard applies to aerospace NDT work in the United States?
facets.a: NAS 410, published by the Aerospace Industries Association and harmonized with EN 4179. Prime contractors flow it down through purchase-order quality clauses, and Nadcap NDT audits verify compliance against it. SNT-TC-1A does not satisfy an aerospace flow-down: its surface-method training hours fall below NAS 410 minimums, so an SNT-TC-1A-only certificate fails aerospace audit on hours alone.

facets.q: How many training hours does NAS 410 require for penetrant testing?
facets.a: 16 formal hours for Level 1 and 16 more for Level 2 — 32 cumulative; a candidate certifying directly to Level 2 owes the full doubled total up front. SNT-TC-1A 2020 recommends 4 and 8 hours for the same levels, 12 cumulative, making penetrant the method with the largest training-hour multiple between the two documents.

facets.q: Is SNT-TC-1A mandatory or only recommended?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice. It binds no one until an employer adopts it through a written practice, and that written practice can modify the recommended hours with documented technical justification. Codes give it teeth indirectly: ASME, API and AWS documents reference certification per SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, so contract compliance still requires a conforming program.

facets.q: Can one written practice cover both NAS 410 and SNT-TC-1A?
facets.a: Yes — one document with a branched hours table is the lower-maintenance structure, since vision, recertification and exam mechanics largely align. Aerospace personnel certify against the NAS 410 columns; industrial personnel against SNT-TC-1A. Each certificate must name its governing standard, and training records must meet NAS 410's course-documentation bar for any hours claimed on the aerospace side.

facets.q: When can a NAS 410 candidate take the specific and practical exams?
facets.a: The specific examination is administered after the candidate has logged at least 75% of the required experience hours, and the practical examination only after 100%. SNT-TC-1A has no equivalent sequencing rule. The gate makes a current, signed OJT log a prerequisite for exam scheduling on aerospace programs, not an after-the-fact formality.

facets.q: How do experience hours compare between the two standards?
facets.a: Surface methods: NAS 410 totals 400 penetrant and 530 magnetic-particle hours to Level 2, against SNT-TC-1A's 210 and 280 in-method — though SNT-TC-1A's total-NDT column reaches the same 400 and 530. Volumetric methods invert: SNT-TC-1A's 840 in-method UT hours exceed NAS 410's 800, inside a 1,600-hour total-NDT demand.

sections.heading: Two documents, two kinds of authority
paragraphs: NAS 410 is published by the Aerospace Industries Association as a National Aerospace Standard, and it is written in requirement language: once a prime contract or purchase order invokes it, its minimums become contractual obligations that auditors check line by line. It is technically harmonized with EN 4179, its European counterpart, so multinational aerospace programs treat the two as interchangeable. SNT-TC-1A is a different kind of document — ASNT publishes it as a recommended practice, and its tables carry no force until an employer adopts them.

The instrument that gives SNT-TC-1A its force is the employer's written practice. The company documents how it trains, examines and certifies each level in each method, and it can adjust the recommended hours where it can justify the change with technical rationale. NAS 410 removes that discretion. An aerospace employer's written practice must meet or exceed the standard's minimums, and both prime-customer auditors and Nadcap treat any shortfall as a nonconformance rather than a judgment call.

That difference in posture explains nearly every numeric difference between the two hour tables. A recommended practice can publish a floor and trust each employer to build on it where the work demands more. A flowed-down aerospace requirement bakes the conservatism into the numbers themselves, because fracture-critical hardware leaves no room for a thin training file. Read the comparison table on this page with that context in mind.

sections.heading: The headline gap: surface-method training hours
paragraphs: Liquid penetrant carries the largest multiple. NAS 410 Revision 5 requires 16 hours of formal training at Level 1 where SNT-TC-1A 2020 Table 6.3.1A recommends 4 — four times as much before a trainee reaches the first exam. Cumulative to Level 2 the gap is 32 hours against 12, roughly triple. For the method many shops treat as the easy one, the aerospace standard demands the most disproportionate classroom investment.

Magnetic particle follows the same pattern at lower intensity: 16 hours versus 12 at Level 1, and 32 versus 20 cumulative to Level 2. The volumetric methods converge. Ultrasonic, eddy current and single-format radiography all require 40 hours per level under both documents, so a UT technician's classroom path is identical whichever standard governs. The one volumetric exception is radiography covering both film and non-film techniques, where NAS 410 raises the requirement to 60 hours per level.

Direct entry to Level 2 changes the arithmetic, not the ratio. NAS 410 doubles the training requirement for a candidate certifying to Level 2 without prior Level 1; SNT-TC-1A states that a direct Level II must complete the sum of both levels' hours. Either way the cumulative columns in the table on this page are the honest comparison. Per-method detail for every technique sits in /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

sections.heading: Experience hours: closer than the training gap suggests
paragraphs: Surface methods show a real but smaller experience gap. NAS 410 requires 130 penetrant hours at Level 1 plus 270 more for Level 2 — 400 total. SNT-TC-1A recommends 70 plus 140 in-method, but layers a separate demand on top: 400 total NDT hours for PT certification. Magnetic particle lands the same way: NAS 410 totals 530 hours to Level 2, and SNT-TC-1A's total-NDT column for MT is also 530.

In the volumetric methods the tables invert. NAS 410 asks 200 hours at Level 1 and 600 more at Level 2 for UT and ET — 800 total. SNT-TC-1A recommends 210 plus 630 in-method, 840 hours, inside a 1,600-hour total-NDT requirement. The industrial recommended practice demands more seat time in UT than the aerospace standard does. The divergence is philosophical: NAS 410 front-loads rigor into structured training, SNT-TC-1A into accumulated bench hours.

Radiography under NAS 410 runs in ranges because the standard splits film and non-film techniques: 200 to 220 hours at Level 1 and 600 to 780 additional at Level 2, depending on the formats held. Whichever scheme you run, none of these hours exist unless they were logged and signed as they were earned — the documentation rules, entry formats and reconstruction paths live in /blog/ndt-ojt-hours-log-requirements.

sections.heading: Two rules only NAS 410 has
paragraphs: NAS 410 sequences its examinations against the experience log. The specific examination is administered only after the candidate has accumulated at least 75% of the required experience hours, and the practical only after 100%. SNT-TC-1A imposes no such gate; an employer can examine a trainee on whatever schedule its written practice sets. On an aerospace program, an out-of-sequence exam date next to an incomplete hours log is an audit finding waiting to be written.

Training delivery is the second structural rule. NAS 410 expects formal, documented courses with defined outlines and qualified instructors, approved within the employer's program — informal shop-floor familiarization does not satisfy the hour counts. SNT-TC-1A describes recommended course content but leaves delivery format to the written practice. Both documents require near-vision examinations on an annual cycle, so vision files rarely separate the two programs in practice; training evidence separates them constantly.

sections.heading: Which standard binds you: the contract decides
paragraphs: Stop asking which document is better and read your purchase orders. If you machine, weld, process or inspect hardware that ends up on an airframe or engine, the prime's quality clauses flow NAS 410 (or EN 4179) down to you, and Nadcap NDT audits will verify compliance against it. Defense subcontracts under the major aerospace primes carry the same flow-down. Your preference does not enter into it — the contract names the standard.

Everything else in US heavy industry runs on the ASNT documents. ASME Code fabrication, B31 piping, API 510, 570 and 653 plant-inspection NDT, and AWS D1.1 structural work all reference employer-based certification per SNT-TC-1A — or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, its mandatory-language sibling, when the contract names it. Nuclear work under ASME Section XI is the notable case where CP-189 rather than SNT-TC-1A is the expected basis for the program.

For a shop serving both markets, the asymmetry is the decision: a technician trained and certified to NAS 410 minimums meets or exceeds every SNT-TC-1A training recommendation in the surface methods, while the reverse fails aerospace audit on hours alone. Dual-market shops certify to the stricter table once instead of maintaining two shortfalls. The full aerospace requirement set — vision, exams, interrupted-service rules — is broken down at /nas-410-certification-requirements.

sections.heading: The Level 3 divide
paragraphs: NAS 410 concentrates program authority in a named Responsible Level 3: the individual who approves the written practice, procedures, training materials and examinations, and who answers to prime customers and Nadcap auditors for the program's technical health. Small and mid-size aerospace suppliers rarely carry that role on payroll, which is why the contracted outside-agency model exists — the scope, accountability and engagement structure are detailed at /consulting/nas-410-responsible-level-3.

SNT-TC-1A assigns a Level III comparable duties — preparing the written practice, approving procedures, administering examinations — but leaves the employer wide latitude in how the role is staffed and evidenced. An ASNT NDT Level III certificate is the conventional basis for the role in both worlds. The practical difference is accountability: the aerospace Responsible Level 3 signature is a contractual control point, and primes review the person, not just the paperwork.

sections.heading: Running both without doubling the paperwork
paragraphs: Dual-standard shops make one early documentation choice: two written practices, or one document with a branched hours table. One document wins on maintenance — vision requirements, recertification intervals, exam structures and grading largely align between the standards, so a single spine with NAS 410 columns for aerospace personnel keeps revisions in one place. Each certificate must state which standard it was issued under; a certificate that names neither fails both audits.

Cross-crediting is where merged programs go wrong. Training hours delivered as an approved NAS 410 course credit cleanly toward SNT-TC-1A qualification, but hours logged under an unstructured SNT-TC-1A program cannot be claimed backward into a NAS 410 file without course documentation and instructor records. Build the training file to the aerospace evidentiary standard from day one, and both certificates draw from the same folder without a finding.

sections.heading: What the delta costs — and where to get help
paragraphs: Price the gap in schedule, not sentiment. Taking a penetrant trainee to Level 2 costs 12 classroom hours under SNT-TC-1A and 32 under NAS 410 — an extra half-week per technician, multiplied across a crew, plus the course development and instructor qualification the aerospace standard obliges you to evidence. Surface-method-heavy shops feel nearly all of the difference; UT-centric shops feel almost none of it, because the volumetric tables match.

Atlantis NDT builds employer programs to either table: Level I and II method training aligned to NAS 410 or SNT-TC-1A hour requirements, written-practice authoring, and contracted Responsible Level 3 coverage for aerospace suppliers. ASNT Level III-led, affordable, accessible and fully customizable to your contract base — request a quote or a program review, and start from the standard your customers actually invoke rather than the one your last employer used.

faq.q: Is NAS 410 the same as EN 4179?
faq.a: They are twin standards maintained in technical harmony — NAS 410 by the Aerospace Industries Association in the US, EN 4179 by ASD in Europe. Requirements track each other closely, and multinational programs accept certification to either. The practical difference is oversight: EN 4179 operates with national aerospace NDT boards, while US programs run on employer certification under prime-customer and Nadcap audit.

faq.q: Does an SNT-TC-1A Level II transfer into a NAS 410 program?
faq.a: Not automatically. The receiving aerospace employer must qualify and certify the technician under its own NAS 410-compliant program, and the existing training file rarely evidences the required course structure or surface-method hours. Documented experience transfers as evidence; the certification itself does not. Expect gap training in PT and MT and a fresh examination cycle.

faq.q: What are the recertification intervals under each standard?
faq.a: Both run five-year maximum certification periods, and employers are free to impose shorter intervals in the written practice. Both also require annual near-vision examinations. Lapse handling is the sharper edge on the aerospace side: an expired NAS 410 certification means requalification under the employer's procedures before the technician touches flight hardware again.

faq.q: Which standard is harder to reach Level 2 under?
faq.a: In penetrant and magnetic particle, NAS 410 — roughly triple the cumulative classroom hours, delivered as documented formal courses. In ultrasonics, SNT-TC-1A's experience columns ask for more total bench time: 840 in-method hours against NAS 410's 800. Difficulty is method-shaped: aerospace surface-method technicians face the steeper training path, industrial UT technicians the longer experience path.

faq.a: Yes. Atlantis provides contracted Responsible Level 3 services for aerospace suppliers — written-practice authoring, procedure and training approval, examination administration and audit representation — alongside Level I and II training built to NAS 410 hour tables. Engagements are affordable, accessible and fully customizable; request a quote through /consulting/nas-410-responsible-level-3.

title: NDT OJT Hours: What Counts, Who Signs, How to Log Them
description: What counts as NDT on-the-job experience, the fields a compliant log entry needs, who signs it, and how to rebuild undocumented hours with employer attestation.
h1: The OJT Hour Log That Survives an Audit — and the One That Doesn't
answer: OJT hours are supervised, hands-on time performing the method — setup, calibration, scanning, interpretation and reporting — not classroom study or site standby. A compliant log entry records date, hours, method and technique, equipment, the part and procedure, the activity performed, and a certified Level II or III supervisor's signature. Undocumented hours can be reconstructed through inspection reports, job travelers and a signed employer attestation.
expansion: OJT hours are the documented, supervised, hands-on portion of NDT qualification — the number SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, NAS 410 and ISO 9712 all demand before certification, and the number candidates most often cannot prove. Creditable time covers surface preparation, equipment setup, calibration, data acquisition, evaluation against acceptance criteria and report writing performed under a certified Level II or III. Classroom and e-learning hours count as training, never experience; standby time counts as nothing. A defensible log entry carries date, hours, method, technique, equipment ID, part and procedure reference, the activity performed, and the supervisor's signature and certification level. When years went unlogged, hours are rebuilt from inspection reports, job travelers and timesheets, then bound by a signed employer attestation a Level III reviews and accepts. Under NAS 410 the log gates the exams themselves: specific exam at 75% of hours, practical at 100%.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020 edition, Table 6.3.1A; 2024 edition, para. 6.4); NAS 410 Rev 5 (September 2020); ASNT NDT Level III eligibility criteria, certification.asnt.org

facets.q: What activities count toward NDT OJT experience hours?
facets.a: Hands-on, supervised performance of the method: part preparation and setup, instrument calibration and standardization, data acquisition, evaluation of indications against acceptance criteria, and preparation of the resulting report. Production work carries the most audit weight; supervised laboratory and mock-up work counts to the extent the employer's written practice defines. Observation without performance earns nothing.

facets.q: Does classroom or online training count as experience?
facets.a: No. Training hours and experience hours are separate tables in every scheme — SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, NAS 410 and ISO 9712 list them independently, and an hour sits in only one column. E-learning, seminars and instructor-led courses accrue to the training requirement. SNT-TC-1A 2024's paragraph 6.4 lets a written practice credit a defined percentage of laboratory practical time against extended experience recommendations — practical time, not coursework.

facets.q: Who is qualified to sign an OJT log entry?
facets.a: The certified Level II or Level III who supervised the work, in the same method, identified by name and certification level. The signature asserts that the activity occurred, the hours are accurate and the supervision was qualified. A quality manager without method certification can countersign employment facts but cannot validate method supervision. The candidate signs each entry as well.

facets.q: How many experience hours does SNT-TC-1A recommend per method?
facets.a: In-method: PT 70 hours for Level I plus 140 for Level II; MT 70 plus 210; UT, RT and ET 210 plus 630 each; VT 70 plus 140. On top of these sit total-NDT-hour requirements: 400 for PT and VT, 530 for MT, and 1,600 for UT, RT and ET (SNT-TC-1A 2020, Table 6.3.1A).

facets.q: Can undocumented hours from a previous employer be recovered?
facets.a: Yes, through reconstruction: gather inspection reports, travelers and timesheets that anchor the period, build a conservative method-split estimate, and bind it with a signed attestation from that employer's Level III or quality authority. The current program's Level III reviews and accepts the package into the certification file. Self-declared hours with no corroborating artifact are rejected across every scheme.

facets.q: What does NAS 410 require of the log before exams?
facets.a: Currency. NAS 410 administers the specific examination only after at least 75% of required experience hours are logged and the practical examination only after 100%, so exam scheduling is blocked until the signed log proves the threshold. That sequencing makes month-end batch logging an operational problem on aerospace programs, not just an audit-day one.

sections.heading: The silent gap that stalls Level III candidacies
paragraphs: ASNT's Level III eligibility is arithmetic: one year of Level II-comparable NDT experience with a four-year engineering or physical-science degree, two years with two academic years of study, four years with neither — and every month of it must be certified by an employer on the application. Candidates rarely fail the arithmetic. They fail the evidence, because the hours were worked across three employers and logged contemporaneously by none of them.

The same file gates every scheme below Level III. SNT-TC-1A's experience tables, CP-189's mandatory equivalents, NAS 410's per-method hour counts and ISO 9712's employer-verified experience all assume a contemporaneous record exists. When it does not, certification stalls — not because the candidate lacks competence, but because nobody can prove where the hours came from. The certification pathway itself is mapped at /asnt-certification; this page owns the log that carries you along it.

sections.heading: What counts as OJT — and what never does
paragraphs: Creditable experience is hands-on performance of the method under qualified supervision: surface preparation and part setup, instrument calibration and standardization, data acquisition and scanning, evaluation of indications against acceptance criteria, and writing or assisting with the resulting report. Time spent performing NDT on production hardware carries the most audit weight, and written practices commonly recognize supervised mock-up and laboratory work as a defined share of the total.

Four categories never count as experience. Classroom and e-learning time is training — a separate table with separate hours. Standby, travel and site-induction time is nothing, even on an inspection contract. Unsupervised practice by an uncertified trainee fails the supervision requirement. And general QC duties — dimensional checks, document review, paint inspection — sit outside the method regardless of who performed them. Logs padded with these categories are the ones auditors unravel first.

SNT-TC-1A 2024 formalized one useful credit: a new paragraph 6.4 recognizes a percentage of direct practical laboratory experience against the extended experience recommendations in its tables. That is a written-practice decision, not an automatic entitlement — the employer's document must adopt it and define the percentage before anyone claims it. Candidates working under older written practices gain nothing from the 2024 text until the employer revises and reissues its document.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a log entry that survives audit
paragraphs: A defensible entry answers five questions without a follow-up phone call: when, what method, on what equipment and part, doing what, witnessed by whom. The table on this page shows the seven fields that answer them, with copy-ready examples. Every field ties the entry to a record an auditor can independently pull — a calibration certificate, a work order, a controlled procedure — and that traceability is what separates evidence from assertion.

Granularity matters as much as content. Same-day or same-week entries in mixed handwriting or timestamped software carry credibility that a single neat month-end page never will. Round-number streaks — eight hours of UT, every day, for a year — invite exactly the scrutiny they deserve. Log the real number, including the 2.5-hour days, and the file reads like what it is: a contemporaneous record of a working technician rather than a reverse-engineered total.

sections.heading: Who signs, and what the signature asserts
paragraphs: The supervising signature belongs to the certified individual who directed the work — a Level II or Level III in the same method, identified by name and certification level. That signature asserts three things: the activity happened, the hours are accurate, and the trainee worked under qualified direction. A quality manager's countersignature can close the employer's record, but it cannot substitute for method supervision the manager is not certified to provide.

The candidate signs too, and the dual signature makes retroactive falsification uncomfortable in both directions. At certification time, the employer's Level III totals the log against the written-practice table and accepts or rejects it. Under NAS 410 that acceptance happens progressively, because the specific exam is administered only after 75% of required hours are logged and the practical only after 100%. An unsigned log delays exams, which delays certification, which delays billable capability.

sections.heading: Scheme by scheme: where the rules diverge
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A leaves log format entirely to the written practice — the tables set the hours (70 experience hours for PT Level I, 210 for UT Level I, 630 more for UT Level II) and the employer defines the record. CP-189 carries the same structure in mandatory language: documentation of experience is a requirement, not a recommendation, and audits read the log as a compliance record. Full per-method hour tables live at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

NAS 410 is the strictest in practice because of its exam-sequencing rule: with the specific exam gated at 75% of hours and the practical at 100%, the log has to be current before anything can be scheduled. ISO 9712 differs in structure — a central certification body certifies, but the employer still attests documented experience, and gaps surface at application review rather than internal audit. Reconciling one log to several schemes at once is routine Level III consulting work.

sections.heading: Rebuilding undocumented hours: the attestation path
paragraphs: Reconstruction starts with objective artifacts, not memory: inspection reports bearing the candidate's name or stamp, job travelers and work orders, daily timesheets, contract assignment records, prior certificates. Each artifact anchors a period and a method. From those anchors, a defensible hour estimate is built period by period — conservative, method-split, and explicitly labeled as reconstruction rather than contemporaneous logging. The moment an estimate outruns its artifacts, the file stops being evidence and becomes a liability.

The binding document is an employer attestation: a letter on company letterhead, signed by the supervising Level III or the responsible quality authority of that era, stating employment dates, methods practiced, the basis for the hour estimate and the records consulted. The current employer's Level III then reviews the attestation, accepts it into the certification file, and notes the acceptance in the written-practice records. For ASNT Level III applications, the employer's certification of experience on the application form performs the same function and carries the same personal accountability.

When a former employer no longer exists, the fallback hierarchy is: records the candidate lawfully retained, attestation from a former supervisor as an individual with their certification history stated, and client-side records from facilities where the work was performed. A Level III weighing such a file documents the rationale for acceptance. What no scheme accepts is a self-declaration with no corroborating artifact — that is the file that ends candidacies.

sections.heading: Multi-method shifts and split hours
paragraphs: Technicians run two methods on one shift constantly — MT and PT on the same weld, UT thickness checks after visual. Hours split; they do not double. A ten-hour shift yields ten hours of experience allocated across methods in the proportion actually worked, and the log entry shows the split explicitly. Written practices that adopt concurrent multi-method experience provisions define the allocation rule; the log's job is to make that allocation auditable line by line.

The total-NDT column catches what method splitting misses. SNT-TC-1A requires both in-method hours and total NDT hours — 400 total for PT certification, 1,600 for UT — so hours worked in any method still advance the total column for every method. A candidate strong in one method and thin in the total column has a different gap than one short in-method, and the log must be structured to report both numbers on demand.

sections.heading: Make the log self-maintaining
paragraphs: The reliable fix is structural: capture hours where the work is already documented. If every inspection report records technician, method, date and duration, the OJT log becomes a query, not a chore — and reconstruction never happens again, because the artifacts and the log are the same record. Weekly supervisor sign-off inside a digital system timestamps the approval chain that paper logs imitate badly and month-end batches destroy entirely.

Atlantis NDT's reporting software captures technician, method, procedure and time on every report as native fields, so experience accrual falls out of normal reporting; our ASNT Level III consultants also run log audits and reconstruction reviews for shops with candidates blocked on evidence. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a demo, and bring your worst log to the first call. Your next Level III candidacy should stall on nothing.

faq.q: Is a payroll timesheet acceptable as an OJT log?
faq.a: As corroborating evidence, yes; as the log, no. A timesheet proves presence and duration but records no method, technique, equipment, procedure or supervising certificate holder — five of the seven fields a compliant entry needs. Pair timesheets with inspection reports during reconstruction; going forward, log method-level detail at the point of work.

faq.q: Do OJT hours expire?
faq.a: The hours persist as history; what expires is certification. Lapsed certificates trigger requalification under the employer's written practice, and reviewers of Level III applications read the recency of Level II-comparable work closely. The safe practice is a continuous log that follows the technician across employers, exported and personally retained at every job change.

faq.q: Who owns the log — the technician or the employer?
faq.a: The employer owns the certification record; the technician should own a personal copy. Employer-based schemes keep the official file, and it stays behind when you leave — the root cause of most reconstruction projects. Export or photocopy your signed log at every departure. No scheme forbids a personal duplicate, and every future Level III will thank you for it.

faq.q: How do I log hours when two methods share a shift?
faq.a: Split the shift by the actual proportion worked and write both entries with the split visible — six hours MT, two hours PT, never eight of each. Concurrent-method credit rules come from the written practice, and the total across methods can never exceed clock hours. Auditors sum entries against payroll; overlapping totals are the fastest way to lose an entire log's credibility.

faq.q: Can Atlantis NDT help reconstruct a blocked Level III candidacy?
faq.a: Yes. Our ASNT Level III consultants run evidence audits: artifact gathering, method-split hour estimation, attestation drafting for former employers, and written-practice acceptance documentation. We also set up report-integrated hour capture so the gap never reopens. Affordable, accessible and fully customizable — request a consultation with the certification records you have, however incomplete.

title: CWI vs API 577 vs NDT Level II: What Each Lets You Sign
description: Signature authority, prerequisites, exam formats and 2026 fees for AWS CWI ($1,255+), API 577 ($380) and employer-based NDT Level II — compared for US contractors.
h1: Three Credentials, Three Signatures: Choosing for a US Contracting Firm
answer: The CWI signs visual weld acceptance under AWS D1.1 and is the credential structural contracts name. An employer-certified NDT Level II signs accept/reject on UT, MT or PT reports, letting a firm self-perform inspection it now subcontracts. API 577 authorizes no signature — it is a knowledge credential that strengthens refinery bids. Exam fees: CWI $1,255 AWS-member, API 577 $380 API-member; Level II costs are employer-borne.
expansion: For a US contracting firm the three credentials answer different bid questions. The AWS CWI is a personal, portable certification that AWS D1.1 names for weld inspector qualification — structural, DOT and AISC-audited work asks for it by name, and it costs $1,255 (AWS member) to sit. An SNT-TC-1A NDT Level II is an employer certification: it lets your own technician calibrate, test and sign accept/reject on UT, MT or PT reports, converting subcontracted inspection spend into self-performed scope. API 577 is the outlier: a $380 (API member) closed-book knowledge exam with no signature authority of its own, valuable as a differentiator on refinery and turnaround bids and as a supplement to API 510/570/653 inspectors, who qualify for it automatically. Prerequisites diverge sharply — five years for a high-school CWI candidate, three for API 577, while Level II runs on logged training and experience hours.

facets.q: Which certification does structural steel work require?
facets.a: The AWS CWI. AWS D1.1 accepts a current CWI as a qualified welding inspector, and state DOTs, public owners and AISC-audited fabricators name the credential in contracts and quality manuals. Neither API 577 nor an NDT Level II substitutes for it on visual weld acceptance — Level II authority covers NDT method reports, and 577 carries no signature authority at all.

facets.q: What does API 577 qualify a person to do?
facets.a: To evidence welding-inspection and metallurgy knowledge against API RP 577 — nothing more. It authorizes no weld acceptance, no report signature and no code sign-off by itself. Its value is supplemental: API 510, 570 and 653 inspectors qualify automatically and deepen the competence behind repair decisions they already sign, and contracting firms cite it as welding depth on refinery and turnaround bids.

facets.q: What does an employer-certified NDT Level II sign?
facets.a: Accept/reject dispositions and inspection reports for the method certified — UT, MT, PT, RT, ET or VT — performed under the employer's written practice and the governing code. Certification is per method and per employer: it authorizes nothing at a new company until that employer certifies the technician under its own program. That structure makes it a company capability rather than a personal license.

facets.q: How much does each credential cost in third-party fees?
facets.a: AWS CWI: $1,255 exam fee for AWS members, $1,520 for non-members on the 2026 price list, with renewal every three years and nine-year recertification. API 577: $380 members, $440 non-members, recertification $265/$320, on a three-year term. Employer-based NDT Level II: no certification-body fee — the employer funds training hours, examinations and the written practice.

facets.q: Can one person realistically hold all three?
facets.a: Yes, and the combination is common in senior inspection roles. AWS counts NDT performed on welded products as welding-related experience, so Level II field years satisfy the CWI's experience requirement in parallel; API 577's petrochemical experience ladder overlaps the same work history. The binding constraints are exam scheduling and three separate renewal cycles — not eligibility.

facets.q: Which credential should a contracting firm fund first?
facets.a: Follow the backlog. Structural and D1.1-governed work makes the CWI the bid-qualifying credential and funds it first. Refinery mechanical work favors employer-based Level II in MT and PT for immediate self-perform margin. Firms already employing API 510/570/653 inspectors add 577 at once — automatic eligibility and a $380 member fee make it the fastest credential decision on this page.

sections.heading: 'Better ROI' is a signature question
paragraphs: Strip the marketing and each credential is a signature. The CWI signs visual weld acceptance and the inspection reports structural contracts demand. An SNT-TC-1A NDT Level II signs accept/reject on ultrasonic, magnetic-particle or penetrant results — the reports a contracting firm now pays a subcontractor to sign. API 577 signs nothing by itself; it is a knowledge credential that changes how a bid reads, not who can release work. Return on investment follows the signature, because the signature is what contracts price.

The three also live in different ownership models. CWI and API 577 are personal, portable certifications that walk out the door with the inspector. Employer-based Level II is a company asset: the certification exists inside your written practice and ends when the technician leaves, but the program that produced it keeps producing. A contracting firm buying credentials is really choosing between renting individual authority and building organizational capability.

sections.heading: AWS CWI: the contract gatekeeper
paragraphs: AWS D1.1 accepts a current CWI as a qualified welding inspector, and the public owners, DOTs and AISC-audited fabricators that govern US structural work write the credential into contracts by name. That is the CWI's ROI mechanism: jobs a firm cannot bid, or cannot self-inspect, without one on staff. The exam fee is $1,255 for AWS members and $1,520 for non-members on the 2026 price list, before any seminar costs.

The exam is three parts: Part A fundamentals at 150 questions, Part B practical at 46 questions built around a book of specifications and replica welds, and Part C open-book code application at 50 to 65 questions — 72% minimum on each part, with no averaging across parts. Certification renews every three years and requires full recertification at nine, by exam, endorsement or 80 professional development hours. Part-by-part failure patterns are broken down in /blog/cwi-pass-rate-by-part-a-b-c-breakdown.

sections.heading: API 577: the cheapest exam, and the one that signs nothing
paragraphs: API 577 certifies knowledge of welding inspection and metallurgy against API RP 577 — 110 closed-book questions, of which 100 are scored, in 3.25 hours, offered at test centers or by remote proctoring. At $380 for API members and $440 for non-members, with recertification at $265/$320 on a three-year term, it is the cheapest credential on this page by a factor of three. What it does not do is authorize anyone to accept a weld, release a repair or sign an inspection report.

Its leverage is positional. Inspectors holding current API 510, 570 or 653 certifications qualify for the 577 exam automatically, and for plant-inspection firms the endorsement deepens the weld-repair competence those authorized inspectors already sign under. For everyone else, entry runs from one year of petrochemical experience with an engineering degree to five years with no degree. On a refinery turnaround bid, 577 on the org chart reads as welding depth; on a structural bid it reads as nothing, because D1.1 work asks for the CWI.

sections.heading: NDT Level II: the self-perform revenue play
paragraphs: An employer-certified NDT Level II converts subcontracted inspection line items into self-performed scope. Under SNT-TC-1A, the Level II calibrates equipment, performs the test, interprets and evaluates results against the governing code, and signs the report — per method. The firm's written practice issues the certification after the recommended training and experience hours are met: 80 cumulative training hours and 840 in-method experience hours for UT, 12 and 210 for PT, 20 and 280 for MT under the 2020 tables.

There is no central-body fee because there is no central body: the employer funds training, examinations and the written practice, and ASNT also operates central examination programs for firms that want third-party paper behind the employer certificate. The ROI arithmetic is a utilization question — a mechanical contractor performing its own MT and PT on welds it already makes captures the inspection margin it currently pays out and removes a scheduling dependency from every job. The build-out path from welder to certified technician is mapped in /blog/welder-to-ndt-inspector-us-career-path-2026.

sections.heading: Prerequisites: who can sit tomorrow
paragraphs: CWI entry is the steepest. AWS scales required welding-related experience against education: one year with a bachelor's in welding engineering, three with engineering coursework toward a degree, five with a high-school diploma, out to twelve with less than an eighth-grade education — and welding-related work explicitly includes NDT performed on welded products, which is how NDT technicians qualify. A vision test is required at application, and the experience must be documented.

API 577 asks for petrochemical-industry experience on a shallower slope — one year with a BS in engineering or technology, two with a two-year technical degree, three with a high-school diploma, five with no formal education — and waives all of it for current API 510/570/653 holders. Employer-based Level II has no biographical entry bar at all: any trainee the employer accepts starts logging training and experience hours immediately, which makes it the only credential of the three a firm can begin building today with the workforce it already has.

sections.heading: Exam formats, compared honestly
paragraphs: The CWI is the hardest test day of the three: separate parts each pass/fail at 72%, a practical requiring inspection-tool handling against replica welds, and a code part demanding speed inside a codebook many candidates have never navigated under a clock. API 577 is one closed-book multiple-choice sitting with no practical component; a candidate with field welding-inspection background prepares for it through structured reading of RP 577 and the referenced fundamentals.

Level II examination is employer-administered under the written practice: a general exam on method theory, a specific exam on the employer's procedures and equipment, and a hands-on practical with flawed specimens, graded to a composite minimum of 80%. Difficulty tracks the Level III who builds the exams, and the credibility of the certificate tracks the rigor of the program behind it — which is exactly what customer auditors probe when they review a self-perform NDT program before awarding work.

sections.heading: ROI by firm type
paragraphs: A structural steel fabricator or erector buys the CWI first, because D1.1 work is the revenue and the CWI is the license to inspect it. Rework disputes, DOT verification inspection and AISC audit findings all resolve against a CWI's signature. A second credential only enters the picture once self-performing NDT on structural welds — ultrasonic testing on complete-joint-penetration groove welds above all — turns the Level II business case on.

A mechanical or piping contractor in refining and petrochemical flips the order: employer-based Level II in MT and PT first for immediate self-perform margin, UT next as volume justifies the longer hours path, with API 577 layered on cheaply to sharpen turnaround bids. A plant-services firm already employing API 510/570/653 inspectors takes 577 immediately — automatic eligibility, a $380 member fee and a three-year term — and treats the CWI as the strategic add for shops that also chase structural scope.

sections.heading: Stacking order for one inspector
paragraphs: For an individual building toward inspection leadership, the sequence that compounds is Level II first, CWI second, 577 third. Level II hours start accruing from the first supervised shift and produce a billable technician fastest. Five years of that work — NDT performed on welded products — simultaneously satisfies the CWI's high-school-diploma experience track, so the second credential's clock runs inside the first's. API 577 then costs one reading cycle and a $380 member fee.

The stack is more than a resume. A CWI who also signs UT reports covers both the visual acceptance and the volumetric verification on the same weld — a two-person scope in one salary — and that combination is what senior inspection roles at contracting firms are built around. The full arc from welder through technician to dual-credential inspector, with US salary bands at each step, is mapped end to end in /blog/welder-to-ndt-inspector-us-career-path-2026.

sections.heading: Where Atlantis fits
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT trains and certifies the Level II leg of the stack: method training built to SNT-TC-1A hour tables, written-practice authoring, and ASNT Level III oversight for firms standing up self-perform NDT programs — affordable, accessible and fully customizable, with a quote on request. We do not sell CWI or API exam preparation; we build the employer program those personal credentials plug into, and the audit file that survives customer review.

If the decision is live — a contract requiring a CWI signature, a subcontracted inspection line item worth self-performing, a turnaround bid that needs welding depth on the org chart — bring the contract language to a consultation. The right first credential is written in your backlog, and reading it against your crew's existing logged hours takes one session with a Level III. Request a demo or a quote through the consulting pages.

faq.q: Does API 577 replace a CWI on refinery welding work?
faq.a: No. They answer different questions: the CWI is a qualification to inspect and accept welds; API 577 evidences welding knowledge inside API's plant-inspection ecosystem. Refinery owners staff repair inspection with API-authorized inspectors under their programs, while D1.1-scoped structural work on the same site still calls for a CWI. Firms serving both markets carry both.

faq.q: Is an NDT Level II certification portable to a new employer?
faq.a: Employer-based Level II under SNT-TC-1A is not portable — the new employer must certify you under its own written practice, though your documented training and experience hours transfer as evidence and shorten the path. ASNT's central certification programs put third-party paper behind your qualifications. Keep signed copies of your hour logs and certificates at every job change.

faq.q: How long does each credential take from a standing start?
faq.a: API 577 is weeks: eligibility check, a study cycle, one 3.25-hour exam. A CWI is bounded by its experience requirement — five years with a high-school diploma, less with technical education — plus preparation for the three-part exam. Employer-based Level II sits between: cumulative training plus in-method experience hours, 12 and 210 for PT, 80 and 840 for UT, logged under supervision.

faq.q: What are the renewal obligations across the three?
faq.a: CWI: renew every three years, recertify at nine by exam, 80 professional development hours or endorsement. API 577: three-year term, recertification at $265 members / $320 non-members. Employer-based Level II: recertification on the written-practice interval — five years under SNT-TC-1A's recommendation — with annual near-vision exams throughout. Budget renewals as a program cost, not a surprise.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT provide CWI or API 577 training?
faq.a: No — Atlantis does not sell CWI or API exam preparation. We build and run the employer side: SNT-TC-1A method training to Level I and II, written practices, and ASNT Level III program oversight that lets a contracting firm self-perform and sign NDT. For firms sequencing all three credentials, our consultants map the stack against your contracts. Quote on request.

title: Interim NDT Level III Cover Before an Audit: What It Fixes
description: An audit date and no designated NDT Level III. What interim cover closes — designation, written practice, exams, audit presence — and what it cannot backdate.
h1: Interim NDT Level III cover when the audit date will not move
answer: An interim NDT Level III engagement gives a US employer designated Level III authority within days: a written designation letter, written-practice review and re-approval, examination administration and grading, and attendance at the audit. It cannot retroactively create training hours, experience, or exam records that were never generated. Certification authority stays with the employer throughout.
expansion: Interim Level III cover exists because employer-based certification is an employer function that requires a designated Level III to hold it up. SNT-TC-1A puts the written practice, the examination questions and the certification recommendation in Level III hands, and Section 13 treats an employee's certification as revoked when employment ends. A resignation therefore removes the approval authority behind every certification file at once, and the audit date does not move to accommodate it. An interim engagement restores that authority inside days rather than months. The contracted Level III accepts a written designation naming methods, scope and dates, re-reads the written practice against what the shop actually does, rebuilds and administers the examination set, restores vision currency, and stands in the room on audit day to answer for the approvals. Certification signature stays with the employer. Atlantis structures these engagements around a fixed audit date and hands off to permanent cover.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024), Sections 5, 7, 8, 9, 12 and 13; NAS 410 Rev. 5 and EN 4179 definitions of Responsible Level 3 and outside agency; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120(e) and T-120(f); ASNT NDT Level III certification scheme education, experience and examination requirements.

table.note: Durations assume records exist and are retrievable. Under SNT-TC-1A the certifying authority named in the written practice must be an employee of the firm, so certification signature remains an employer function for the whole engagement.

facets.q: Can a contracted Level III certify our technicians?
facets.a: No. Under SNT-TC-1A the certifying authority named in the written practice must be an employee of the firm. A contracted Level III administers and grades examinations, approves the question sets, and states that written-practice criteria were met. The employer signs the certification. Letting a consultant sign creates a defect harder to remediate than the vacancy it was meant to solve.

facets.q: How quickly can an interim Level III be designated?
facets.a: Designation itself takes a day: employer management signs a letter naming the individual, the methods in scope, the authorities granted and the effective dates. Useful work starts immediately. What takes longer is the written practice review, which runs five to ten working days, and examination rebuild, which runs two to four weeks per method depending on specimen availability.

facets.q: Must the interim Level III re-approve our NDT procedures?
facets.a: Yes, for every method inside the designated scope. A procedure carries the approval of a Level III who no longer holds certification, which auditors treat as an unapproved procedure. Re-approval is a technical review, not a countersignature: technique, calibration, scanning parameters, acceptance criteria and reporting are read against the code of construction and the customer specification before signature.

facets.q: What happens to certifications issued after our Level III left?
facets.a: They go on hold pending review rather than becoming automatically void. Where the examination was administered by a valid administrator and the question set had prior Level III approval, the file survives with a documented review. Where a Level II administered the examination to a peer or subordinate, SNT-TC-1A's rule was broken and re-examination is the only close.

facets.q: Can an interim Level III run the practical examination?
facets.a: Yes, and that is frequently the reason for the engagement. Practical examinations require specimens containing known discontinuities appropriate to the method and the employer's product, a documented grading scheme, and a checklist recording candidate performance. Specimen sourcing sets the schedule more than examiner availability does, which is why it is scoped in week one rather than week six.

facets.q: How long should an interim engagement run?
facets.a: Name the destination on day one and the length follows. Where an internal candidate already meets the ASNT experience threshold, six to nine months covers application processing, Basic and Method examinations, and handover. Where the candidate is short on experience, the bridge equals the shortfall. Engagements without a named destination become permanent by accident and cost more than either alternative.

sections.heading: The trigger: a fixed audit date against a vacant Level III seat
paragraphs: Interim Level III demand has one shape. A company holds an audit date — a Nadcap reaccreditation window, a customer surveillance visit, an ASME survey, an AS9100 or ISO 9001 stage — and the person who approved its written practice, its examination questions and its NDT procedures is gone. The technicians are competent and the equipment is calibrated. What has vanished is the approval authority that makes the certification files valid. Auditors test that authority first, because everything downstream inherits from it.

SNT-TC-1A makes the loss immediate rather than gradual. Section 13 treats an employee's certification as revoked on termination of employment for any reason, unless that individual holds third-party certification. The departing Level III's own employer-based credential lapses the day they leave, and with it the documented basis on which they approved the written practice. A signature block on a controlled document now names someone who no longer holds the certification the document depends on. That is a finding an auditor can raise without opening a single technician file.

Interim cover means a contracted Level III designated in writing to act for the employer over a defined period, with a defined method scope and a defined end date. It is not a permanent appointment and it is not a rubber stamp on work already done. The engagement exists to restore approval authority, reconstruct what can be reconstructed, and give the employer a defensible position on audit day. The event that starts it is covered in /consulting/ndt-level-3-resigned-what-to-do.

sections.heading: The designation letter and what it actually authorizes
paragraphs: The designation letter is the first artifact, and it is signed by employer management rather than by the Level III. It names the individual, lists the exact NDT methods within scope, states the effective and expiry dates, and enumerates the authorities granted: approving the written practice, approving examination questions, approving and qualifying procedures, and recommending personnel for certification. An auditor reads this letter before anything else, because it establishes whether the person answering questions has standing to answer them at all.

NAS 410 and EN 4179 define a Responsible Level 3 as a Level 3 designated by the employer with the responsibility and authority to ensure the standard's requirements are met and to act on the employer's behalf. Both standards define an outside agency as an independent organization providing NDT services to implement those requirements, and both include consultants and self-employed individuals inside that definition. Contracting the role is anticipated by the standards. The written designation is what makes it operative rather than informal.

The letter does not transfer certification authority. Under SNT-TC-1A the certifying authority is a person designated in the written practice, and an outside agency cannot certify the employer's personnel. The contracted Level III states that examinations were administered and passed and that written-practice criteria were met; the employer signs. Employers that let a consultant sign certification records create a defect harder to remediate than the vacancy it was meant to solve. The boundary is set out in /consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do.

sections.heading: Written practice review is the first deliverable, not the last
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A requires the employer to establish a written practice for the control and administration of NDT personnel training, examination and certification, requires that practice to be reviewed and approved by the employer's NDT Level III, and requires it to be maintained on file. Three separate obligations, and a vacancy breaks the middle one. Re-approval by the interim Level III is the single highest-value hour in the engagement, because it re-anchors every personnel record that references the document.

Re-approval is not a signature pass. The review reconciles the document against what the shop actually does: methods listed against methods performed, the training-hour and experience tables against real personnel files, the examination structure against examinations actually given, the stated recertification interval against certification dates in force, and the vision requirements against the eye-exam records on file. Where the document and the practice disagree, one of them changes — and the document is not always the one that is wrong.

The basis standard matters as much as the content. ASME Section V Article 1 requires personnel qualification in accordance with the employer's written practice, T-120(e) requires that practice to follow SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, and T-120(f) permits other national or international central certification schemes where the written practice says so. A written practice built on the wrong basis document, or silent about which basis it invokes, produces a finding that no amount of record-keeping repairs afterwards.

sections.heading: Examination administration and the subordinate rule
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A states that in no case shall a certification examination be administered by one's self or by a subordinate. In a shop where the departed Level III was the only qualified administrator, this rule is why an outside Level III becomes the only lawful route to a valid examination — a constraint, not a convenience. Employers that had a Level II administer examinations to peers during the vacancy will find those examinations challenged, and the certifications resting on them challenged with them.

The Level III approves all in-house certification examination questions. An interim engagement therefore rebuilds or reviews the general, specific and practical examination sets for each method in scope, method by method. General examinations test method principles. Specific examinations test the employer's own procedures, equipment and acceptance criteria, which means they cannot be lifted from a generic bank. Specific examinations are where audit exposure concentrates, because they are the set most likely to have been copied rather than written.

Practical examinations set the schedule. They require specimens containing known discontinuities appropriate to the method and the employer's product forms, a documented grading scheme, and a checklist recording what the candidate did. Sourcing or verifying specimens is the step that decides whether examinations finish before audit day. An interim Level III scopes specimen availability in the first week rather than the last, because a missing reference block cannot be solved by working longer hours.

sections.heading: What an interim engagement cannot fix before audit day
paragraphs: It cannot create training hours or documented experience that were never accrued. SNT-TC-1A allows the employer to modify its program but not to eliminate training, experience, testing or recertification. Where a technician's file shows no classroom hours for a method they have been performing, the honest outcome is a documented restriction on their certification scope until the hours are completed. Reconstructing hours from memory, or issuing a certification that assumes them, converts a records finding into an integrity finding.

It cannot make the contracted Level III the employer's certifying authority, and it cannot convert an outside recommendation into an employer certification by force of urgency. It also cannot backfill a vision examination for a period that has already elapsed. SNT-TC-1A calls for annual near-vision acuity examination — Jaeger Number 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches — with color contrast differentiation at initial certification and at five-year intervals. A test performed today evidences today, not last year.

It cannot compress ASNT NDT Level III certification for an internal candidate. First-time applicants sit the Basic examination plus at least one Method examination, application processing runs two to four weeks before scheduling, and the experience thresholds are twelve months with a four-year engineering or physical science degree, twenty-four months with two years of post-secondary study, and forty-eight months without a degree. Sponsorship is the right permanent answer and the wrong answer to an audit six weeks out.

sections.heading: The realistic 30/60/90 sequence
paragraphs: Days one to thirty are diagnosis and containment. The designation letter is issued, and the interim Level III reads the written practice against the standard, pulls a sample of personnel files across every method and level, checks vision currency and recertification dates, and lists the exposures in the order an auditor will meet them. Any certification action taken since the vacancy is placed on hold pending review rather than defended. The output is a written exposure list with owners and dates, not a verbal briefing.

Days thirty-one to sixty are construction. The written practice is revised and formally approved, NDT procedures are reviewed and re-approved or requalified, the examination bank is rebuilt and approved, examinations are administered and graded, and vision examinations are brought current. Records are assembled to the content SNT-TC-1A calls for: examination copies or evidence of successful completion, composite grades, level and method with any limitations, education and experience, training completion, and vision results for the current certification period.

Days sixty-one to ninety are proof. Certification files are reissued by the employer on the interim Level III's recommendation, an internal audit runs against the same criteria the external auditor will use, and a mock audit exercises the answers out loud. Remaining items move into a corrective action log with root cause and evidence of implementation, because auditors credit a documented open finding under active correction far more than a gap presented as closed without evidence behind it.

sections.heading: Audit day and the scope discipline that protects you
paragraphs: Presence is a deliverable, not a courtesy. Auditors ask who approved the written practice, who approved the examination questions, who qualified the procedures and who signs certifications. Those four questions are answered in person by the individual holding the designation letter, with the letter on the table. An employer who answers them by producing a consultant's business card and an email thread has demonstrated the opposite of what the standard asks for, and the finding writes itself.

Scope discipline keeps the engagement honest. The interim Level III answers for what was reviewed and approved under the designation and declines to defend records generated before it. Where a predecessor's work is deficient, the correct response names it, points at the corrective action, and gives the completion date. Auditors draw a sharp line between a program that found its own problems before the visit and a program that is discovering them in the room.

Nadcap accreditation cycles reward that distinction directly. Initial accreditation runs twelve months. Eighteen- and twenty-four-month merit depend on consecutive cycles clear of Non-Sustaining Corrective Actions, verification of corrective action audits and Type C auditee advisories. A finding closed with a fix that does not hold costs a merit cycle even when it clears the immediate audit, which is why interim work is written to survive the next audit rather than only to pass this one.

sections.heading: The handoff to permanent cover
paragraphs: Three permanent outcomes exist, and the interim engagement should name which one it bridges to on day one. The employer hires an employed Level III. The employer sponsors an internal Level II through ASNT Level III certification. Or the employer retains a contracted Level III on a standing rather than interim basis, with the certifying authority remaining an employee of the firm. Engagements that never name the destination become permanent by accident and cost more than either alternative.

Sponsorship arithmetic decides the bridge length. A candidate holding a four-year engineering degree needs twelve months of documented experience in the applicable methods; a candidate without a degree needs forty-eight. Add application processing of two to four weeks, examination scheduling, and the Basic plus Method sequence. ASNT certification renews on a five-year cycle thereafter. Where the candidate already meets the experience threshold, a six-to-nine-month bridge is realistic; where they do not, the bridge equals the shortfall.

The handoff package is what makes the next Level III effective in week one rather than month three: the approved written practice with revision history, the approved examination bank with grading keys, the procedure set with qualification records, a personnel matrix showing method, level, limitations and next recertification date, the vision currency schedule, and the open corrective action log. Atlantis builds interim engagements to a fixed audit date and to that handoff package. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a scoping call or a quote.

faq.q: Is an interim Level III the same as an outside Level III?
faq.a: Both are contracted rather than employed. An interim engagement is time-boxed to an event — an audit, a vacancy, a certification cycle — and ends on a stated date with a handoff package. A standing outside Level III arrangement is ongoing with no terminal date. The authority limits are identical in both cases: the employer remains the certifying authority.

faq.q: Will an auditor accept a contracted Level III?
faq.a: Yes. NAS 410 and EN 4179 define outside agency to include consultants and self-employed individuals, and SNT-TC-1A anticipates outside agency involvement in training and examination. What auditors test is whether the designation is in writing, whether it names the methods, and whether certification signature stayed with an employee of the firm.

faq.q: Do we need a separate designation letter for each method?
faq.a: One letter with an explicit method list works. What matters is that the scope is written rather than assumed. Authority extends only to methods in which the designated Level III holds certification, so a letter naming methods the individual is not certified in creates its own finding. List the methods, list the levels, list the dates.

faq.q: Can the interim Level III also cover our welding inspection program?
faq.a: The designation covers the NDT methods written on the letter. Welding inspection under AWS or a code of construction is a separate qualification and a separate designation. Where the same individual holds both credentials, two designations can run in parallel. Where they do not, the NDT scope stands alone and the welding scope needs its own cover.

faq.q: Our audit is in three weeks. What is achievable?
faq.a: Designation, written practice review and re-approval, vision currency restoration, procedure re-approval, and audit-day presence. Examination rebuild starts but will not finish for every method. Time-bound gaps convert to documented restrictions on certification scope, recorded before the audit rather than discovered during it. That is a defensible position; a silent gap is not.

title: NDT Program Gap Assessment: Findings Taxonomy and Sequencing
description: How an NDT program gap assessment samples records, classifies findings by remediation path, and sequences fixes against a fixed audit date. US programs.
h1: What an NDT program gap assessment samples, finds and sequences
answer: A gap assessment tests the employer's written practice against what technicians actually do. It samples personnel files, graded examination papers, vision currency, procedure revision control and inspection records, then classifies each gap by whether it is documentable now, requires re-examination, or requires elapsed time. Sequencing matters more than the finding count: time-bound gaps must start first.
expansion: A gap assessment compares three artifacts that drift apart in every NDT program: the written practice as approved, the procedures as issued, and the work as actually performed and recorded. It samples personnel files across every method and level, traces inspection reports back to the procedure revision and certification scope in force on the examination date, and reads the retention clause the employer wrote for itself before checking whether graded examination papers survive against it. What separates an assessment from a findings list is classification. Each gap is sorted by remediation path rather than severity: documentable now, requiring re-examination, requiring elapsed calendar time, or structural. Structural gaps — an absent Level III designation, a written practice on the wrong basis standard — invalidate everything beneath them and are sequenced first. Time-bound gaps start next, because their clocks run whether or not anyone works on them. Atlantis delivers a clause matrix, a findings register and a sequenced plan against a named audit date.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024), Sections 1, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 12; ANSI/ASNT CP-189; NAS 410 Rev. 5 and EN 4179 vision and Responsible Level 3 provisions; Nadcap AC7114 audit criteria and PRI accreditation length and merit rules; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120.
