Technician certification across all of the above
Employer written practice under ASNT SNT-TC-1A
The written practice itself, and each individual certification record
Training hours, examination scores, vision tests, and the Level III's own certificate
table.note: IACS UR Z17 section 4.4 makes certification conditional on a practical demonstration of the specific service, and section 5.2 sets renewal at intervals not exceeding five years, shortened to three years for firms engaged in thickness measurement. Class application and audit fees are set by the society. Treat the demonstration as a scheduled, staffed event rather than a formality.

facets.q: Does a refinery-built NDT written practice cover shipyard work in Houston?
facets.a: No. SNT-TC-1A qualifies people by method and by technique, and hull gauging on coated plate is not the same technique as vessel-wall thickness on cleaned steel. IACS UR Z17 Annex 1 requires pulsed echo multiple-echo single-crystal instruments on coated surfaces. A written practice that never names that technique cannot certify anyone to use it, and the surveyor rejects the readings.

facets.q: What does IACS UR Z17 require of a Houston hull gauging crew?
facets.a: Operators certified to a recognised industrial NDT standard, with adequate knowledge of ship structures to select representative measurement positions, plus a minimum of one year of tutored on-the-job training. The responsible supervisor needs at least two years as an operator in that activity and certification to a recognised standard. A one-person firm must itself meet the supervisor requirement.

facets.q: Who has to approve NDT procedures for hull welds?
facets.a: The ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds states that procedures and techniques shall be established and approved by personnel certified to NDT Level 3 in the applicable inspection method. Method by method. A Level III certified in ultrasonics cannot sign your radiography technique. Interpretation and evaluation of results is restricted to Level 2 or Level 3 personnel.

facets.q: How often does a Houston tank barge face a drydock and internal structural examination?
facets.a: Under 46 CFR 137.300, a towing vessel in saltwater more than six months a year needs examination at least twice every five years, with not more than 36 months between them. A vessel in saltwater six months or less a year needs it at least once every five years. Houston's coastwise fleet mostly falls on the shorter cycle.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III certify our technicians, or must we employ one?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A certification is employer-based, so your company issues the certificate. The Level III does not have to be your employee. The ABS guide describes a Level 3 as authorised to assume full responsibility for an NDT facility and staff, establish and validate techniques, and manage qualification examinations. An outsourced Level III performs those functions under a service agreement.

facets.q: What does the Gulf Copper newbuild programme change for Houston subcontractors?
facets.a: Repair work is judged against a surveyor's satisfaction on the day. Newbuild is judged against a documented quality system that a prime contractor audits before you are cleared to bid. Davie Defense is investing up to a billion dollars in the Galveston and Port Arthur yards to build three Arctic Security Cutters, and sub-tier NDT firms will be audited accordingly.

sections.heading: The Houston market is a barge fleet first and a shipyard second
paragraphs: Ask an inspection firm in Pasadena what marine work looks like and it will describe a drydock. In Houston the volume sits elsewhere. The Ship Channel complex runs more than 200 private terminals alongside eight public ones and carries roughly twelve percent of all United States waterborne tonnage, and the vessels moving most of that cargo are tank barges. Kirby Corporation, headquartered in Houston, is the largest inland and coastal tank barge operator in the country and runs fleeting, towing and shifting services across the Gulf Coast and the inland rivers. It absorbed Higman Barge Lines, a Houston, Gulf Intracoastal Waterway and Mississippi River operator, in 2018.

That fleet is not a side market. Kirby runs its own San Jac Marine yard at Channelview with four floating drydocks lifting between 900 and 2,000 tons, which means a large share of Houston hull steel work happens inside an operator-owned facility on the operator's schedule rather than in a commercial yard. Buffalo Marine Service, also Houston based, runs bunkering tugs and barges on the channel through subsidiaries including Shamrock Marine. An inspection firm that markets only to drydocks makes itself invisible to the largest buyers in its own city.

The consequence for your certification programme is structural. Most Houston marine NDT is plate and structural weld work on hulls under United States Coast Guard authority, punctuated by classed ocean-going tonnage calling at the terminals. Two regimes, two sets of paperwork, one crew. A Level III who builds the programme around only one of them leaves you unable to bid half the market. Mapping that split is the first thing an [outsourced ASNT Level III consultant](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) should do before writing a single procedure.

sections.heading: Galveston Bay repair yards are being pulled into a shipbuilding quality regime
paragraphs: Gulf Copper has run ship repair and marine services out of Galveston and Port Arthur for over seventy-five years. Davie Defense completed its acquisition of those Texas yards in December 2025 and broke ground on a modernisation programme that could reach a billion dollars, with the first phase scheduled for completion in 2028. Under a Coast Guard contract finalised in May 2026, the Gulf Copper facilities will build three of five Arctic Security Cutters, first delivery expected in 2028 and the full run delivered by February 2035. A 2025 economic study projected roughly 2,400 direct jobs.

That is a change of category, not a change of volume. The Galveston yard historically handled jack-ups, semi-submersibles, barges and multi-service vessels, and was selected to carry out repairs on the Battleship Texas. Repair work is accepted by a surveyor's judgement at the dock. Newbuild for a government customer is accepted by a documented quality system that a prime contractor audits before your name appears on an approved supplier list. Malin International Ship Repair and Drydock also works the Galveston waterfront and faces the same shift in what buyers ask for.

For an inspection subcontractor the practical difference is evidence. A newbuild prime wants procedure qualification records, technician practical examination results, calibration traceability for every gauge and every reference block, and a signature from a Level III certified in the method. Not a certificate scan and a rate sheet. Building that file is ordinary [NDT technical procedure development](/consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development) work, but it takes weeks, and no yard schedules a bid window around a subcontractor's paperwork.

sections.heading: Why a refinery-built written practice fails a marine audit
paragraphs: Houston has the deepest NDT labour pool in the United States and almost all of it was trained on refinery and petrochemical assets. Those technicians are genuinely expert. The problem is that ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualifies people by method and by technique, and the written practice that certified them lists the techniques their employer intended them to use. Corrosion mapping on a cleaned pressure vessel wall is not the same technique as hull gauging through a coating system, and a written practice that never names hull gauging cannot certify anyone to perform it.

IACS UR Z17 Annex 1 is explicit about the equipment. On coated surfaces, instruments using the pulsed echo technique are required, either oscilloscope or digital instruments using multiple echo, single crystal. Single echo instruments may be used only on uncoated surfaces that have been cleaned and ground. A refinery-trained technician arriving with a single-echo gauge and applying it to coated hull plate is producing readings the attending surveyor is entitled to reject, and the rejection lands on your report, not on the technician.

The fix is not a new company. It is a marine annex inside your existing programme that names hull gauging, coated-surface multiple-echo technique, structural weld inspection and the acceptance criteria that apply to each, with the training and examination hours to match. Firms that already run [petrochemical NDT consulting](/consulting/petrochemical-ndt-consulting) scopes keep that side of the business entirely intact; the marine capability is added to the programme, never substituted for it, through targeted [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development).

sections.heading: What class service supplier approval actually costs you in paperwork
paragraphs: IACS UR Z17 sets the floor for firms providing services that surveyors rely on. Section 4.2.2 requires operators, technicians and inspectors to have a minimum of one year of tutored on-the-job training. Section 4.2.3 requires the responsible supervisor to have at least two years of experience as an operator in the activity being approved, and states that where the supplier consists of one person, that person must meet the supervisor requirements. Section 4.2.4 requires personnel records covering age, formal education, training and experience for every approved individual.

Annex 1 adds the thickness measurement specifics. The responsible supervisor is to be qualified to a recognised national or international industrial NDT standard, ISO 9712 Level II being the named example, and operators to the equivalent Level I, with adequate knowledge of ship structures to select a representative position for each measurement. Documented work procedures must cover survey preparation, selection and identification of test locations, surface preparation, protective coating preservation, calibration checks, and report preparation and content. The surveyor must verify each separate job and sign the report.

Then come the recurring costs. Section 4.2.5 requires equipment records including maintenance and calibration. Section 4.4 makes certification conditional on a practical demonstration of the specific service. Section 5.2 sets renewal or endorsement at intervals not exceeding five years, cut to three years for firms engaged in thickness measurement. That three-year clock is why a Houston firm that scraped through once so often fails at renewal: the original Level III has moved on and nobody re-signed the procedures.

sections.heading: The hull weld rules your Level III personally owns
paragraphs: The ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds is short and unambiguous about authority. Section 7 states that procedures and techniques shall be established and approved by personnel certified to NDT Level 3 in the applicable inspection method. Inspection shall be performed by certified Level 1, 2 or 3 personnel, and interpretation and evaluation of results shall be performed by personnel certified to Level 2 or Level 3. A Level 1 may classify results only with the prior written approval of a Level 3.

Section 5.9.1 describes what a Level 3 may be authorised to do: assume full responsibility for an NDT facility and staff, establish and validate techniques and procedures, interpret codes and standards, designate the particular test methods and techniques for specific work, and manage qualification examinations where the certification body authorises it. Section 5.9.2 adds that the individual must have enough practical background in materials, fabrication and product technology to select methods, establish techniques and help set acceptance criteria where none exist.

Read together, those clauses describe a role, not a certificate on a wall. Every method your firm offers needs a Level III certified in that method to sign its technique. If you offer four methods and your Level III holds two, two of your procedures are unsigned and every report produced under them is challengeable. That gap is the single most common finding when an outsourced Level III first opens a Houston inspection firm's document control.

sections.heading: Higher-strength steel changes when you are allowed to test
paragraphs: Section 9.1 of the same ABS guide sets hold times before nondestructive testing may begin on weldments in higher-strength steel, because hydrogen-induced cracking is delayed. For steels of 400 N/mm2 yield strength, equivalent to 58,000 psi, testing is to be conducted a minimum of 24 hours after welds have been completed and cooled to ambient temperature. For steels above that yield strength the minimum is 72 hours. The surveyor may require a longer interval or additional random inspection at a later period.

There is a documented relief. At the surveyor's discretion the 72-hour interval may be reduced to 24 hours for radiographic or ultrasonic inspection, provided a complete visual and random magnetic particle or penetrant inspection is carried out 72 hours after the welds have been completed and cooled. If delayed cracking is encountered in production, previously completed welds are to be reinspected, and the surveyor may require requalification of procedures.

This is a scheduling clause disguised as a technical one. A yard that quotes a three-day turnaround on a high-strength steel repair has already committed to a hold time it cannot compress without a written arrangement with the attending surveyor. Your NDT procedure should state the hold time, the yield threshold that triggers it, and the reduced-interval option, so that the yard's planners are working from the same document as your technicians rather than from an assumption.

sections.heading: Subchapter M and the tank barge fleet
paragraphs: The Coast Guard side of the Houston market runs on 46 CFR Subchapter M. Section 137.300 sets the examination cycle by saltwater exposure: a towing vessel exposed to saltwater more than six months a year must undergo drydock and internal structural examinations at least twice every five years, with not more than 36 months between examinations, while a vessel exposed six months or less a year needs them at least once every five years. The cognizant Officer in Charge, Marine Inspection may require additional examination where hull damage or structural deterioration is found or suspected.

Operators using the towing safety management system option with an internal survey programme carry extra obligations. Section 137.210 requires that the interval between successive surveys of any item does not exceed one year unless otherwise prescribed, and requires personnel carrying out those surveys to hold qualifications comparable to a surveyor from a third-party organisation as described in section 139.130. Section 137.135 governs what the examination report must contain.

For your firm this means the acceptance criteria are not yours to invent. Wastage limits come from the operator's approved standards and the attending surveyor's requirements, and your procedure has to reference them rather than restate a generic percentage. A Level III writing that procedure has to read the operator's programme first. That is a different exercise from writing a class gauging procedure, and both are needed if you intend to work the whole channel.

sections.heading: The third Houston market: offshore structure and rig work
paragraphs: Galveston Bay and the wider Texas coast still carry a substantial rig and offshore structure repair trade. The Gulf Copper Galveston facility has historically supported conversion, survey, repair, retrofitting and maintenance across jack-ups, semi-submersibles, barges and multi-service vessels. That work does not follow class hull rules. It follows the contract specification, which is usually written around AWS structural welding requirements or ASME Section V, with the acceptance criteria set by the customer's engineering department.

The same weld can therefore have three different acceptance criteria depending on which document the job was sold under, and a technician who applies the wrong one produces a technically correct report against the wrong standard. This is a written practice and procedure control problem, not a skills problem. Your procedure set needs to be organised by controlling document, and your job packs need to name which one applies before a technician mobilises.

Firms that split their week between the channel and a fabrication yard find the boundary work useful revenue and dangerous exposure in equal measure. Structuring it properly is the substance of [offshore NDT consulting](/consulting/offshore-ndt-consulting), and the discipline is simple to state and hard to enforce: no technician mobilises without a job pack naming the controlling document, the acceptance criteria that apply and the revision of the procedure being worked to. The Level III's job is to make sure that boundary is written down before anyone crosses it.

sections.heading: What an outsourced Level III delivers in the first ninety days
paragraphs: The sequence matters more than the speed. First a gap read: the existing written practice against every scope you actually bid, the certification file for every technician, and the signature status of every procedure. Most Houston firms discover at this point that they hold current certificates issued under an expired or method-incomplete written practice, which means the certificates themselves are difficult to defend in an audit. That finding is uncomfortable and it is better found by your own consultant than by a client's auditor.

Then the rebuild: a written practice covering the marine annex alongside your existing industrial scopes, method by method, with training hours, examination content and vision requirements specified. Then examinations, administered and documented, which is the part firms most often try to shortcut and the part auditors most reliably check. Independent oversight of that step exists precisely because self-administered examinations are the weakest link in an employer-based certification system, and an auditor testing your programme will start there rather than with your equipment.

Then procedures, signed by method, and a dry run of the class demonstration test before the surveyor is booked. Firms working both the Texas and Louisiana Gulf frequently run the same programme across two states, which is why the [New Orleans and Lower Mississippi maritime programme](/consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-new-orleans) is built to the same structure with a different regulatory emphasis. Bring the audit date to the conversation and [request a scoped quote](/contact) against it.

faq.q: Do we need class society approval to gauge hulls in Houston?
faq.a: If a class surveyor relies on your readings to make a decision affecting classification or statutory certification, yes. IACS UR Z17 exists because societies must verify the performance of third-party services their surveyors depend on. Coast Guard work on unclassed barges under Subchapter M is a separate route. Most Houston firms need both, and the two sets of paperwork do not overlap as much as owners expect.

faq.q: Can our refinery-certified Level II technicians work shipyard jobs?
faq.a: They can once your written practice names the marine techniques and they have been trained and examined in them. The certificate follows the written practice, so adding scope means reissuing the practice, delivering the training hours, running the examinations and documenting all of it. The people are usually fine. The paperwork almost never is until someone rebuilds it deliberately.

faq.q: How long should we allow to prepare for a class service supplier audit?
faq.a: Work back from the evidence the standard requires. Operators need a documented year of tutored on-the-job training, and the responsible supervisor needs two years as an operator in that activity. If those records do not already exist, no consultant can create them. Where the experience is real and only the documentation is missing, a focused programme rebuild plus a demonstration dry run is a matter of weeks.

faq.q: Does Atlantis act as the Level III of record or just supply documentation?
faq.a: Both, depending on what the scope needs. An outsourced Level III can author and sign the written practice, write and approve procedures by method, administer and document qualification examinations, and stand in front of the auditor or surveyor. Where you already have an internal Level III we work alongside them on the methods they do not hold. Scope and terms are quoted on request.

faq.q: Our Level III resigned three weeks before a client audit. What now?
faq.a: Your procedures are unsigned from the date of departure and your authority to issue new certifications lapses, so the immediate task is establishing coverage rather than re-papering history. An outsourced Level III can take the responsible role, review and re-approve the procedure set method by method, and stand in front of the auditor. This is a common and recoverable situation.

faq.q: Which methods matter most for Houston Ship Channel work?
faq.a: Ultrasonic thickness gauging carries the volume, because hull and barge structural assessment is fundamentally a wastage question. Magnetic particle and penetrant carry weld surface inspection, with radiography and ultrasonics for subsurface examination of full penetration welds. The ABS hull weld guide directs radiographic or ultrasonic inspection for internal examination and magnetic particle or penetrant for surface inspection of welds.

title: New Orleans Brown-Water NDT: Two Survey Clocks, One Written Practice
description: Inland towboats get one drydock exam every five years; Gulf boats need two. One written practice covers both plus class. What an outsourced ASNT Level III signs.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting for the New Orleans and Lower Mississippi Fleet
answer: A Mississippi River towboat in saltwater six months or less gets one drydock and internal structural examination every five years. A Gulf coastwise boat needs two, with not more than 36 months between them. 46 CFR 137.300 sets both. An outsourced ASNT Level III writes one written practice that satisfies both cycles plus class survey work.
expansion: New Orleans is the only United States metro where an inspection firm routinely serves two regulatory populations with the same crew in the same week. The brown-water fleet, run by operators such as Canal Barge Company, founded in New Orleans in 1933 and running roughly 800 vessels, and Blessey Marine Services, a predominantly unit-tow operator moving residual fuels, asphalt, lubricating oils, petroleum feedstocks, refined products, petrochemicals and alcohols, spends most of its life in fresh water. The blue-water and offshore population, built and repaired down Bayou Lafourche at Bollinger and Edison Chouest yards, is classed and surveyed. Those two populations sit under different documents, different examination intervals and different acceptance criteria, and a written practice built for one will not carry the other. The commercial answer is a single certification programme with two annexes, authored and signed by a certified Level III.
source: Verified against 46 CFR 137.300, 137.210 and 137.135 and the third-party organisation surveyor qualification reference at 46 CFR 139.130; IACS UR Z17 Annex 1 section 1 and sections 4.2 to 5.2; the ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds, Section 1; Bollinger Shipyards location and Arctic Security Cutter contract disclosures; Conrad Shipyard, Canal Barge Company, Blessey Marine and Edison Chouest Offshore company information; and Port of South Louisiana and Port of New Orleans facility data.

The cognizant OCMI may require additional examinations where hull damage or structural deterioration is discovered or suspected, may require internal inspection of affected spaces and fuel tanks, and may adjust intervals to monitor structural condition. Plan technician availability against the demand cycle, not against the regulation.

facets.q: Why do inland and Gulf towing vessels have different examination intervals?
facets.a: 46 CFR 137.300 keys the interval to saltwater exposure. A vessel in saltwater more than six months a year needs drydock and internal structural examinations at least twice every five years with not more than 36 months between them. A vessel in saltwater six months or less a year needs them at least once every five years. Salt drives the corrosion rate, so the regulation follows exposure rather than vessel type.

facets.q: Does an inland barge fleet need class society approval for its gauging contractor?
facets.a: Not for the Subchapter M examination itself, which is a Coast Guard and third-party organisation matter. Class approval under IACS UR Z17 becomes necessary the moment a class surveyor relies on your readings for a classification or statutory decision. Louisiana firms working both the inland fleet and offshore supply vessels need both routes, because the same technicians cross between them constantly.

facets.q: What qualifications do surveyors under an internal survey programme need?
facets.a: 46 CFR 137.210 requires an owner or managing operator using the towing safety management system option with an internal survey programme to ensure the management system specifies personnel with qualifications comparable to those of a surveyor from a third-party organisation as described in 46 CFR 139.130. It also caps the interval between successive surveys of any item at one year unless otherwise prescribed.

facets.q: Can one written practice cover both inland and class work?
facets.a: Yes, and it should. A single employer written practice under SNT-TC-1A can carry separate annexes for Subchapter M structural examination support and for class-approved hull thickness measurement, each naming its own techniques, training hours, examinations and acceptance references. Two separate programmes create two sets of certification records for the same people, which is the fastest way to fail an audit on a currency question.

facets.q: What does a Louisiana yard's newbuild programme demand from a subcontractor?
facets.a: Documented evidence rather than assurance. Bollinger operates ten ISO 9001 certified shipyards across south Louisiana and Mississippi, and its Houma yard is the base for four Coast Guard Arctic Security Cutters under a contract valued at 2.14 billion dollars. Sub-tier inspection firms on programmes at that level are audited on procedure qualification records, technician examination results and calibration traceability.

facets.q: Where does the New Orleans market differ from Houston?
facets.a: Houston concentrates its marine work around one ship channel and a bay. Louisiana spreads it down a bayou corridor: Bollinger at Lockport, Houma, Larose, Amelia, Morgan City and Harvey, Conrad at Morgan City and Amelia, Edison Chouest's North American Shipbuilding at Larose. Mobilisation distance, not technical scope, is the dominant cost driver, and your procedures have to work unsupervised at six sites.

sections.heading: Two fleets, two clocks, one quality department
paragraphs: The defining feature of the New Orleans inspection market is not the port. It is that a single firm here serves two vessel populations governed by different examination cycles. 46 CFR 137.300 draws the line at saltwater exposure. A towing vessel exposed to saltwater more than six months a year must undergo drydock and internal structural examinations at least twice every five years, with not more than 36 months between examinations. A vessel exposed six months or less a year needs them at least once every five years.

That single clause explains why brown-water and blue-water NDT demand behave so differently. A Mississippi River fleet on the longer cycle generates lumpy, plannable work concentrated in known windows. A Gulf coastwise fleet on the shorter cycle generates steadier, tighter-deadline work with wastage trending that actually matters between examinations. Most Louisiana inspection firms serve both, and staff to the average, which means they are overstretched in one season and idle in the other.

The regulation is a floor, not a schedule. The cognizant Officer in Charge, Marine Inspection may require additional examination where hull damage or structural deterioration is discovered or suspected, may call for internal inspection of affected spaces and fuel tanks, and may adjust intervals to monitor structural condition. Your written practice has to certify people for scope that appears without notice, which is a different design problem from certifying for a predictable annual programme.

sections.heading: The yards are a bayou corridor, not a waterfront
paragraphs: Bollinger Shipyards, founded three-quarters of a century ago and headquartered at Lockport, operates ten ISO 9001 certified shipyards positioned across south Louisiana and Mississippi, with Louisiana sites including Lockport and Houma for new construction, Larose, Amelia, Morgan City, Fourchon and a quick repair operation at Harvey. Conrad Shipyard runs five yards, among them Morgan City and Amelia in Louisiana and Orange in Texas, building and repairing offshore support vessels, tugs, ferries, inland push boats, inland and offshore tank barges, deck barges and dredge equipment.

Edison Chouest Offshore, based at Cut Off since 1960, operates its own shipyards including North American Shipbuilding at Larose, established in 1974 on the Dixie Delta Canal. Textron's Marine and Land Systems operation at Slidell sits on the other side of the metro with an entirely different customer. The result is that Louisiana marine NDT work is distributed across parishes rather than concentrated at a single dock, and technicians spend real hours on the road between Lafourche, Terrebonne and St. Mary.

Distributed work changes what a procedure has to do. A technique sheet that assumes a supervisor is present at the next bench will not survive a two-hour drive to a yard where your firm has one technician on site. Procedures written for this market need to be executable unsupervised, with decision points written out rather than implied. That is a specific style of [NDT technical procedure development](/consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development), and it is the difference between a document that passes review and one that works.

sections.heading: What Subchapter M actually asks of your inspectors
paragraphs: Operators who chose the towing safety management system route and demonstrate vessel compliance through an internal survey programme carry an explicit personnel obligation. 46 CFR 137.210 requires the management system to include procedures for surveying and testing, identification of the equipment and systems needing assessment, documentation and reporting of non-conformities and deficiencies, and assignment of personnel with qualifications comparable to those of a surveyor from a third-party organisation as described in 46 CFR 139.130. It also caps the interval between successive surveys of any item at one year unless otherwise prescribed.

That comparability requirement is where inspection firms get caught. A technician holding a current ultrasonic Level II certificate is qualified in a method. Being comparable to a third-party organisation surveyor is a broader claim about vessel knowledge, and it is not something an NDT certificate alone establishes. Firms bidding internal survey support need to document the marine experience separately, in the same personnel file, against the same individual.

Section 137.135 governs what the examination report has to contain, which means your report template is a compliance artefact rather than a marketing document. Report content, wastage figures, location identification and the basis for acceptance all need to trace back to a procedure that a Level III has signed. Getting that chain intact is the practical core of [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) for a Louisiana inland fleet contractor.

sections.heading: Where inland gauging and class gauging diverge
paragraphs: Inland structural examination and class hull thickness measurement look identical from a distance. Both are ultrasonic wall thickness on steel. They are not the same technique and they are not accepted by the same person. Class gauging sits under IACS UR Z17 Annex 1, which requires operators certified to a recognised national or international industrial standard, ISO 9712 Level I being the named example, with adequate knowledge of ship structures sufficient to select a representative position for each measurement, and a responsible supervisor at Level II or equivalent.

The equipment clause is where the divergence becomes physical. On coated surfaces, Annex 1 requires instruments using the pulsed echo technique, either oscilloscope or digital instruments using multiple echo, single crystal. Single echo instruments may be used only on uncoated surfaces that have been cleaned and ground. Coated internal structure is normal on both populations, so a firm carrying only single-echo gauges is limited to prepared surfaces and will be found out at the first class job.

Documented procedures under Annex 1 must cover survey preparation, selection and identification of test locations, surface preparation, protective coating preservation, calibration checks, and report preparation and content. The surveyor must verify each separate job and document that verification by signing the report. Nothing in Subchapter M imposes that per-job surveyor signature, so a firm that has only ever worked inland has no habit of building it into the workflow.

sections.heading: Offshore supply vessels put you straight back under class
paragraphs: The offshore service vessel fleet operating out of Fourchon, Houma and Larose is classed, and the moment a class surveyor relies on your readings for a classification or statutory decision, your firm needs approval as a service supplier. IACS UR Z17 section 4.2.2 sets a minimum of one year of tutored on-the-job training for operators, technicians and inspectors. Section 4.2.3 requires the responsible supervisor to have at least two years of experience as an operator in the approved activity, and states that a one-person supplier must itself meet the supervisor requirements.

Approval is not a document exercise. Section 4.4 makes certification conditional on a practical demonstration of the specific service, so a crew has to perform in front of the society. Section 4.2.5 requires equipment records including maintenance and calibration. Section 5.2 sets renewal or endorsement at intervals not exceeding five years, shortened to three years for firms engaged in thickness measurement. Three years is short enough that Louisiana firms routinely reach renewal with a Level III who has since left.

Firms whose work skews toward the offshore population rather than the inland fleet will find the sequencing, evidence requirements and demonstration logistics set out in more depth under [offshore NDT consulting](/consulting/offshore-ndt-consulting). The Louisiana specific is that very few firms actually get to choose between the two. The inland fleet pays the bills through a slow winter and the offshore fleet pays for the equipment, so most operators here carry both routes and both sets of records, which is precisely why one written practice with two annexes beats running two separate programmes.

sections.heading: The newbuild chain and what a prime contractor audits
paragraphs: Louisiana newbuild is running at scale. Bollinger signed a contract to build four Coast Guard Arctic Security Cutters, with the work based at its Houma yard and supported by its workforce across multiple Gulf Coast facilities under a contract valued at 2.14 billion dollars. Conrad continues to build inland and offshore tank barges, deck barges, ferries and dredge equipment across its Morgan City and Amelia yards. Both types of programme audit their sub-tier inspection suppliers before awarding work.

What the prime asks for is narrow and specific. Procedure qualification records. Technician practical examination results with the actual scores, not a summary. Calibration traceability for gauges and reference blocks. A written practice with a revision history. And a Level III certified in each method whose signature appears on each corresponding technique. The audit is not looking for capability. It is looking for whether the evidence exists in the form the contract requires.

The most common Louisiana failure is method coverage. A firm offering ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle and penetrant services with a Level III certified in only two of them has two unsigned procedures. Under the ABS hull weld guide, procedures and techniques shall be established and approved by personnel certified to NDT Level 3 in the applicable inspection method, which makes the gap a finding rather than a technicality.

sections.heading: Hull weld inspection on the river and in the yard
paragraphs: For weld inspection the method assignment is set by the guide, not by preference. Radiographic or ultrasonic inspection, or both, is used for internal subsurface inspection. Magnetic particle or penetrant inspection, or another equivalent approved method, is generally used for surface inspection of welds. The extent and location of inspection follow the applicable rules, the material and welding procedures involved, the quality control procedures in use, the results of visual inspection, and the surveyor's satisfaction.

Personnel authority is tiered and enforced. Inspection may be performed by certified Level 1, 2 or 3 personnel, but interpretation and evaluation of results is restricted to Level 2 or Level 3 in the applicable method, and a Level 1 may classify results only with the prior written approval of a Level 3. A Level 1 is not to be responsible for the choice of test method or technique. Job packs that send a Level 1 out alone to make calls are non-compliant on their face.

Delayed hydrogen cracking adds a timing rule that catches yards more often than inspection firms. Testing of weldments in steels of 400 N/mm2 yield strength, equivalent to 58,000 psi, is to be conducted a minimum of 24 hours after welds are completed and cooled to ambient temperature, and a minimum of 72 hours above that yield strength, unless specially approved otherwise. Write the hold time into the procedure so the yard planner sees it.

sections.heading: The lower Mississippi is the customer behind the customer
paragraphs: The reason this fleet exists is the cargo base. The Port of South Louisiana stretches 54 miles of Mississippi River frontage between New Orleans and Baton Rouge from its headquarters at LaPlace, and handles roughly sixty percent of all raw grain shipments leaving the American heartland. The channel from New Orleans to Baton Rouge carries a 48 foot draft. The Port of New Orleans operates the Napoleon Avenue Container Terminal with an annual container capacity around 840,000 twenty-foot equivalent units, served on dock by the New Orleans Public Belt Railroad.

For an inspection firm that cargo profile is a demand forecast. Grain, petrochemical and refined product movements determine how many barges are in service, which determines how many hulls hit a drydock in a given quarter, which determines whether your technicians are billable in March. Firms that plan capacity against the regulatory cycle alone misread the market, because the cycle sets the minimum and the cargo sets the actual volume.

It also shapes the training question. A Louisiana firm growing into class work needs technicians who can gauge coated internal structure competently, and that capability is built through a structured programme rather than absorbed on the job between tows. On-site delivery through [corporate NDT training](/corporate-ndt-training) is how most firms here close that gap, because it keeps the crew in the parish and lets the documented training hours count toward the tutored on-the-job experience the class route demands anyway.

sections.heading: Building one programme that survives both regimes
paragraphs: The design goal is a single employer written practice with two clearly separated annexes: one for Subchapter M structural examination support, one for class-approved hull thickness measurement and hull weld inspection. Each annex names its own techniques, its own training hours, its own examination content and its own acceptance references. One certification record per person, listing every technique that person is qualified in, so a currency question has exactly one answer.

The sequence is a gap read against every scope you actually bid, then reissue of the written practice, then training, then examinations properly administered and documented, then procedures signed method by method. The examination step is the one firms most often compress and the one auditors most reliably interrogate, which is why it is worth separating the person who administers the examination from the person who wrote the training material that prepared the candidates for it.

An outsourced Level III has real limits worth understanding before you engage one, and those boundaries are set out plainly in the guidance on [what an outside NDT Level 3 can and cannot do](/consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do). Firms working both the Texas and Louisiana Gulf usually run the same structure across both, which is why the [Houston and Galveston Bay maritime programme](/consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-houston) mirrors this one. Bring your examination window and [request a scoped quote](/contact).

faq.q: Our boats never leave fresh water. Do we still need drydock examinations?
faq.a: Yes. 46 CFR 137.300 requires drydock and internal structural examinations at least once every five years for a towing vessel exposed to saltwater six months or less a year. The reduced frequency is the concession for lower corrosion exposure, not an exemption. The cognizant Officer in Charge, Marine Inspection may also require additional examinations where hull damage or deterioration is found or suspected.

faq.q: Do we need class approval if we only work inland barges?
faq.a: Not for the Subchapter M work itself. Class service supplier approval under IACS UR Z17 applies where a class surveyor relies on your measurements for a classification or statutory decision. Most Louisiana firms eventually take offshore supply vessel work and need approval anyway, so the practical question is when to build the evidence, not whether.

faq.q: Can the same technician cover an inland structural examination and a class hull gauging job?
faq.a: Only if your written practice certifies that person in both techniques and your class approval covers them as an operator. The class route additionally requires a documented year of tutored on-the-job training and adequate knowledge of ship structures to select representative measurement positions. The competence is usually there. The documentation usually is not until someone builds it.

faq.q: How does Atlantis work with firms spread across several bayou parishes?
faq.a: By writing procedures that execute unsupervised and building one certification programme that travels with the technician rather than with the site. Programme authorship, procedure approval by method, examination administration and audit attendance can be delivered remotely and on site as the schedule requires. Scope, cadence and terms are quoted on request against your actual examination calendar.

faq.q: What happens to our certifications if our Level III leaves?
faq.a: Certification under SNT-TC-1A is employer-based, so the certificates remain your company's, but your authority to issue new ones and to approve procedures lapses until a qualified Level III is in place. Procedures signed by the departed individual come under scrutiny at the next audit. The recovery order is coverage first, then a method-by-method review and re-approval of the entire procedure set.

title: Mobile Shipyard NDT Runs on NAVSEA Tech Pub 271, Not ABS Rules
description: Austal and Alabama Shipyard work is qualified to NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, and aluminum rules out magnetic particle. What an outsourced ASNT Level III signs.
h1: Maritime and Naval NDT Consulting for Mobile, Alabama
answer: Mobile's naval work answers to NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, which sets its own personnel, procedure and equipment qualification rules. Austal's aluminum structure rules out magnetic particle entirely. An outsourced ASNT Level III writes a Tech Pub 271 written practice, qualifies technicians in penetrant, radiography and ultrasonics, and signs every procedure before a government source inspector sees it.
expansion: Mobile is a naval shipbuilding town with a commercial repair yard attached, and that inverts the certification problem compared with every other Gulf port. Austal USA employs over 3,000 people in Mobile inside roughly 1.5 million square feet of indoor manufacturing space, has delivered 34 ships to the Navy since 2009, and now runs both an aluminum line and a steel line alongside submarine module fabrication and outfitting for the Virginia and Columbia classes. That work is not qualified against classification society rules. It is qualified against NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, which covers radiographic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, ultrasonic, eddy current and visual inspection and contains the minimum requirements to qualify NDT personnel, procedures and equipment. A Mobile inspection firm holding an ABS-oriented written practice is holding the wrong document for the largest employer in its market.
source: Verified against NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, Requirements for Nondestructive Testing Methods; the ASNT Naval Shipbuilders NDT Level III certification programme description and its eligibility restrictions; the ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds, Section 1; Austal USA published programme, facility and workforce information; Alabama Shipyard published service and project information; Port of Mobile and Alabama Port Authority terminal data; and public information on Airbus, AM/NS Calvert and the Bayou La Batre shipyards.

table.note: The aluminum constraint is physics, not policy, and it changes staffing rather than paperwork alone. A firm whose weld surface inspection capability rests mainly on magnetic particle technicians has no usable surface method on an aluminum hull, and penetrant on production aluminum weldments is slower, more consumable-intensive and more sensitive to surface condition than magnetic particle on steel.

facets.q: Why can't magnetic particle be used on Austal's aluminum hulls?
facets.a: Magnetic particle inspection works by magnetising the part and detecting flux leakage at discontinuities. It requires a ferromagnetic material. Marine aluminum alloys are not ferromagnetic, so there is nothing to magnetise and no leakage field to reveal. Surface inspection on aluminum structure falls to liquid penetrant, with radiography and ultrasonics covering subsurface examination and eddy current available for specific applications.

facets.q: Which document governs NDT qualification for Mobile naval work?
facets.a: NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, commonly called Tech Pub 271. It covers radiographic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, ultrasonic, eddy current and visual inspection, and it contains the minimum requirements necessary to qualify NDT personnel, procedures and equipment. Classification society rules and guides govern commercial classed hulls, not the naval programmes that dominate Mobile's shipbuilding employment.

facets.q: Can we send our Level III to the ASNT Naval Shipbuilders examination?
facets.a: Probably not. That examination is restricted, aimed at Level III test examiners contracted as prime contractors or sub-tiers within specific naval shipbuilding chains, and applicants must apply through a naval shipyard administrator rather than register directly. It is not available to the general public. Most Mobile subcontractors therefore qualify people employer-based under a written practice that satisfies Tech Pub 271.

facets.q: What does employer-based certification mean if the exam is restricted?
facets.a: It means your company issues the certificate, under a written practice signed by a certified Level III, with training hours, examinations and vision testing documented in each individual's file. The restricted ASNT examination is one route to establishing a Level III examiner within a particular prime contractor chain. It is not the only way to satisfy Tech Pub 271 personnel requirements as a supplier.

facets.q: How much aerospace competition is there for Mobile NDT technicians?
facets.a: Substantial. Airbus opened its A320 family assembly plant in Mobile in 2015, added A220 production in August 2019, and employs around 2,000 people. AM/NS Calvert employs about 1,600 in steel. Those employers qualify inspectors under aerospace and industrial regimes rather than naval ones, and they bid for the same certified technicians your yard contracts need.

facets.q: What kind of work does Alabama Shipyard bring to local inspection firms?
facets.a: Ship repair covering maintenance, overhaul, conversion and upgrades, marine construction including pier work and heavy lift crane services, and shipbreaking covering vessel and barge dismantling including nuclear. Its project history includes Military Sealift Command vessels such as USNS Comfort, USNS Brittin and USNS Gordon. It holds ISO 9001 certification, which shapes what it expects from a subcontractor's documentation.

sections.heading: Mobile is a naval yard town with a commercial repair yard attached
paragraphs: Austal USA has been building in Mobile since 1999 and expanded onto Blakeley Island in 2005. It now employs more than 3,000 people locally out of over 3,500 nationwide, operates roughly 1.5 million square feet of indoor manufacturing space, and has invested about a billion dollars in United States shipyard facilities. It has delivered 34 ships to the Navy since 2009. Its current portfolio spans Independence class littoral combat ships, Spearhead class expeditionary fast transports, Heritage class offshore patrol cutters for the Coast Guard, and landing craft utility hulls.

The company has also moved well beyond aluminum. It runs a steel construction line alongside its aluminum fabrication, and since 2022 has performed Virginia class and Columbia class submarine module fabrication and outfitting, with a dedicated module manufacturing facility for submarine components. In July 2026 it launched AFDM 15, a Navy dry dock and the largest vessel it has launched to date, and in August 2026 delivered the first in class LCU 1710.

Alongside that sits Alabama Shipyard, an ISO 9001 certified operation whose scope runs from ship repair covering maintenance, overhaul, conversion and upgrades, through marine construction including pier work and heavy lift crane services, to shipbreaking that extends to vessel and barge dismantling including nuclear. Its project record includes Military Sealift Command vessels such as USNS Comfort, USNS Brittin and USNS Gordon. Between them these two yards define what a Mobile inspection firm must be qualified for, and neither is primarily a classification society customer.

sections.heading: Aluminum removes a method from your menu
paragraphs: Magnetic particle inspection detects discontinuities by magnetising a component and finding flux leakage where the material is interrupted. It requires a ferromagnetic material to work at all. Marine aluminum alloys are not ferromagnetic. There is no way to magnetise the part, no leakage field, and therefore no indication. On an aluminum hull or superstructure, magnetic particle is not merely inadvisable, it is physically inoperative, and no procedure or technique variation changes that.

The consequence is that surface weld inspection on aluminum structure falls entirely to liquid penetrant, with radiography and ultrasonics carrying subsurface examination and eddy current available for specific applications. That is a real production burden. Penetrant on production aluminum weldments is slower than magnetic particle on steel, consumes more material, is more sensitive to surface condition and cleaning, and demands more careful dwell and developer control. Throughput planning built on steel-yard assumptions will be wrong.

For an inspection firm this is a staffing question before it is a paperwork question. If your weld surface inspection capability rests mainly on magnetic particle technicians, you have no usable surface method for the largest shipbuilder in your metro. Rebalancing toward penetrant depth means training hours and examinations, and it means a written practice that certifies people in the penetrant techniques the customer's specification actually calls for.

sections.heading: Tech Pub 271 governs here, not the ABS guide
paragraphs: NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 is the controlling document for Mobile's naval work. It covers nondestructive testing method requirements for radiographic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, ultrasonic, eddy current and visual inspection, addressing the requirements for conducting NDT used in determining the presence of discontinuities in metals. Critically for a supplier, it also contains the minimum requirements necessary to qualify NDT personnel, procedures and equipment. Those three qualification streams are what an auditor works through.

This matters because a Mobile inspection firm that built its programme around commercial marine practice is holding a document set aimed at a different acceptance authority. Class guides describe what a surveyor will accept. Tech Pub 271 describes what a government programme will accept, and the evidence chain runs through the prime contractor rather than a society. The technical methods overlap heavily. The qualification and acceptance paperwork does not.

The practical output is a written practice authored specifically to satisfy Tech Pub 271 personnel requirements, with procedures written to its method requirements and signed by a Level III certified in each method. That is standard [outsourced ASNT Level III consulting](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) work, but the source document is different from the one a Houston or New Orleans firm starts with, and copying a Gulf-standard programme into Mobile produces a programme that fails on its first naval audit.

sections.heading: The naval Level III examination is probably closed to you
paragraphs: ASNT operates a Naval Shipbuilders NDT Level III certification whose specific examination aligns with Tech Pub 271 requirements. It is a one-part open-book examination of 2.5 hours and 50 questions on naval shipbuilding industry standards. It is also restricted. It serves NDT professionals working as Level III test examiners within specific naval prime contractor chains, applicants must be contracted as prime contractors or sub-tiers, and applications go through a naval shipyard administrator rather than direct registration. It is not available to the general public.

That restriction is the single most misunderstood fact in the Mobile market. Firms assume the naval examination is the credential they need, discover they cannot sit it, and conclude they cannot serve the market. The conclusion does not follow. Tech Pub 271 sits inside an employer-based certification system, and the standard route for a supplier is a company written practice, signed by a certified Level III, that satisfies the publication's personnel qualification requirements.

Building that is a documentation and examination exercise, not a credentialling roadblock. It requires a Level III certified in each method you offer, a written practice that names the techniques your contracts require, documented training hours, properly administered qualification examinations and vision testing on file. Independent oversight of that examination step matters more here than in commercial work, because the acceptance authority is a government customer whose record expectations outlast the contract itself.

sections.heading: You are hiring against Airbus, and it changes your written practice
paragraphs: Mobile's NDT labour market is not only maritime. Airbus opened its A320 family assembly plant in the city in 2015, the first in the United States, assembling A319, A320 and A321 aircraft, added A220 production in August 2019, and employs around 2,000 people. AM/NS Calvert employs roughly 1,600 in steel upriver. The University of South Alabama and the Mobile County Public School System are the two largest employers in the metro, which tells you how tight the technical labour pool actually is.

Aerospace and aerospace supply work in this labour market qualifies inspectors under a completely different regime. Firms serving that side run against NAS 410 and prepare for Nadcap audits rather than naval or class acceptance, and the [Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness](/consulting/nadcap-ac7114-audit-readiness) requirements and the [NAS 410 responsible Level 3](/consulting/nas-410-responsible-level-3) role are structurally different from anything in Tech Pub 271. A technician certified under one is not automatically usable under the other.

For a Mobile inspection firm the strategic question is whether to build one programme covering both worlds or to specialise in one. Firms serving marine and aerospace customers simultaneously need parallel written practices with clean separation between them, because an auditor from either side reads cross-contamination between regimes as a loss of document control. Firms that specialise should say so plainly in their bids. A programme that gestures at both regimes without committing to either reads as unfocused to both audiences and loses work it could have won.

sections.heading: The port itself is a break bulk and bulk market
paragraphs: The Port of Mobile operates 42 berths handling containerised, bulk, break bulk, roll-on roll-off and heavy lift cargo, alongside private bulk terminal operators. It is the largest break bulk forest products port in the United States and runs McDuffie Terminal, one of the nation's largest coal terminals and its largest import coal facility. The Alabama Port Authority also operates dedicated steel, general cargo and finished automotive facilities, with a channel maintained at 45 feet and a deepening programme to 50 feet.

Break bulk and bulk handling generates a different inspection demand profile from container terminals. Cargo handling structure, cranes, conveyors, ship loaders and terminal steelwork all corrode and fatigue, and the customer buying that inspection is a terminal operator rather than a vessel owner. The acceptance criteria come from the equipment manufacturer or a structural standard, not from a marine survey document.

That is a genuine adjacent market for a Mobile inspection firm, and it is the one most often ignored because it does not look like ship work. Bringing it inside the same certification programme means naming the structural and equipment techniques in the written practice explicitly, which is straightforward [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) once someone decides the scope belongs there rather than treating it as occasional side work.

sections.heading: Bayou La Batre and the small yard problem
paragraphs: Half an hour southwest of the city, Bayou La Batre supports a cluster of shipyards largely owned and operated by local families, including Metal Shark, formerly Horizon Shipbuilding, Steiner Ship Yard, Rodriguez Boat Builders, Master Boat Builders and Williams Fabrication. These yards build and repair working vessels for customers well beyond the Gulf, in both steel and aluminum, and they sit alongside the seafood processing industry that gave the town its name.

Small family yards face a specific version of the certification problem. They need a written practice and signed procedures to bid the work, but the volume rarely justifies a salaried Level III, and the one they can afford is usually certified in one or two methods rather than the four or five their contracts touch. The result is a programme that is genuinely competent in practice and indefensible on paper the moment a customer sends an auditor.

This is exactly the gap an outsourced arrangement is designed for. One certified Level III can hold the responsible role across several yards at once, authoring each written practice separately, approving procedures method by method and administering qualification examinations, without any single yard carrying a full-time salary. The arrangement has real boundaries worth agreeing in writing before it starts, particularly around who holds signature authority when the Level III is unreachable, and how quickly procedures get re-approved after a customer changes specification.

sections.heading: Commercial repair still runs under class rules
paragraphs: Not everything in Mobile is naval. Alabama Shipyard's commercial repair, conversion and upgrade work on classed tonnage brings classification society requirements back into play, and the ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds is explicit about who owns what. Procedures and techniques shall be established and approved by personnel certified to NDT Level 3 in the applicable inspection method. Inspection may be performed by certified Level 1, 2 or 3 personnel, but interpretation and evaluation is restricted to Level 2 or Level 3.

The method assignment follows the same logic on steel hulls everywhere: radiographic or ultrasonic inspection for internal subsurface examination, magnetic particle or penetrant for surface inspection of welds, with extent and location determined by the applicable rules, the materials and welding procedures involved and the surveyor's satisfaction. Higher-strength steel weldments carry hold times before testing, a minimum of 24 hours at 400 N/mm2 yield strength and 72 hours above it.

So a Mobile firm serving both yards genuinely needs two acceptance frameworks living inside one certification programme, with every procedure stating on its face which one it was written against. That is more document control than most small firms run, and it is the reason a Mobile programme is harder to build than a purely commercial Gulf one. The contrast is instructive: the [New Orleans and Lower Mississippi programme](/consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-new-orleans) is built around Coast Guard examination cycles rather than naval qualification, because the fleet on that stretch of river is a different animal entirely.

sections.heading: What an outsourced Level III delivers into a Mobile audit
paragraphs: The first deliverable is a scope decision, written down. Which yards you intend to serve, which acceptance authority each answers to, and therefore which controlling document each of your procedures is written against. Firms that skip this step end up with a single generic procedure set that satisfies nobody, because the naval customer wants Tech Pub 271 traceability and the commercial customer wants class rule traceability and the two look different on the page.

The second is the written practice itself, authored to cover every method you offer, with the aluminum reality built in rather than bolted on. That means penetrant treated as a primary surface method with the training hours to match, not as a fallback for when magnetic particle is unavailable. Then examinations administered and documented, then procedures signed by a Level III certified in each specific method.

The third is presence when it counts. Sitting with the auditor, answering the personnel qualification questions directly, and producing the file rather than describing it. Where technician depth is the real constraint rather than documentation, structured [corporate NDT training](/corporate-ndt-training) delivered on site closes it faster than recruiting against Airbus wages. Bring the audit or bid date and [request a scoped quote](/contact) built backwards from it.

faq.q: Is our ABS-oriented NDT programme usable for Austal work?
faq.a: Not without rework. Naval construction qualifies personnel, procedures and equipment against NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, and the evidence chain runs through the prime contractor rather than a classification society. The methods overlap almost entirely. The qualification documentation, acceptance references and traceability expectations do not, and an auditor works from the controlling document your contract names.

faq.q: We only hold magnetic particle and ultrasonic capability. Can we bid aluminum hull work?
faq.a: Not for surface weld inspection. Magnetic particle requires a ferromagnetic material and marine aluminum is not one, so it produces no indication at all. You would need liquid penetrant capability, which means qualified technicians, a written practice naming the penetrant techniques your customer specifies, and a procedure signed by a Level III certified in penetrant testing.

faq.q: Do we need the ASNT Naval Shipbuilders Level III credential to work in Mobile?
faq.a: For most suppliers, no, and for many it is not even obtainable. That examination is restricted to Level III test examiners within particular naval prime contractor chains and is not open to the general public. Tech Pub 271 operates within an employer-based certification system, so a company written practice signed by a certified Level III is the standard supplier route.

faq.q: Can one Level III cover several Bayou La Batre yards at once?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the normal arrangement for yards of that size. A single certified Level III can hold the responsible role across multiple employers, authoring each written practice, approving procedures method by method and administering qualification examinations. Each yard issues its own certifications under its own practice. The limits of the arrangement are worth agreeing in writing before you commit to it.

faq.q: How do we compete for technicians against Airbus and the steel mill?
faq.a: By certifying people internally rather than buying them certified. Airbus employs around 2,000 in Mobile and AM/NS Calvert around 1,600, and both bid above what a small inspection firm can sustain for an already-qualified inspector. Training an existing employee through a documented programme to Level II in the methods you actually sell is usually faster and more durable than recruiting.

faq.q: What should we prepare before a prime contractor audit?
faq.a: A current written practice with revision history, one certification file per technician showing training hours, examination scores and vision testing, procedures signed by a Level III certified in that specific method, and calibration traceability for every instrument and reference standard. Auditors test whether the evidence exists in the required form. Capability is assumed; documentation is what gets checked.

title: Puget Sound Runs Three NDT Approval Regimes, Not One
description: Bremerton runs on NAVSEA Tech Pub 271, the ferries on Coast Guard inspection, the Bering Sea fleet on class. One outsourced ASNT Level III holds all three.
h1: Outsourced ASNT Level III Support for Seattle and Puget Sound Shipyards
answer: A Puget Sound inspection firm faces three separate approval regimes. Navy availabilities at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard and Vigor run on NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, which makes SNT-TC-1A mandatory rather than advisory. Washington State Ferries drydockings answer to the Coast Guard. The Bering Sea catcher-processor fleet answers to class. One outsourced ASNT Level III signs the written practice all three demand.
expansion: Puget Sound is not one maritime market. Puget Sound Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility at Bremerton employs roughly 15,000 people across six dry docks and is the only US facility certified to recycle nuclear-powered ships. Vigor's Harbor Island yard holds a Master Ship Repair agreement and dry-docks Navy, Coast Guard and Washington State Ferries hulls. Lake Union Dry Dock, Pacific Fishermen in Ballard and Everett Ship Repair carry the North Pacific catcher-processor fleet berthed at Terminal 91 and Fishermen's Terminal. Each customer accepts NDT under a different authority. Navy work runs on NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, which converts ASNT SNT-TC-1A from a recommended practice into mandatory minimums and requires a Level III Examiner to certify every inspector and sign every procedure. Class and Coast Guard work run on other rules entirely. A firm bidding across all three needs one Level III who keeps all three sets of paperwork straight.
source: Verified against NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Rev 1 (paragraphs 1.5.2, 1.5.3, 1.5.5, 1.6, 1.6.1.1, 1.6.3, 1.6.4, 1.6.7, 1.6.8, 1.6.9, 1.6.10, 1.7.1-1.7.4); IACS Unified Requirement Z17 Rev.15 and Rev.16, including Annex 1 sections 1 and 15; the Puget Sound Ship Repair Association member roster showing Master Ship Repair and Agreement for Boat Repair categories; the Port of Seattle Terminal 91 fishing fleet briefing; the WSDOT Washington State Ferries fact sheet of February 2025; NAVSEA PSNS and IMF public facility data; NOAA Fisheries 2026 Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands groundfish harvest specifications and the 20 January A-season opening; and the ASNT published Level III examination fee schedule and experience routes.
