table.note: USIBD's LOA bands are specified at the 95 percent confidence level, which is two sigma: LOA20 spans 5 cm to 15 mm, LOA30 spans 15 mm to 5 mm, LOA40 spans 5 mm to 1 mm. Scanner datasheets are published at one sigma. Writing LOA30 into a scope while quoting a 2 mm instrument specification compares two numbers built on different statistics, and the comparison flatters the instrument by a factor of two.

facets.q: What is the difference between instrument accuracy and network accuracy?
facets.a: Instrument accuracy describes one measured point relative to the scanner head — the figure on the datasheet. Network accuracy describes how well a point at one end of the unit relates to a point at the other, hundreds of metres and many setups away. The second is always worse than the first, and it is the number that governs whether a tie-in fits.

facets.q: How many setups before registration error dominates?
facets.a: It dominates as soon as setups are chained rather than tied to control. Independent registration errors between successive setups combine as the root sum of squares, so the disagreement between the first and last station grows steadily along an unconstrained chain. Closing loops and observing control targets bound that growth; adding setups without either lets it run.

facets.q: Do I still need targets if my scanner registers itself?
facets.a: On-board tracking such as Leica's visual inertial system or Trimble's IMU-based Registration Assist handles local alignment well and removes most field target work over short chains. Across a full unit, surveyed targets or control anchor the whole network to something external. Read the registration report: bundle and cloud-to-cloud errors climbing along a chain are the signal that control is required.

facets.q: How do I write an accuracy requirement into a scope of work?
facets.a: State four things. The USIBD LOA band required, separately for Measured Accuracy and Represented Accuracy. The confidence level, since LOA is written at 95 percent and datasheets at one sigma. Whether the requirement is absolute or relative, and over what extent. And the verification method to be applied at handover, with pass criteria agreed before mobilisation.

facets.q: How is scan accuracy verified when the data arrives?
facets.a: Independent check measurements, agreed in advance. Surveyed check distances between features at opposite ends of the unit, compared against the same distances extracted from the cloud, test network accuracy directly. ASTM E3125-17 formalises the equivalent instrument-level test, evaluating derived-point to derived-point distance errors against manufacturer-specified maximum permissible errors across the work volume.

facets.q: What tolerance is achievable across a whole unit versus one vessel?
facets.a: They are different problems. One vessel scanned from a few setups sits close to the instrument specification, because few registration links exist. A full unit spanning hundreds of metres is governed by the control network, and its achievable tolerance is set by the survey that established that control rather than by the scanner. Specify each extent separately.

sections.heading: Three different numbers all get called accuracy
paragraphs: The word accuracy carries three distinct meanings on a scanning project, and conflating them is the root of nearly every dispute at handover. Instrument accuracy is a property of the hardware and describes one point measured from one station. Registration accuracy describes how well separate setups agree with one another after alignment. Network accuracy describes how well a point at one end of a unit relates to a point at the far end, and it is the only one that governs whether a fabricated spool arrives and fits.

USIBD's C120 specification separates these formally. Absolute Accuracy is defined there as a standard deviation related to a given reference frame such as a building or state coordinate system — a global figure over the whole object, and one that is independent of distance or the number of setups. Relative Accuracy is defined as a standard deviation related not to a superior datum but within an object's region or within one or more setups. The specification notes plainly that accuracy dilutes over distance through the concatenation of multiple setups.

That last clause is the whole subject in one sentence. A vendor can be truthful about a 2 mm scanner and still deliver a unit dataset where opposite ends disagree by far more, because concatenation is doing exactly what the standard says it does. The remedy is never a better scanner. It is control, and it must be specified in advance alongside the [deliverable rung you are buying](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-to-cad-as-built-deliverables).

sections.heading: What the manufacturer's figure covers, and the conditions printed beneath it
paragraphs: Scanner datasheets are honest documents that get read carelessly. Leica publishes 3D point accuracy for the RTC360 of 1.9 mm at 10 m, 2.9 mm at 20 m and 5.3 mm at 40 m, built from a range accuracy of 1.0 mm + 10 ppm and an angular accuracy of 18 arcseconds. Beneath the table sits the qualifier that matters most: all accuracy specifications are stated at a level of confidence of 68 percent according to JCGM100:2008, and the figures apply at 89 percent albedo.

FARO states 3D point accuracy of 2 mm at 10 m and 3.5 mm at 25 m for the Focus S, with a ranging error of ±1 mm defined as a systematic measurement error at around 10 m and 25 m, and instructs that for distances larger than 25 m a further 0.1 mm per metre of uncertainty is added. Its footnote states that all accuracy specifications are one sigma, after warm-up and within the operating temperature range. Trimble publishes 2.4 mm at 10 m, 3.5 mm at 20 m and 6.0 mm at 40 m for the X7, at one sigma, valid when the instrument is levelled within ±5 degrees.

Three consequences follow. Accuracy degrades with range in every case, because the angular term opens into an arc. Every figure is one sigma, so restating it at the 95 percent confidence that engineering specifications use doubles it. And every figure applies to a warm, level instrument shooting a bright surface square-on. The datasheet describes laboratory conditions honestly; a process unit supplies none of them.

sections.heading: The surface is part of the measuring system
paragraphs: A scanner and the thing it points at form one measurement system, and the target contributes error the instrument cannot correct. FARO publishes the effect openly: range noise at 10 m of 0.1 mm against a 90 percent reflectivity white target and 0.9 mm against a 2 percent black target for the Focus S Plus, rising to 1.6 mm at 25 m on black. Maximum range collapses in parallel, from 0.6–350 m at 90 percent reflectivity to 0.6–50 m at 2 percent, stated for a Lambertian scatterer.

Incidence angle compounds reflectivity. A beam striking a pipe wall at a grazing angle spreads its footprint into an ellipse across a curved surface, and the returned point is computed from the centroid of an energy distribution that is no longer symmetric. Every one of these effects is largest on exactly the geometry that matters: the sides of vessels, the far faces of large-bore lines, and any surface documented from a single distant station because closer access was denied.

Industrial surfaces are systematically hostile. Weathered aluminium jacketing is specular rather than diffuse. Coke-covered and soot-blackened steel sits at the low end of the reflectivity scale. Wet surfaces after washdown scatter unpredictably. Damp or dusty air attenuates the return. None of this appears in a scope of work that names only a scanner model, and all of it degrades the same geometry you later want for [mapping damage mechanisms across an asset](/digital-twins/rbi-visualisation-damage-mechanism-mapping).

sections.heading: How registration error is measured, and what a good report shows
paragraphs: Registration error is the disagreement between overlapping setups after alignment, and it is the term buyers most rarely ask to see. Leica's Cyclone REGISTER 360 defines Bundle Error as the overall indicator of the link quality forming the bundle, calculated as the average of cloud-to-cloud and target errors. Cloud-to-Cloud error is described as the average of all cloud-to-cloud errors encountered in the links, a reliable indicator directly reflecting the effectiveness of visual alignment. Target error is the average distance between pairs of connected targets in an individual setup.

Two supporting metrics carry as much information as the error figures themselves. Overlap is the average percentage of overlapping area in links, indicating how much two clouds share. Strength describes how well data is translated and represented across the X, Y and Z axes. A link with low error and low overlap is not a good link — it is a link with too little shared geometry for its error figure to mean anything. Trimble's Registration Assist reports project and station average error, overlap and consistency in the same spirit.

Demand the report as a deliverable and read three things. Whether every setup is connected by more than one link, since a single-link station has no redundancy and no way of revealing its own error. Whether overlap percentages support the reported errors. And whether the chain closes on control or simply runs from one end of the site to the other. Leica's own documentation pairs the numerical metrics with visual verification through slice tools, and that combination is the correct standard of proof.

sections.heading: How error accumulates when setups chain across a unit
paragraphs: Registration errors between successive setups are largely independent, which means they combine as the root sum of squares rather than adding directly. A chain of setups running from a unit's north boundary to its south accumulates disagreement steadily along its length, and the two ends are the worst-related pair of points in the entire dataset. Nothing about the instrument changes along that walk. The relationship between distant points does, and it degrades monotonically.

This is why a scan can pass every local check and fail the only one that matters. Measure a nozzle-to-nozzle distance inside one vessel and it agrees with the tape. Measure between a pipe rack support at one end of the unit and a foundation bolt at the other, and the disagreement is far larger than any datasheet suggests. USIBD anticipates this directly, noting that a relative standard deviation is used when higher demands arise for particular parts of a building, knowing that accuracy dilutes over distance through concatenation of multiple setups.

The practical consequence is that unit-scale tolerance must be specified as an absolute requirement against a defined reference frame, not as a relative one. It also means the question "what accuracy will I get" has two answers on the same project — a tight one within any single asset, and a looser one across the site — and both belong in the scope. Getting this right is what makes [thickness data trended against real geometry](/digital-twins/thickness-trending-on-asset-geometry) reliable years later.

sections.heading: Control networks and targets are what break the chain
paragraphs: A control network is a set of physical points whose coordinates are established independently of the scanning, usually by total station traverse or GNSS observation, then adjusted and reported with residuals. Scans register to those points rather than to each other. The chain of accumulation is broken because every setup relates to the same external frame, and the network's own accuracy becomes the ceiling for the whole dataset instead of the sum of every link before it.

This is the single highest-value decision in a unit-scale scope, and it is routinely omitted because on-board registration works so convincingly at small scale. Modern instruments have made local alignment nearly effortless — Leica's visual inertial system tracks scanner movement between setups in real time, and Trimble's X7 performs full automatic calibration of range and angular systems in 25 seconds without user interaction or targets. Neither provides an external datum. They make a well-formed chain, not an anchored one.

Targets remain worth their field time on large jobs for a second reason: they are checkable. A surveyed target gives an independent coordinate that the registered cloud can be tested against, producing evidence rather than a vendor assurance. Specify the control network, its observation method, its adjustment report and the target layout in the scope, with the same discipline applied to [writing a technical procedure that has to survive audit](/consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development).

sections.heading: One vessel versus a whole unit: two different tolerances
paragraphs: A single vessel scanned from a handful of surrounding setups sits close to instrument specification. Ranges are short, so the angular term stays small. Links are few and mutually redundant, so registration error stays low and is easily checked. Surfaces are approached square-on because the scanner can be positioned freely around the object. This is the regime where 2 to 3 mm is a realistic expectation, and where deviation analysis against a nominal cylinder produces trustworthy out-of-roundness results.

A full process unit is governed by entirely different physics. Ranges lengthen because access is restricted. Setups multiply because congestion demands them. Links chain because a straight line of sight rarely exists between distant areas. Surfaces are shot at whatever angle the walkway permits. The achievable tolerance across such a dataset is set by the control survey, and expecting the scanner specification to describe it is a category error.

Write both into the scope explicitly. A clause reading "LOA30 relative within any individual asset, LOA20 absolute across the unit, both at the 95 percent confidence level stated in USIBD C120" is precise, achievable and verifiable. A clause reading "scanning to 2 mm accuracy" is none of those things, and it will be interpreted by the vendor in the way most favourable to the vendor — reasonably, because it is the only reading the sentence supports.

sections.heading: Writing an accuracy clause that survives delivery
paragraphs: USIBD C120 supplies the vocabulary. Its Level of Accuracy bands, specified at the 95 percent confidence level, run from LOA10 with a lower range of 5 cm, through LOA20 spanning 5 cm to 15 mm, LOA30 spanning 15 mm to 5 mm, LOA40 spanning 5 mm to 1 mm, to LOA50 spanning 1 mm to zero. The framework derives from DIN 18710, which prescribes five accuracy levels in terms of standard deviation, and it notes that any LOA higher than the one specified is acceptable because it exceeds the requirement.

The specification's most useful contribution to a scope is its split between Measured Accuracy and Represented Accuracy. Measured Accuracy is the standard deviation achieved by the final measurements, however acquired, affected by the sensor, by how measurements are joined into a common coordinate system, and by the object itself in terms of incidence angle, reflectivity, colour and roughness. Represented Accuracy is the standard deviation achieved once that data is processed into another form such as linework or a model. Error is always introduced in that conversion, so specify both.

Add the verification method and the pass criteria before mobilisation, never after delivery. ASTM E3125-17 provides the formal instrument-level analogue: it establishes requirements and test procedures for evaluating derived-point to derived-point distance measurement performance throughout the work volume of medium-range 3D imaging systems, from 2 m to 150 m, by comparing measured distance errors against manufacturer-specified maximum permissible errors. That structure — a declared figure, a defined test, an agreed pass mark — is what an enforceable clause looks like.

sections.heading: Verifying the data on the day it arrives
paragraphs: Three checks catch nearly everything, and all three are cheap. First, independent check distances: survey a set of distances between identifiable features at opposite ends of the site with a total station, then extract the same distances from the delivered cloud and compare. This tests network accuracy directly, which no software report does, and it is the only check that reveals accumulated chain error.

Second, read the registration report against the geometry rather than accepting its headline number. Confirm every setup carries more than one link, that overlap percentages are consistent with the reported cloud-to-cloud errors, and that the strength metric is balanced across all three axes. A dataset with excellent error figures and single-link stations has no redundancy, and no redundancy means no evidence.

Third, check coverage before checking accuracy, because missing data cannot be repaired at any price once the crew demobilises. Walk the coverage map against the asset list, confirm which elevations were captured, and get the inaccessible areas listed in writing. Atlantis writes these clauses, runs the capture, and delivers the verification evidence alongside the data. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Send an asset list and a tolerance requirement through [contact](/contact) for a quote or a demonstration.

faq.q: Why does my scan not match the tape measure on site?
faq.a: Compare like with like first. A datasheet figure is one sigma, so roughly one measurement in three falls outside it, and a 95 percent comparison doubles the allowance. Then establish which accuracy you are testing: a short distance within one setup tests the instrument, while a long distance across the site tests registration and control, which are almost always the larger terms.

faq.q: Does a more expensive scanner give a more accurate unit survey?
faq.a: Not materially, at unit scale. Published 3D point accuracy across current professional instruments clusters within a couple of millimetres at 10 m — 1.9 mm for the RTC360, 2 mm for the Focus S, 2.4 mm for the X7. Across hundreds of metres and dozens of setups, registration and control dominate that difference entirely. Spend on the control network, not on the head.

faq.q: What confidence level should I write into a specification?
faq.a: Ninety-five percent, matching USIBD C120, which states its LOA bands at that level. Then convert any manufacturer figure before comparing, since scanner datasheets are published at one sigma. Leica states this explicitly, referencing 68 percent confidence per JCGM100:2008. Stating the confidence level in the clause removes the most common source of argument at handover.

faq.q: Can registration error be fixed after the crew leaves site?
faq.a: Partially. Re-processing improves alignment where sufficient overlap exists, and adding constraints from surveyed control corrects a chain that was observed but never anchored. What cannot be fixed is inadequate overlap or missing coverage, because no algorithm recovers geometry that was never measured. This is why coverage is verified before accuracy, and both before demobilisation.

faq.q: How does surface condition change what I should specify?
faq.a: Tighten the setup plan rather than the tolerance. Dark, sooty or specular surfaces cut both range and precision — FARO publishes range noise rising from 0.1 mm to 0.9 mm at 10 m between 90 percent and 2 percent reflectivity. Specify shorter maximum ranges and higher point density on identified problem surfaces, and require the vendor to state the ranges actually used.

faq.q: Who should own the accuracy specification on a plant project?
faq.a: Someone accountable for the downstream use, working with a specialist who understands the measurement chain. The pattern matches how competent inspection programmes are written: a defined requirement, a documented method, and independent verification. Atlantis writes scan accuracy scopes alongside its inspection and [Level III consulting work](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services), so the geometry and the inspection data hold to one standard.

title: Build Order for a Startup NDT Program: Practice Before Equipment
description: The sequence a new US inspection firm has to follow: written practice, procedures, personnel, records, then the client audit, and what buying equipment first costs.
h1: Standing Up an NDT Program From Nothing, in the Right Order
answer: Build in this order: written practice, then procedures, then personnel qualification, then records, then the audit. The practice governs which methods you certify, so writing it after buying a phased array unit forces a rewrite. Classroom training compresses into weeks; the 1,600 hours of NDT experience behind a UT Level II accrues in real time and cannot be bought.
expansion: Most new US inspection companies build in exactly the wrong order: buy a flaw detector, hire two technicians, sign the contract, then discover at the client's audit that nothing on file supports the levels printed on the technicians' cards. The written practice is the governing document. It fixes which methods you certify, at which levels, against SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, with what training hours, what examinations, what recertification interval and what vision requirements. Every other record in the programme is evidence of compliance with it. Written last, it has to be reverse-engineered around certifications already issued, and an auditor reads that in the dates. Written first, it takes two to four weeks with a Level III and tells you which equipment you actually need. Sequencing cannot fix experience: SNT-TC-1A puts 1,600 total NDT hours behind a UT Level II, and those accrue one hour per hour.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition with addendum), Table 6.3.1A and paragraphs 1.4, 5.x, 8.1.1, 12.0 and 13.0; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2020); ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120 (2023 edition); ASNT NDT Level III certification requirements, certification.asnt.org.

table.note: Hours are from SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A and are cumulative across Level I and Level II. Build times are programme build effort, not experience accrual; steps 1-4, 6 and 7 run in parallel with step 5, which runs in real time.

facets.q: Can a startup use its client's written practice instead of writing one?
facets.a: No. SNT-TC-1A makes the employer responsible for qualifying and certifying its own personnel, and a client's practice certifies the client's people against the client's scope. Borrowing it leaves you with certification records that reference a document you do not control and cannot revise. Clients ask for your practice by name at audit, and the version-control trail has to be yours.

facets.q: Do certifications my technicians hold from a previous employer transfer to my company?
facets.a: Employer-based certifications do not transfer. SNT-TC-1A treats certification as revoked when employment ends unless the individual holds a third-party credential such as an ASNT NDT Level III certificate or an ISO 9712 certificate. You may credit the documented training and experience hours from the previous employer toward qualification, then examine and certify the technician under your own written practice.

facets.q: How long before a startup can put a certified UT Level II on site?
facets.a: Classroom training and examinations compress into weeks. Experience does not. SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A puts a UT Level II at 80 hours of training, 840 hours in the method and 1,600 hours of total NDT experience, cumulative across Level I and Level II. A startup meets that by hiring people who already hold the hours, not by accruing them in its first quarter.

facets.q: Do I need to own equipment before writing procedures?
facets.a: You need to know the equipment class, not own the serial number. A UT procedure names the instrument type, transducer frequency and size range, couplant, calibration block and reference reflectors. Writing the practice and the procedure first tells you the calibration blocks and probe set the technique needs, which is a shorter and cheaper purchase list than the one a distributor assembles for you.

facets.q: Can a contracted Level III sign my technicians' certifications?
facets.a: A contracted Level III qualifies personnel, writes and approves procedures, sets and grades examinations and approves the written practice. The certification itself is issued by the employer. An outside agency states that the examinations were passed and the written practice criteria met; the employer's authorised signatory certifies. Keep both signatures on the certification record so the split is visible at audit.

facets.q: What is the first finding a client auditor writes against a startup?
facets.a: A certification signed before the written practice was approved, or signed to a revision that did not yet exist. It surfaces in thirty seconds because the auditor compares two dates on two documents. The second most common is an examination administered by the candidate's own supervisor, which SNT-TC-1A paragraph 8.1.1 rules out: no one is examined by themselves or by a subordinate.

sections.heading: The purchase order that arrives before the programme
paragraphs: The pattern is consistent. A founder wins a first contract, quotes UT and MT, and spends the mobilisation budget on a flaw detector, a yoke, a set of probes and a couple of calibration blocks. The written practice gets written six weeks later, by which point the scope of the programme has been decided by a distributor's quotation rather than by the contract. Firms end up certified in methods they never sell and uncertified in the one the client actually buys.

The written practice decides scope. It names the methods and levels the company certifies, the standard it works to, the training hours it requires, how examinations are built and graded, the recertification interval, vision requirements and the records it keeps. Equipment is downstream of that document, not upstream. A practice written first produces a purchase list keyed to the techniques you will actually run, including the calibration blocks and reference reflectors your procedures call out by name.

Reverse-engineering costs more than the delay it avoids. Certifications signed before an approved practice existed have to be reissued against the approved revision, examination records have to be rebuilt to match the question counts the practice specifies, and the dates on the reissued documents tell an auditor exactly what happened. Two to four weeks of [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) at the start removes a rework cycle that otherwise lands in the middle of your first job.

sections.heading: What compresses into weeks and what accrues one hour per hour
paragraphs: Four things move as fast as you are willing to work. The written practice takes two to four weeks with a Level III. Method procedures take two to six weeks each. Examination sets, vision screening, the certification file structure and the equipment calibration register take a fortnight together. A mock audit against your own practice takes a week. A disciplined startup has a defensible programme skeleton inside ninety days, and none of that work requires a single piece of equipment to be delivered.

Experience does not compress. SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A puts a UT Level II at 80 hours of classroom training, 840 hours of experience in ultrasonics and 1,600 hours of total NDT experience, cumulative across Level I and Level II. A PT Level II sits at 12 training hours, 210 hours in penetrant and 400 hours total. An MT Level II sits at 20, 280 and 530. Those hours accrue in real time under documented supervision, and no consultant creates them.

That leaves three honest routes to a certified crew on day one. Hire technicians who already hold the documented hours from a previous employer and re-examine them under your practice. Subcontract the method you cannot staff, and inspect the subcontractor's certifications the way your client will inspect yours. Or scope the first contract to the methods you can genuinely staff and add the rest as hours accrue. Startups that sign the certification and hope are the ones that lose the contract at audit.

sections.heading: Your Level III on day one, and what that person can and cannot sign
paragraphs: You cannot approve your own written practice into existence. SNT-TC-1A requires the practice to be reviewed and approved by the employer's NDT Level III, and it requires the Level III to approve in-house examination questions. Until a Level III is designated, the programme has no approval authority, which means no valid practice, no approved procedures and no gradeable examinations. This is why the Level III is the first appointment a startup makes, ahead of the first technician and well ahead of the first instrument.

The distinction that trips new owners is between qualification and certification. A contracted Level III qualifies personnel, writes and approves procedures, builds and grades examinations, and approves the practice. The employer certifies. An outside agency states that the examinations were passed and the criteria in your written practice met; your authorised signatory issues the certification. Recording both signatures keeps the split visible, and it is the arrangement an auditor expects to see written into the practice itself.

For a firm with one contract and no payroll headroom, an [interim NDT Level III](/consulting/interim-ndt-level-3) supplies the designation, the approvals and the examination oversight without a full-time salary line. The practice names the individual, the certification records carry the qualification signature, and the scope of the engagement is documented. That arrangement is standard in the first two years of a US inspection company and it is what most first-contract clients expect to see.

sections.heading: Procedures: how many, and driven by which code
paragraphs: The customer's code decides. ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120 requires personnel performing examinations to the Code to be qualified and certified in accordance with a written practice, and the 2023 edition moved the exceptions to SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 into T-120(e), deleting the former Mandatory Appendices III and IV. A shop working to Section VIII with Section V examinations, a pipeline contractor on API 1104 and a structural fabricator on AWS D1.1 each generate a different procedure set from the same written practice.

Write procedures only for the methods on the contract in front of you. A startup with a UT thickness and MT weld inspection scope needs two method procedures, not eight. Each one names the instrument class, transducer or yoke specification, calibration block, reference reflectors, surface condition, scanning coverage, acceptance criteria referenced to the customer code, and the reporting format. Anything you cannot demonstrate on site during the first job does not belong in the procedure at all.

Keep technique sheets separate from the procedure. The procedure is the approved, revision-controlled document your Level III signs; the technique sheet is the job-specific instance recording the actual block, the actual calibration and the actual scan plan. Separating them means a new job does not trigger a procedure revision cycle. That structure is the working core of [NDT technical procedure development](/consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development), and it is what keeps a growing document set manageable past the tenth contract.

sections.heading: Qualifying your first technicians without inheriting someone else's paperwork
paragraphs: Employer-based certification does not travel. When a technician leaves a previous employer, that employer's certification is treated as revoked unless the individual holds a third-party credential such as an ASNT NDT Level III certificate or an ISO 9712 certificate. The card in their wallet is history, not qualification. What does travel is the documented training and experience, which you credit toward qualification under your own practice after verifying it with the previous employer in writing.

Qualification then runs the normal route: training to the hours your practice sets, general, specific and practical examinations, and vision screening. SNT-TC-1A recommends near-vision acuity sufficient to read Jaeger Number 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, administered annually, with colour-contrast differentiation at initial certification and at five-year intervals. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 tightens the near-vision requirement to Jaeger Number 1 at not less than 12 inches. Set the standard once, in the practice, and screen everyone against it.

One examination rule catches almost every startup. SNT-TC-1A paragraph 8.1.1 states that in no case shall a certification examination be administered by oneself or by a subordinate. In a five-person company, the person who trained the candidate is the person who wants to grade them, and that is exactly the arrangement the clause blocks. Independent [NDT Level III exam oversight](/consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight) removes the conflict and produces an examination record an auditor accepts without argument.

sections.heading: The five files an auditor opens first
paragraphs: An auditor's first hour is predictable. They ask for the written practice and check its approval signature and revision date. They ask for the certification file of one named technician working on site that day. They ask for the procedure that technician is working to and confirm it is the approved revision. They ask for the examination records behind the certification. They ask for the calibration record of the instrument in that technician's hand.

Every one of those five has to reconcile with the others. The technician's certification must reference a practice revision that existed on the signing date. The examination record must show the question count and pass mark the practice specifies. The vision record must sit inside its interval. The calibration record must cover the serial number in use, not a similar instrument sitting in the van. Reconciliation failures, rather than missing documents, produce the majority of findings against young companies.

Build the register before the volume arrives. Fifty certification files, a calibration schedule and a recertification diary are trivial on a spreadsheet and unmanageable at three hundred. Set up certification records, expiry dates, vision dates and equipment calibration in one place from the first month, with a named custodian, so that growth does not quietly convert an orderly programme into four disconnected folders on a shared drive.

sections.heading: The first-client-audit trap
paragraphs: The trap is timing. Most first audits happen after award and after mobilisation, not before the contract is signed. Procurement qualifies you on price and on certifications claimed; quality audits you when your crew is already standing on their site. A finding at that point stops work on a job you are already staffing and already spending against, and the commercial cost of that pause dwarfs the cost of the programme you postponed.

The findings repeat. A certification predating the practice that governs it. An examination graded by the candidate's supervisor. A procedure with no Level III approval signature. A technician whose vision record expired. A calibration certificate for a different serial number. An OJT log with no hours recorded by method. None of these are technical failures, and every one of them reads to an auditor as a company that started work before it built a programme.

Run the audit against yourself first. A structured [NDT program audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) against your own practice, sampled the way a client samples, surfaces the reconciliation failures while they remain cheap to fix. Do it before mobilisation on the first contract, and again after twelve months, when the volume of records has grown past what one person keeps in their head and the drift starts without anyone noticing.

sections.heading: SNT-TC-1A or CP-189: decide before you certify anyone
paragraphs: The choice changes who can be your Level III. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer's Level III is permitted to be qualified by employer-administered examination. Under [ANSI/ASNT CP-189](/compliance/ansi-asnt-cp-189), the employer's certification of a Level III has to include an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in the applicable method. If your first contract or your target market invokes CP-189, an employer-qualified Level III does not satisfy it, and the programme gets rebuilt around someone holding the ASNT certificate.

The second difference is flexibility. SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice: the employer adapts it through the written practice, and paragraph 1.4 stops you deleting the basic provisions of training, experience, examination and recertification. CP-189 is a consensus standard whose minimum requirements cannot be reduced, and it prescribes the contents of the certification record. A startup expecting aerospace, nuclear or federal work assumes the tighter regime at the outset rather than discovering it at the first audit.

Switching later is expensive because it is retrospective. Moving a programme from SNT-TC-1A to CP-189 means re-examining personnel whose original examinations do not meet the standard, replacing a Level III who was employer-qualified, and rebuilding certification records to the prescribed content. Decide at the practice-writing stage, while nothing has been certified, and write to the stricter of the two when your sales pipeline touches both regulated and commercial work.

sections.heading: A realistic first ninety days
paragraphs: Weeks one and two: designate the Level III, decide between SNT-TC-1A and CP-189, list the methods and levels the first contract genuinely needs, and start the written practice. Do not order equipment. Do not print certification cards. The only deliverable in this window is a document stating what the programme is, and it is the document every other record in the company will be measured against for as long as the company exists.

Weeks three to six: approve the practice, write the two or three method procedures the contract requires, build the examination sets, and stand up the certification file structure, vision screening and calibration register. Equipment is ordered in this window, because the procedures now specify it by class, block and reflector. Technician qualification starts here: verify prior training and experience in writing, close the training gap, and schedule independent examinations.

Weeks seven to twelve: certify, then audit yourself. Issue certifications under the approved practice, populate the records register, run technique sheets on a trial job, and put the whole programme through a gap assessment sampled the way your client will sample it. Close the findings before mobilisation. To have this build order applied to your first contract rather than described, [tell us what that contract requires](/contact). Demo and quote on request.

faq.q: What does a brand-new inspection company need before its first job, at minimum?
faq.a: An approved written practice, a designated Level III, an approved procedure for every method on the contract, certified personnel whose training and experience are documented, vision records, a calibration register for every instrument in use, and a certification file per technician that reconciles with all of the above. That set answers the first hour of any client audit.

faq.q: How much does the standard itself cost a startup?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A is published by ASNT and purchased from the ASNT store; CP-189 likewise. Buy the current edition, which is SNT-TC-1A 2024 with addendum, rather than working from a PDF of the 2011 or 2016 revision circulating online. Auditors check the edition your practice invokes against the edition the customer's code requires.

faq.q: Can the owner of the company also be the Level III?
faq.a: Yes, when the owner holds the qualification the practice requires. The constraint is examination independence: SNT-TC-1A paragraph 8.1.1 blocks anyone from being examined by themselves or by a subordinate, so an owner-Level III cannot grade their own recertification, and cannot have a direct report grade it either. Bring in an outside Level III for that specific step.

faq.q: Which methods should a startup certify first?
faq.a: The ones on the signed contract, plus the one method your client most frequently adds mid-job. PT and MT carry the lowest experience burden under Table 6.3.1A. UT, RT and ET each demand 1,600 hours of total NDT experience at Level II, which makes them hiring decisions rather than training decisions in year one.

faq.q: Do I have to recertify technicians on a fixed cycle?
faq.a: Your written practice sets the interval and SNT-TC-1A recommends a maximum of five years. Put the dates in a diary on day one. Expired recertification and expired vision records are the two findings that appear in year three at companies that built a good programme and then stopped maintaining the calendar behind it.

title: NDT Level III Succession Planning: What Lapses the Day They Leave
description: What stops and what survives when a firm's only NDT Level III retires or resigns: certifications, designation transfer, records custody, and building bench depth.
h1: Planning for the Day Your Only Level III Is Gone
answer: Three things lapse the moment your sole Level III leaves: their employer certification, their authority to approve procedures and grade examinations, and the signature holding up your written practice. Technician certifications the employer already issued stay valid. The incoming Level III reviews and re-approves the practice and procedures. They do not re-certify your workforce from zero.
expansion: Every US inspection company with one Level III is running an undocumented single point of failure. Retirement is the common trigger, resignation the fast one, and death the one nobody has a folder for. The damage is not that certifications evaporate; employer certifications already issued survive, because the employer issued them. The damage is that approval authority stops. No new procedure is approved, no examination is graded, no new technician is qualified, no revision to the written practice is valid, and the practice itself now carries an approval signature belonging to someone no longer employed. Contract clauses requiring a named Level III start to bite within days. The fix is structural rather than heroic: a practice that names roles instead of a person, records held by the company rather than in a personal laptop, a documented designation transfer, and a standing relationship with a second Level III before the resignation letter arrives.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition with addendum), paragraphs 5.x, 8.1.1, 12.0 and 13.0; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2020); ASNT NDT Level III certification and recertification requirements, certification.asnt.org; O*NET/BLS occupational data for Non-Destructive Testing Specialists (17-3029.01), May 2025 wage data; 10 CFR 34.42 and Texas DSHS radioactive material licensing guidance.
